div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT. THE GOVERNMENT DEFEATED.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT. THE GOVERNMENT DEFEATED.

The Conservative Government in four local Parlie- silent suffered their first defeat on Tuesday evening when the division on the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton's Bill "to remove misconceptions as to the nature of the relations existing between Church and State "-took place. There was a good attendance and the debate was entered into with considerable keenness. Mr. R. DONE (C., Newport) contended that there was, no institution in this country which was so misrepre- sented as the Church of England at the present time. The time-honoured phrase" the Church of England as by law established" implied to a great many people that the State at some time or other singled out the Church of England from a lot of denominations for special privileges. That was not the case, because the Church was in existence before the State. A great question which excited animosity was that of the Bishops sitting in the House of Lords. There were no Bishops in the House of Lords as bishops; they were called there as barons. It was not a special ecclesiastical privilege to have a seat in the House of Lords, because all the bishops (lid not sit in that assembly. The words" by law established "as used of the Church of England were words of limitation. They applied to the time commonly called the Refor- mation when the Ecclesiastical Courts ceased to have power in their own affairs and were subjected to the secular Courts. He contended that Noncenformist bodies were also "established "in the sense that they had to go to secular Courts to decide whether a minister was fulfilling the trust deeds or not. The Church owed her temporalities to an Act of Parliament ; the Non- conformists held their properties by various trust deeds. That was the difference. Mr. T. BARNES Evesham), protested against the introduction of such questions before the House where there were so many different religious opinions. The question was one for Churchmen alone. It was a waste of time to bring in a Bill to remove misconceptions when the introducer of the BILL created misconceptions by the speech he made last week. Dealing with the question of tithes, Mr. Barnes protested against Non- conformists having to pay to a Church they did not believe in. He contended that tithes were originally voluntary but Parliament, under the tutillage of the Church, had made them compulsory. Many imposts which had been put on the country in the past were most unjust and iniquitous. The member for Newport had said all people an -the country were on a level. No thanks were due to the Church party for that. It had been forced from them by the Noncon- formists and Roman Catholics. Catholic emancipation was granted, as the Duke of Wellington said, from fear of revolution. He would also point out that all religions were not on an equality in this land. As everyone knew, no Roman Catholic could become Lord Chancellor of the country to-day. (Hear, hear, from the Nationalist benches). The PRIME MINISTER (Mr. W. H. Stansfield), wished to make it, perfectly clear that this was not going to be a party measure. (Cries of "Oh, Oh,' and "Shame."). It had been brought in to remove mis- conceptions in all parties,and he was sorry to sap that amongst Conservatives there were misconceptions as to establishment and disestablishment. The Church bad never been established by law. If anyone maintained that it had been, let them give the date of the Act of Parliament which established it. The Church of Eng- land Liturgy had however the sanction of the law. At the time of the Reformation there was one Church in this land. Their forefathers objected to certain abuses which had crept in, and the Church reformed itself. That course received the sanction of the clergy and of the great majority of the people,. and later cn the liturgy was revised to exclude everything that was objectionable. That received the sanction of Parliament but it did not establish the Church. Since the Toleration Act was passed all religious bodies had been established and sanctioned and upheld by the law of this country. All places of religious worship were exempt from rates and taxes and were so far established; previously it was not so The word established did not mean set up or founded by the State. The Church was a Divine institution founded by Jesus Christ and the Apostles. Dealing with the question of indifference to public worship the speaker said the prevailing idea was that as long as men were honest, clean and true in their private lives they need not go to church or chapel; they did not consider they were called upon to make any public corporate pro- • feesion at all, and if they setup by disestablishment the idea that the State repudiated as a State all public connection with religion—and many people seemed to think an Act of Parliament must be right—they lowered the ideals of the people. The Church of England as a Church had not a single endowment—in fact the Church of England as a legal corporation did not exist at all. The endowments had been left to the separate parishes. Similarly, there were endowments belonging to the church in Cairo-street, but they were not administered by the whole of the Unitarian Church, but by the local trustees. So it was with the various endowments of the Church of England. (Applause). Mr. H. RIGBY (N.' Scotland Division of Liverpool) said the attitude of his party would he one of detach- ment and neutrality. If the conditions under which many endowments were given were fulfilled to the letter, Masses would have to be offered for the respose of the souls of the donors. That condition applied to Boteler Grammar School. The Right Hon. gentleman sought to strengthen and justify his position by appeals to certain Acts of Parliament and certain commissions. Those acts of Parliament were, however, forced through a servile Parliament by a tyrranical monarch, to cover illegal and confiscatory acts already committed by him. He said distinctly that these commissions were frauds and that every record of them which came to light went to prove that-He warned the hon.member forßurton- on-Trent and his friends against repeating such processes. He would remind them that two blacks could not make a white. (Applause.) Mr. A. PERRIS (L.. Central Bradford) said that in introducing the Bill, the Rev. E: C. E. Carleton said he had actually known speeches to be made expressing a desire to disestablish the Church for the good of the Church. He confessed that he (Mr. Perris) was one of thosa individuals himself. He believed from his heart and sonl that disestablishment of the Church in England and Wales would be for the benefit of that church, he believed also that the church people would find out that if the dead hand were taken off the Church then real life would enter the Church, and it would do a great deal more good for the country than it had done for many hundreds of years. They all knew that when the Church was entirely dependent upon endowments the people got into the habit of trusting to those endow- ments and became really pauperised, so that they did not feel the need of the support which every member should render. He believed that it would be to the interest of true religion ..to have disestablishment. (Applause.) Mr. HAWTHORNE (C., E. Belfait), speaking as a Presbyterian, said he believed in a Stete Church because he did not believe in 'an irrere''ious State. He would like to see the Presbyterian Church established in England. (Laughter). The Presbyterian Church and other Nonconformist churches, like the Anglican churches, largely depended upon endowments. The Rev. C. IiARVEY COOK (L., Ashford), said the emphasis of the points he had heard that night revealed to him a very strange mental condition. It had been said that they always used the phrase "Church and State." They admitted that, but they were going to learn a new thing—State first, Church second. ("Hear hear," and "No, no,") That WAS the meaning of democracy and the movement of the times. In the future it was to be the State first and what he had to find fault with the Anglican and Roman Catholic for was that with them the Church was put first and the State second. He believed a man wasa man first before he belonged to a religious society. He belonged to his country first as a citizen of that land. (A voice: "Who made him ?") They would not, continued the reverend gentleman, go into that question, because if he asked the honourable member who made the remark to answer the question himself he would have a diMculty in doing so. (Laughter). An honourable member had stated that the Church was founded by Jesus Christ 2,000 years ago—another extra- ordinary statement? The Church of the livieg God had been ever since men had looked up,wherever they were. What they had now was an organization. They had a spiritual Church, the spiritual man and woman, long long before they had any structure. The Church was a spiritual society, and it was based on great human necessities; it found its voice in great human needs. It was not true that there would not be religion if they had no churches. He did not know but what the time was coming when the dream of the Apocalypse would be true, "I saw no temple therein." He wished to God he could live to see the time when the people would be all righteous and when there would be no need for the parson. (Laughter). If their friends of the Established Church had such tender sensibilities about the word "Establishment," he was not concerned whether they used it or not. To imagine that they were not going to have a religious state if they had not an Established Church was to muddle things up. There never was a time when men were more religious than to-day and , there never was a time when they went to church less. Why ?—because the clergy had lived too remote from the world of actualities. They had spoken to men as if they were children who had to be taught. They, and he spoke for himself, had treated them as if they were infants and the clergy were a sort of a foster father. (Laughter.) Until the Nonconformist as well as the Anglican knew how to win men, no mere change of name was going to work the secret. He admitted that technically the Church of England never had been established by law, but the custom had grown up to think of it as established and the Anglican thought of it as such. Referring to endowments, the speaker said that at the annual speech day in connection with the Boteler Grammar School the Rector spoke ,on the text

One of the choicest features of the opera is the lovely unaccompanied choral singing in "Hail Poetry. Naturally enough, the ladies revel in the " chatteTing" chorus which repeatedly breaks forth during the discourse of ,the lovers in the first act, and the . technical difficulties of this musical novelty are easily surmounted. We cannot speak too highly of the services of the admir- able amateur orchestra which, . while playing with taste and precision, has also the negative but never- theless important virtue of not obtruding itself during the vocal solos. 11 Mr. F. Crossley, whOse interest in the operatic enterprises is beyond all praise, is again to be congratulated upon the entirely satisfac- tory outcome of the tact and skill with which he directs the whole of the forces engaged. Testimony must be borne to the invaluable work of Mr. Foden Williams, who enhances his already high reputation in War- rington as a coach and stage manager. He has been absolutely untiring in his efforts to promote, the success of the performances and it Must be gratifying to him, as well as to his apt and willing pupils, that everything has passed off so smoothly. The whole of the arrangements have been in the hands of a small sub-committee of the Warrington Musical Society with Mr. Henry Bond as hon. secretary and treasurer.

div.p: McDOUGALL'S Patert SELF—RAISING FLOURpArsZ

'Look to the rock whence ye are hewn." He (the speaker) did not for one moment accuse the Rector of any misrepresentation but when he tried to show or let it be understood that the Boteler Grammar School was an Anglican institution, he was not true to history, for it was a fact that the school was established by a Roman Catholic. Mr. E. WYNNE JONES (Leader of the Opposition) said he did not think a more provocative measure had ever been introduced into the House. It was argued that the Church had never been established by law. If that were so, what on earth were they trying to disestablish it for? It was admitted that the liturgy of the Church had been established and if to establish the liturgy was not to establish the Church. what was it? In the Coronation Oath they had the phrase "established by law," and Professor. Freeman, to whose writings Church- men often appealed, admitted that the Church received special protection and a large measure of patronage from the State, while on the other hand it had to sub- mit to a large measure of State control. They had heard nothing in the debate about the great spiritual work to which the clergy were called but they had heard a great deal about the question of property. They admitted that the members of the Church of England had done splendidly in their own way, but, after all, he submitted that the bulk of the property Iwas not the property of the Church, but State property. The bishoprics themselves had been created by the Crown, and to support them large gifts had been made from the Crown' from time to time. The fact that the Bishops had, seats in the House of Lords was hound up with the Establishment of the Church and the Bishops bad by their votes in that House shown that they were there to support the Church. With his party it was no petty quarrel between Churchmen and Dissenters. It was a great national policy. They believed that a State Church system was wrong and they believed that if the practical application of religious equality could only be applied it would be really advantageous to Christian religion and to the social and political interests of the country at large. (Applause). The MINISTER or EDUCATION (Rev. E. CI E. Carle- ton), in reply, asked the Leader of the Opposition to cite a case where Parliament had drawa up a canon, rubric or table of lessons. . Those things were not done by Parliament, but by Convocation. ' Mr. E. WYNNE-JONES : Parliament can smash rubrics.

The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON : Parliament can do nothing of the kind. Continuing the rev, gentleman contended that Mr. Asquith's Bill fer the disestablish- ment of the Church in Wales was pure vandalism. As to the allegation that the Church had not the confidence of the Welsh people, he admitted it had not the confi- dence of the plundering. section. (Laughter.) It was not right to judge a Church by its popularity. They were not concerned with the Church of the people so much as with the Church of Christ, and persecution bad often been a better note of orthodoxy than popularity. Mr. Asquith's Bill was simply an instance of the policy of the Government to attack their political opponents for the benefit of their political friends. The amendment, that the Bill be read that day three months, was then put to the vote with the following result :
For Against
Majority The Nationalists refrained from voting. but all except one of the Independents voted for the amendment. The Bill was, therefore, rejected.

div.head: ELECTORAL REFORM BILL.
div.p: ELECTORAL REFORM BILL.

Next week the Attorney: General (Mr. F. G. Taylor), will introduce the following Bill for the amendment of the law relating to the Parliamentary Franchise:- 1. In addition to those who are at present legally entitled to vote, the following persons shall be entitled to the exercise of the Parliamentary Franchise, viz.: Every male adult who shall, (a). Be liable in the event of war to be called on for active service with the Army, Navy, or Territorial Forces. (b). Be a griduate of any British University. (c). Be separately assessed for the payment of Income Tax. 2. Notwithstanding any enactment to the contrary no person whose name appears in the Parliamentary List as one entitled to vote, shall be disqualified by reason only of the transference of his dwelling-place from one Parliamentary Division to another, but shall at the next revision of the list be transferred, if he possess other qualifications than time of occupancy, to the register of the Division into which he shall

have remOved. 3. During the hours of poll in any Parliamentary Division no intoxicating liquors shall be sold in any licensed house, club or other premises wherein the same shall be usually sold, within that Division and a radius of the mile therefrom excepting to bona- fide travellers as defined by the therefrom, Acts. 4. No person shall solicit the vote of any individual voter at a Parliamentary Election at any time after the issue of the writ, nor provide any means of con- veying any voter to poll, excepting in case of physical incapacity. 5. Any person guilty of a breach of section 4 shall be liable on summary conviction to a penalty of not less than £1 nor more than £5, in respect of each voter solicited or conveyed. 6. The addressing of any meeting of voters exceeding 20 in number, or the delivery of any printed matter to any voter shall not be a breach of Section 4. 7. Any Parliamentary voter who shall fail to vote at a contested election shall be struck off the Parlia- mentary register until after the next election, unless he shall satisfy a Commision to be held within three calendar months after the poll than his failure . . .

to vote was occasioned by absence of at least 10 miles from the Division during the entire hours of poll, or by sickness, accident, or %ork at a distance of at least 5 miles from the Division, or by any other cause which the Commissioner shall deem rem sonable. 8. The said Commissioner shall sit at least once in every Parliamentary Borough (or Division of a Borough returning a separate member) and within one mile from every polling station within every Parliamentary Division of a County. One sitting at least in every such place shall be after 7 p.m. Every voter who shall not appear by the marked copy of the Register used at the election to have voted shall be warned at least 7 days before-band of the dates and places at which the Commissioner will sit, and of the provision of section 7 hereof. 9. The Commissioners shall consist of a Barrister-at- law or Solicitor of at least 10 years standing, to be appointed by the Town Council of a Parliamentary Borough, or by the County Council of the County within which a Parliamentary County Division is situate, and the appointing body shall pay the costs of the Commission. 10. After a dissolution of Parliament elections of all Parliamentary Boroughs shall be held upon one fixed day, and the elections of all County Divisions shall also be held upon one fixed day. 11. Parliamentary Representation shall hereafter as between the four countries be readjusted immediately after every census in proportion to the then adult male population, such readjustment to come into effect upon the next dissolution and not in itself to

cause any election. 12. The representation of each country shall be sub- divided (after the aggregate of their numbers has been ascertained as named in section 11.) by bills to be introduced for that purpose. 13. No hereditary peerage shall henceforth be created to a greater degree than to carry a patent of nobility to such direct descendants only of the original recipient as shall be born in his lifetime and similarly all present patents of nobility shall cease in like degree. _ . - _ _ _
11. The-right to sit in the House of Lords shall be limited accordingly.

div.head: THE
div.p: THE
PIRATES OF PENZANCE.
MUSICAL SOCIETY'S OPERATIC PERFORMANCES.

Fresh lustre is added to the notable record of the Warrington Musical Society's operatic section by the performances of "The Pirates of Penzance" at the Parr Hall this week. The society has every reason to be proud of the succession of triumphs achieved since its first' incursion into the realm of light opera six years ago. Much has been accomplished in that time and it . has become a pleasant annual task to bestow well-deserved praise upon those who have shared in the enterprises with such conspicuous success. Quite an interesting variety Of operas— with one exception, the works of those wonderful collaborators,Gilbert and Sullivan—has been presented. Ea every case the production has been so adequate and pleasing as to gain the cordial appreciation of the music-loving public. In one respect the 0 pera Committee have been somewhat unfortunate this year, and that is in chancing upon a week when a surfeit of counter-attractions has made unusually strorg demands upon public patronage. Notwithstanding this initial drawback there has been no sign of discouragement, the audiences, while fairly large numerically, having acclaimed the efforts of the amateurs as enthusiastically as ever, each performance being characterised bY refreshing crispness and gaiety. From the musical and artistic standpoints, the present venture is fully in keeping with the fine traditions ot the society. It shows to a striking degree how rich are the resources at the promoters' command. The personnel of ;he opera company-has undergone considerable changea of late, but several of those who have gained distinction in previous years are happily still to the fore, and the way in which the new aspirants acquit themselves is indeed a pleasant revelation. With such an abundance of promising talent there should be no reason to fear for the future of the Warrington operas—that is if public support is commensurate with the arduous nature of the undertakings. "The Pirates of Penzance" while capturing the public fancy ton remarkable degree, is peculiarly suitable for production by amateur organizations. Abounding in excellent choral numbers,which well repay painstaking study, it does not impose too heavy demands upon the dancing and acting accomplishments of the performers while the general atmosphere is one of bright colour and gay abandon suggestive of fairy-land. The libretto is conceived in that whimsical vein of which Sir W. S. Gilbert is a past master, and it is wedded to delightful, sparkling music worthy to be . ranked with Sullivan's best operatic achievements. The rugged and romantic coast-line of Cornwall forms an ideal scenic setting and we are introduced to a band of marauding pirates, blood-thirsty and ferocious to look upon but in reality singularly tender-hearted, especially when appealed to by "orphans "—of whom, consequently, a surprisingly large number fall into their clutches. A contingent of police—valiant officers who sing lustily of their indomitable daring but tremble with alarm at the pirates' approach—also play a prominent part in the development of the story, and the merriment and animation are considerably enhanced by the fussy Major General Stanley and his s formidable though fascinating bevy of daughters—" blushing buds of ever blooming beauty" as an ardent admirer describes them. The spectacle of a pirate torn 'twist a sense of devotion to duty—i.e. to his questionable calling—as set forth in his indentures, and the laudable desire to enter respectable society would ba most touching were it not so ludicrous. The " plot " is typical of the Gilbertian inventiveness, and round it he has woven a wealth of diverting incident, flavoured with smart quips and cranks;- which appeal irresistibly to the audience's sense of 'humour. It is but voicing the generally-expressed opinion to say that all the performers enter into their respective parts with commendable whole-heartedness and enthusiasm, and there is in most cases an absence of the stiffness and self-consciousness which too often mar amateur efforts. The action of the opera is not allowed to lag for a moment, and everything goes as merrily as the proverbial marriage bell. The group- ing—always an important factor—is admirable in every detail, and there is nothing wanting in the wayof picturesque spectacular effect: The principals have been well chosen, and, generally speaking, do justice to the characters allotted to them. The dramatis personae is as follows :

Major General Stanley Mr. G. H. Smith. The Pirate King Mr. Fred Pleldhouse. Samuel (his lieutenant) 'Mr. Wallace Ray. Frederic (the pirate apprentice) Mr. J. H. Draper. Sergeant of Police Mabel Miss Emily Taylor. Edith {General Stanley's J Miss Dorothy Trusloce. Kate Daughters 1 Miss Annie Warren. Isabel Miss Lily Boyle. Ruth (a pirate maid-of-all-work)

Miss Emily Taylor is a charming Mabel, and not only acts with naturalness and grace but further delights the audience with her beautiful singing. She Makes artistic use of a sweet and flexible voice of good compass, and her interpretation of that captivating song "Poor wandering one " is one of the pleasantest features of the opera. Me. J. H. Draper might with advantage infuse more dash and fervour into his portrayal of the amorous Frederic, which is in other respects meritorious and full of promise or the future. His vocalisation of several interesting numbers, notably the song "Oh, is there not one maiden here" is tasteful-and sympathetic. Mr. Draper is associated with Miss Taylor in that exquisite and pathetic madrigal "Oh, leave me not," which is undoubtedly the gem of the opera and has nightly received an enthusiastic encore. On Monday evening a sharpening of intonation on Mr. Draper's part slightly detracted from the otherwise perfect effect of this beautiful item, but this was excusable in view of the excitement of a debut, and no flaw was detected in the encore rendering. Miss Jennie Armstrong achieves a signal success as Ruth, the dramatic possibilities of the part being finely realised. Possessed of a full, rich contralto voice she sings most expressively and every word is distinctly heard. The duet in which Ruth vainly assails the heart of Frederic gives Miss Armstrong her great opportunity and she makes the most of it, her appeal being marked by much intensity of feeling. In nice con- trast, she imparts a touch of piquancy to the song narrative of the blunder which led to Frederic being apprenticed to a pirate instead of to a pilot, and the pleasure of the audience has found unmistakable manifestation each evening in a warm recall. Mr. G. H. Smith, who leapt into fame in last year's opera, again has a role which suits him splendidly and he possesses the happy knack of invest* it with the maximum of hilarity. Arranged in gorgeous uniform, bedizened with gold braid and medals, he cuts quite an impressive • figure. Whether in rattling off a characteristic patter song, enlisting the pity of the pirates with a tearful recital of the woes of an orphan boy, bestowing his blessing upon the" force " in their hazardous expedition, or in keeping the fair "props of his old age" within bounds, he is equally entertaining and brings to bear a cheery confidence which soon places him on good terms with the audience. Mr. Fred Fieldhouse adds another to his list of operatic successes by a spirited and realiStic impersonation of the Pirate King. Ie appears to be thoroughly at home on the stage and puts a great deal of" go ' into his acting. His principal song "I 'am a pirate King" is given with rare spirit and goes with a grand swing, invariably resulting in an encore. At first sight it is difficult to recognize Mr. J. W. Bibby as the stolid, rotund sergeant of police, so complete is the disguise of the "make-up." This is certainly one of his best character studies, although he has compaiatively little to do, and the quiet humour of the part is ' irresistible. At first he is a model of constabulary dignity but it is amusing to see how he gradually becomes quite affable under the "well-meant intentions of the ladies. Mr. Bibby is heard to distinct advan- tage in the quaint and well-known song "When a felon's not engaged in his employment." The Misses Dorothy Tiuslove, Annie Warren, and Lily Boyle, as Edith, Kate and Isabel respectively, are a dainty and vivacious trio, merry leaders of the irrepressible band of maidens who cast their spell over the pirate gang. Mr. Wallace Ray is a bluff, sturdy Samuel, the inde- fatigable lieutenant of the Pirate King._ The chorus work is especially praiseworthy, the effect of the fine, well-balanced body of voices, heard in such excellent concerted numbers as the rousing finale of the first act being brilliant and inspiring.

div.head: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE MEETING.
div.p: WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE MEETING.
The Compulsory Feeding Question.

There was a large attendance at a meeting promoted by the Warrington Women's Suffrage Society on Monday evening in the Cairo-street School. Alderman Bennett presided and the meeting was also addressed by Mrs. Beckham and Miss Abadam. The ladies were, excellent speakers and the audience was quite favour- able to the principles they advocated. The CHAIRMAN said he was in sympathy with the main objects of that meeting. There were many methods in connection with the advocacy of Women s Suffrage with which • he entirely disagreed. If his friends really wanted the vote they must be prepared to accept the obligation which it entailed. If they interrupted meetings they must be silenced or else put out. If they broke windows they must be punished just the same as male offenders, and anything which savoured of lawlessness must be suppressed with a strong hand. And if they made martyrs of themselves, they must be prepared to suffer. He thought it was childish and not.to be tolerated that they should refuse food; he was not in sympathy with the hunger strikers. It seemed to him that by adopting these tactics they were doing the cause irreparable harm. However much they might disapprove of those tactics, that did not in the least affect the substantial justice of the claims the women made. The cause was as sane and justifiable as any he had been fighting for. He was a believer in adult suffrage. For good or evil they had adopted the policy of democracy and i.e thought the Only solution of the sex problem was adult suffrage— ho was not particular at what age. (Applause.) Every citizen had a right to the government of his own country. If the ladies we equal to themselves, surely by no logical process could they be denied the right of government in the Empire. They Ind admitted the ladies to Boards of Goardians and the County Councils, and why not extend the vote to Parliamentary elections? (Applause.) If they followed that line of argument, some men would say that they would have the ladies in the House of Commons itself. His answer to that was "Why not." (Applause.) Mrs. RACKIIAM said there wits a tremendous wave of progress in their movement end every day the country was becominf-tiper and readier for this great reform. She emphasized the work done at the recent by- elections, and stated that although it was not quite so apparent as that done by tke militants it was never- theless a useful and a wondbrful work. At the last twelve or fourteen by-elections they had been busy collecting the signatures of voters to a petition in favour of women's suffrage, and during the pest twelve mouths they had secured less than 21,000 signatures. (Applause). When the Gbneral Election came they would be busy all over the country collecting the signatures from those in favour of this great reform. Men could not say women did not want the vote; and it was foolish of men to argue that women should not have the vote because there were so many of them. It was urged by some women that they did not want the vote, as they would trust the men to govern for them. She felt, on the contrary, that women's interests could not be represented unless they had the power of the vote. (Applause). When a Bill affecting men voters was introduced before Parliament, bow it seemed to be driven through the House by some unseen force, but when a woman's Bill was brought in, look at the differ- ence ! Was not that strange in a democratic country like theirs? But she thought the great reform could not be long delayed. They had women on their Town Councils, a woman mayor, and women doing such splendid work on the Royal Commissions, especially their poor law, that was it likely they should be denied this most elementary stage of all? They did not ask for the vote because they could do everything better than men. (Laughter). It was because, besides being women, they were human beings, that they desired it. They believed, too, that men could work for the public good better with the aid of women. (Hear, hear). She moved the resolution: "That the time is now ripe for the granting of votes to women on the same terms as they are, or shall be granted to men." (Applause.) Miss ABADAM in seconding the resolution, said that it was not the-majority who asked for the vote, but the intelligent majority. They had emerged from the past, well let them emerge from the present to something better in the future. She did not think women could use their votes much worse than men. (Laughter). Some men thought that a woman was meant to drudge all day. There was a time, before John Burns had achieved fame, when he was addressing a crowd of men in London, and he said "Boys, agitate for an eight hours day, and after you have got it, agitate for an eight hours day fcr your wife" But .Thhn Burns did not say that now. (Laughter). She had ,met women with very superior appearance who said they would have nothing to do with the suffrage question because of the example set by the other women. But the women who were so loyal to their fellow women, though mistaken in their tactics, were gorgeously brave. Who of those present would fast for two days for an ideal? There was no cause left which did not begin with violence. Democracy itself began with the pulling down of guildhalls and riotous murders. Let them talk no more about the "physical force " nonsense. There were millions of women working for the amelioration of humanity. People said that tl-e dap of chivalry were dead. No, I but. the cause was awaking chiveri. 1114 tvOte t,ldl it was not ladylike. But while they were comfortably drinking their coffee at the breakfast table there might be a girl of equal refinement to themselves, refusing food in gaol, suffering because she bad seen a vision. In conclusion the speaker referred to the noble sacrifice made by the three vvriters on the " Daily News " staff who had voluntarily relinquished their posts as a protest against the Government's treatment, of the suffragettes. , -

On the pmposition of Mr. CHARLES PLINSTON seconded by Mrs. STANSFIELD a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman and the speakers, and this resolution was carried by a largo majority, there being only two dissentients.

div.head: WOMEN'S CIRCLE.
div.p: THE WOMEN'S CIRCLE.
Visit From Mr. Cameron, M.P.

A young people's evening in connection with the Warrington Women's Circle was held on Monday inithe new room, Bridge-street. Mr. Dodds presided, and was supported by Mrs. Dodds, Mr. R. Cameron,l M.P. and Mrs. Cameren, Miss Dodds and Mrs. W. J. Walker. There was a large attendance. Mr. DODDS congratulated them upon the circle room. He had no idea that there was such a comfortable room in Warrington and so suitable for their purpose. It mas surprising to see the number of people about Mrs. Letheren and it was surprising to realise the good work that was being done. There was work to be done by women and they were just now determined to help the men in their work—legislative and otherwise. As the women wanted to come and help the men, he for one should be glad to have their help in connection with the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League of which be was the president. The speaker then referred to a speech by Colonel Hall Walker, M.P. for Widnes, in the House of Commons dealing with a duty which was being -put upon the public-house trade. He was reported in the "Manchester Guardian" as having said , that "very little consideration had been shown to the workingmen. The workingraan required two public- houses—one where be worked and one where he lived." Continuing, the Chairman said that as an employer of labour—and he did not say that in a boasting spirit, because he was connected with firms which employed about 20,000 men—the employers did not want public- houses about their works. It had been proved that alcohol was of little good to anybody; it was better for those who went without it and better for everybody else. He would ask the worn n %%hailer it was their desire or the desire of their husbands to have a drinking shop close to their homes as well as close to the works. They saw what the idea of" The Trale " was—as much trade as they could get. He was rather surprised the brewers did not want a half way house--(Laughter.) —as well as one at the home and the works. As a public man he could not let a remark of that kind go, without protesting against it, so that the people should know what the ideas of our Warrington brewers were in regard to the requirements of the workingman as to public houses. He thoueht that at this time of day when the highest authorities had said that alcohol was not necessary, but quite the contrary, they ought to protest against such a thing being said and resolve that there should be fewer public houses. They should support the temperance party which brought in the Licensing Bill last year and which was lost, for reasons which be need not go into. Concluding he hoped that the institution would grow and do for Warrington, as be believed it would, work which could not be done by any other institution in the town, and which would tell for the advantage of the people of :Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. CamEttoN, M.P.,said he would address himself to the ladies on that occasion. He was very pleased with the title "Warrington Women's Circle." He had lead the report and congratulated the leaders on having pro- vided a place where women could come out from the idle world of gossip and flirtation and continue their education, and make their mind and character clearer and stronger. (Applause.) It was a weakness in the education of many that when they left school they left it altogether. Their school age ought to reach to 16 rir 18 years, but if they had left school earlier it was a great gain to be able to con- tinua their education in such an institution as the "Circle." He would speak specially to the younger amongst them. He had seen a great deal of life (he would be 84 next month) and be ought to have learned some of the secrets of growth and success. And first he would say," Take care of your health." (Hear, hear.) Healthy and intelligent parents were the greatest boon they could have. But if they bad not these they must make the best of what health they had. Then "Take care with whom you fall in love." Was he intelligent, likely to get on. nervous, consumptive? They ought to ask such questions as these. In twenty years' time when they saw nothing but his faults they would be sorry they did not ask them sooner. (Applause). A woman's mind was not inferior to a man's. He had often envied a woman's gifts in art, music and literature; and it was possible for the majority of to enter into the realm of , knowledge if they would take the trouble. Let them master some of the great books that women had written and they would see how small some things were and bow much better and nobler life could be. (Applause). It • was the duty of every woman to know bow to use her needle and cook a meal. His own mother could spin the threads of which she made their garments, and her cooking was the most savoury he had ever tasted. Every woman onght also to he half a doctor in her knowledge of nursing and simple medicines. And she must keep the home orderly and clean. The man engaged in the dirtiest work most enjoyed a clew home, and of the home the woman was the inspiring spirit and in that sphere she realized the noblest possibilities. A mother's soul was the divinest thing God had made. Religim as an inner reality, and not as mere cant, was the grclitez;; life power, and parents could not exercise • their richest influence without it. ft was because John Wesley had such a mother that he changed the face of England, and , Thomas Carlyle, whose mother learnt to rend and , write for his sake, said that the greatest thing Provi- dence gave a man in this life was a mother. The true daughter, woman, mother, held the secret of a country's true grotr.ess, (Applause)._ An excellent piogihmme, provided by Mr. and Mrs. Dodds,. was gone through. Mrs. Cameron's songs were enthusiastically received, viz., "We'd better bide a wee" and a little minstrel song entitled" That's the reason why." Miss Plinston sang "Last night." Mrs. Dodds gave a reading "Over the hill to the poor house," and a recitation. A vote of thanks to the speakers was proposed by Mr. W. E. WYNNE-JONES, and seconded by Mr. W. GLEAVE and-carried.
Nest Tuesday eveninz Miss Truda Crostleld will give a talk on "Syria and Palestine."

div.head: HOW LIBERAL LEGISLATION ATTRACTS CAPITAL.
div.p: HOW LIBERAL LEGISLATION ATTRACTS CAPITAL.
An American Trade Invasion.

According to statements made by one in authority to an "Evening Chronicle" representative, the announce- ment that the United States Rubber Regenerating Company are establishing works at Trafford Park is only one of a series of interesting developments in the neighbourhood. Twelve months since there was an inclination to scoff at the enterprise shown—following on the pming of the Patents Acts—with the object of Inducing American and Continental patent holders to come to Trafford Park.

The practical suggestion was then rinde that. in order to rceet firms who, while inclined to manufacture in England were not in a position to establish works, American hive warehouses should be erected.

Notwithstsnding the terrors of the Budget as regards undeveloped land, this policy, it will be found, has been absolutely justified. Indeed the success of the idea is shown in thelfact that the whole of the first warehouse is occupied, and thst eight mapufactnring firms, for the first time in England, are housed under one roof and draw the motive power for the:r plant as well as their other common requirements from one common centre. The chairman of the Estates Co. is also in the happy position of intimating that the experiment has been repeated; that a second warehouse now in course of erection will be completed in six weeks, and that it has alresdy been leased off in sections. "Unquestionably," said the speaker, "the success of this novel venture is due to the Patent Act. Indirectly also the provision of the hive warehouses has sot many medium-sized engineering and other concerns inquiring for ground on which to establish themselves at Trafford Park, and to-day, as almost weekly for the past twelve months, representatives of several firms are prospecting the land still available."

He added that there are many inquiries coming from America, and that, with the substantial return of property on the other side, the nesotiations which had taken place were bound to materialise in the founding of several other great firms by the Canal side. "The only thing that retarded them,' he observed," has been the position of the American money market. Firms with money invested in America would not realise at a loss, but we know that as soon as they can clear they are in a position to deal with us and take up a portion of our land."

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" Miss Hook of Holland,"

One of the most popular musical eomedies ever produced is certainly "Miss Hook of Holland," laic!' has paid its first visit to Warrington this week. 'l6 a result notwithstanding the many other attractions the town, the Royal Court Theatre has been crowd°, every night with audiences which have gone away fal,t of praise and satisfaction. " Miss Hook of Holland is merry from start to finish, and very much of the humour is high-class. The music may not be of thet type which is likely to make a lasting impression, 1; it s tuueful and catchy—about all that is nes"e i for the modern musical comedy. The motif of the piece is only slender—and this too does not matte': much. Mr. Hook, of Holland, is a wealthy distiller the famous liqueur "cream of the sky," on the reee for which his fortunes have been founded. The reoiP° gets lost, and the finding of it is woven into the lor affairs of Miss Hook and her admirers. Halfil action takes place in the cheese market at Arc"ttee. on the borders of the Zuyder Zee, and remainder in the distillery at Amsterdam. T,ilt interior of a distillery hardly seems, at first thougiL; to he the ideal spot for musical comedy, but this iS le distillery unlike all others. The male and feraa employes seem to be equal in number and in privilegei; Thep do more love making than distilling and genial Mr. Hook seems to have no very strong "J'-oi tion, so long as he can sample a sufficient quantityi ie the famous liqueur. There is a big caste for comedy, and Mr. George Dance's CompanY maintains that gentleman's reputation. Mr. Shale is an old favourite on the stage, but we ug whether he has ever done anything better than hll, present role of Mr. Hook. He is inexpressivelY drohe °.;11- and laughter is never silent when Mr. Hook takes , floor. Miss Gertrude Melville makes a charmini Miss Hook of Holland. She is pretty, vivacious, sings sweetly in the lighter numbers which fall to her lot. One of the best things in the whole comedY the part of Simon Slinks, a loafer who has spent,k. lifetime in leaning upr-igainst the canal at ArnuLa Simon is a comical fellow with ideas on the 5a.,c11, cause of labour It is too sacred for him to incl.. in ; but he rubs along pleasantly all the same. lCharles E. Paton's conception of the part is won, fully good. His voice and mannerisms freque.ly, bring down the house. As a foil to Simon .Slicho there is Van Eck" A very ordinary Dutchman, Ivo slouches through life without saying a word, a a wearing little but a vacant smile and sf very old suit. Mr. R. Arunel has no ~e4ah'`, task as Van Eck, and his representation 01 ' part is excellent. Another great fund of lunnoilr found in Mina, the maid to the Hooks. Miss Cisthe Sephton bids fair to make a name for herself in role. She is a second Fanny Fields for dro,leitii;e, queer dancing and comic singing. Her song 'es. Flying Dutchman" receives the heartiest of eno‘m.fer Mr. Chas. Cautley has the hero's part—Bandraast,e. Van Vovt - and he sings and acts in excellent stZ;r. Captain Paep is most martially pourtrayed Wood Mansey, whose baritone voice is frequen;ei, heard to advantage, and Schnapps finds ready ref' sentation in Mr. George Mudie, jun. The comedy is very well mounted and staged, e.c.l, an enlarged orchestra under the direction of AL' Samuel Richardson does full justice to the music'

The kick-oil time from and including to-day, to November 15th is 3 o'clock.

The County Cup ties seem to grow in interest from year to year, and the Competition commencing to-day la being eagerly looked forward to both in Lancashire and Yorkshire. The first-round draw is as follows :
LANCASIMIE CUP,
Leigh v. Barrow. Widnes v. St. Helens. Rochdale Hornets v. Oldham. Wigan v. Warrington.
YORKSHIRE CUP. Brantley v. Halifax. Hunslet v. Bradford Northern. Huddersfield v. Hull Kingston Hovers York v. Hull. Leeds v. Wakefield Trinity.

The Lancashire clubs who have byes are Broughton Rangers, Salford, Swinton, and Runcorn, and they will be engaged in League contests, the fixtures being Ebbw Vale v. Batley. Broughton Rangers v. Swinton. Dewsbury v. Keighley. Merthyr v. Runcorn. Treherbert v. Salford.

Warrington are faced with the heaviest engage- tent of all the first-round ties for the Lancashire Cup, and curiously enough it was their fate last year 10 go to Wigan. After a very fine match Warrington lost 10-15, but they gave a display which did them redit and might easily have reversed the verdict. -PG-day, Wigan are weaker, and-Warrington somewhat stronger, so that there are distinct possibilities of a triumph for the Wirepullers at Central Park. lam fet saying that I expect Warrington to win—but I "Pe they will. After Leigh's performance on the time ground, the Wirepullers should not lack confid- etee in themselves or a backing from their supporters.

Both sides are likely to be at full strength with the exception of Barton, a Wigan forward who is under l'ilspension. Judging by the season's form, Warring- 'ton ought to have a pull at threequarter and half back, where Wigan seem to have fallen away. Much will 4ePend on the result of the forward battle and here it seems to me that Warrington's fortunes lie. The rummagers will need to do some honest work in the Pack. or they will be outpointed for possession—and rPssession is nine points in the game, as well as the lv. Granted that the Warrington six fully hold their OW7II then the honours should go the visitors.

The teams have been selected as follows: Warrington—Tilley, full back; Fish, Dickenson, l'„raylor and Bradshaw, three-quarters; Brookes and „enking, half backs; O'Niell, O'Malley, Shugars, 'llamas, Boardman and Belton, furwards. 'Wigan—Sharrock, full back; Leytham, Jenkins, vrice and Miller, th:ee-quarters ; Ned Jones and (Thomas, half backs; Cheetham, Francis, Whittaker, Ramsdale and Parr, forwdrds.

the way O'Malley will not have the pleasantest recollections of Wigan, for it was at Central Park he earned the distinction of being the only Australian '3ent off the field during the Kangaroos' tour. From I have heard since, the Australian was not to blame 14,1 the matter, but the victim of savagery in the scrum. Ile Wigan forward who was banned on the same Occasion is not playing-to-day—which is just as well.
I3Y way of special training for the Cup-ties the Warrington team on Thursday walked to Northwich alld indulged in the famous brine baths.

• Warrington " A" will be notable for at last includ- N Frawley in the ranks of the threequarters. The ngaroo back has had a long spell of inactivity, and .1"11 be glad indeed to 'get a gallop after the ball day. The match is with Ince in the Combination, 4nd the visitors will meet a team which could win a Ira tell or two in the Senior League if put to it. Hence rice are doomed!

Warring ' Warrington .` 1" will consist of Mclntyre, full ta il ek' • Smith, Frawley, Cartwright, and Jordan, eequarters ; Daintith and Kay, half-backs Harmer, 'llesters, P. Boardman, Gibbs,Worrall and Bradshaw, 40rwards.

lt is not often a visiting team gets a pleasant sur- i it)tise, but that is what Warrington found n store for ,heni at Swinton. The fact that both teams had only V,st one match during the season seemed to ensure 'arrington a very hard struggle, which is their Ilsaal experience in the den of the Lions. To their `llrprise the visitors found that most of the Lions were s?_bs and much more easily tamed than anyone could 'etave expected. They showed their claws during the 7st few minutes, but Warrington soon put the wire ~eand them and had them comfortably carolled before 'us allotted time had expired. Unless they alter, the Ice-famous Lions will have to be re-named the Lambs: A' is a long time since they were really formidable. 11' a matter of fact they have never looked up since '4B Valentines retired from the fray.

nt Warrington's perforbiance was, nevertheless, full ta merit and I question whether any other team will lie 15 points to nil out of the Swinton men on their own ground. The Wirepullers played a dashing and soon had the measure of the opposition. Ve forwards controlled matters in the scrum—where -wihton badly lacked weight—and the backs quite (aktelassed their opponents. Jenkins and Brooks played I_ll improved game, though the passing is not quite up the best standard get. There were signs, too, that centres are coming into form. Taylor has not Vt his speed back and at present runs too far with we ball before passing. Both Fish and Bradshaw onere, great on the attack and as usual each got a very '")ct try.

I think a considerable amount of credit for the success is due to Tilley, The Widnes man IP the finest display I have seen him give since t,a/Tington beat Oldham in the N.U. cup final. He allilot be looked upon as a " back number "yet % to"niie though there may be doubts as to his ability th go through a hard season. On Saturday he kicked than any man on the field, and his catching general headwork were splendid. His reliability ;...a happy effect on the team, and the men in front :1141 played something like their natural game. The Tilliters in the Manchester papers who belittled 1:11. Y'F3 performance must have been blind or

Swinton's greatest deficiencies ,were lack of weight and speed. The men are too small, and though they have plenty of dash, they are not likely to make much impression on any of the crack teams. There is a noticeable want of class about the team and, honestly speaking, I did not see a single player who struck one as being much above "A " team standard. The directors of the young Lions will have the utmost difficulty in keeping their pets in the • top half of the table. They are getting better support, which is something at least to be thankful for.

Free Tride in footballers seems likely to be put a stop to as a result of Warrington's importation of Stuntz from South Australia by cablegram. The N.U. has been considering the question again, and there is every indication that Warrington's venture will be the last of its kind. There is a good deal to be said in favour of protection for the Colonial clubs, and little for the poaching of the Mother Country. Luckily for Warrington they snapped up their prize before prohibition was thought of. Now, I expect there will be a tariff put on by the Australian clubs, which will be upheld by the governing body on this side.

The " A " team made short work of their "friendly" opponents, Salford St. Bart's, and ran up the huge score of 47 points to nil. Smith and Cartwright were a very strong wing,the former getting four tries in brilliant style and the centre three. Mclntyre was not very brilliant at full back, but he kicked seven goals in succession. He ought to seriously study the perfec- tion of his game as a custodian.

div.head: Warrington's Fine Victory at Swinton.
div.p: Warrington's Fine Victory at Swinton.

Warrington had a fair following at Swinton on Satur- day and rejoiced their supporters by a substantial victory on the Lions ground. Both sides were well represented, and with the Swinton ground for once in a Way quite firm and dry the conditions favoured a fast game. The 5,000 people present bad no reason to com- plain on this score, for the game was lively from beginning to end. Mr. W. Taylor of Hunslet was the referee and the teams were.:

Swinton—G. Thomas, back; H. Davies Young, Parker and Wharton, three-quarter backs ;'Jones and Fairhurst, half backs ; Pollitt, D. Davies, Neen, Preston, Simister (captain), and Gartrell, forwards, Warrington—Tilley, back ; Fish, Dickenson (captain) Taylor, and Bradshaw, three-quarter backs; Brooks and Jenkins half backs ; Niel], Thomas, Boardman, Flamer, and Bolton, forwards. Swinton won the toss and bad the slope in their favour when Thomas started. The Blue forwards were immediately active and some fast following up gave Tilley a lot of work which be performed excellently. Gradually Warrington found their feet and drove Swinton back, Thomas kicking at goal from a penalty and only being a few feet under the bar. Swinton made another spasmodic rush which Tilley checked and then Warrington took command of the game. Tilley hit the post with drop at goal, and soon after Fish put in a long run on the left. O'Neill took up the passing in mid-field and threw out to Taylor who ran down touch and then centred cleverly. The home defence was caught napping and Jenkins scored easily under the bar, Thomas gcaling. Warrington were now quite overplaying the homesters and five minutes later from a cbner throw by Jenkins, Brooks and Dickenson made an opening for Fish. The left-winger left the Blues full- back standing and scored under the posts again,himself adding the goal. The locals made several loose rushes, but lack of speed prevented them getting far. Brooks had to kick dead once, and a hot melee followed near the Warrington line, but Jenkins and Taylor safely got the ball away. Just before the interval the home full back was tackled by Boardman and sustained a leg-sprain which prevented him taking any further part in the match. Half-time: Warrington 10 points, Swinton nil. Warrington appeared to ease up somewhat in the second half, and their play was nothing like so attractive. Brooks broke through a time or two but his passes went astray, and the home line had some marvellous escapes. A fine passing run followed a long pass by Thomas, but Taylor held a shade too long and was collared near the line. From a punt by the same player the home full back was beaten at centre and in the race for the ball Bradshaw easily beat his centre and scored a good try, which Thomas improved upon. Near the close Swinton had several chances to score but bungled them by bad passing and were finally beaten pointless. Warrington, 3 goals, 3 tries, 15 points; Swinton, nil. ST. HELENS v. TREHERBERT : THE VISITORS BADLY BEATEN.
Played at St. Helens, before 5,000 spectators. The "Saints" included their latest captures hi the forwards —Tom Crellin, of Maryport, and John Hodgson, of Irookland Rovers. - - -

Galloway started for the visitors before a strong breeze. St. Helens pressed esrly on, an.l from a passing movement between Bradley and Briers,the latter crossed, for C.Creevey to improve. After a spell of even thid-field play the home backs opened out, and Barton scored close in, Creevey convecting. Et. Helens were holding the upper hand at this stage, and " Butcher "

Prescott trapping up the leather, scored. The place kick failed. Flanagan scored after running half the length of the field, and Creevey crossed under tbe posts, Turtill improving one. Half-time score—St. Helens 3 goals 5 tries (21 points), Treherbert nil. Turning round, Prescott started, and the " Saints " had to defend, Turtill clearing from Duncan. St. Helens were penalised, and Duncan made a poor attempt to place a goal. St. Helens combined, and Flanagan scored a try, Turtill improving. Eveleigh crossed the St. Helens line twice, but the attempts at goal were poor. End-to-end play followed, and Barton went through the visitors' team and scored, Turtill improving. The visitors broke away several times, and from their rushes Francis and Cox scored. Edwards made miserable attempts to convert. Near the call of time Flanagan again forced his way over, Creevey adding the extra points. Result—St. Helens 6 goals 8 tries (36 points. Treherbert 4 tries (12 points).
WIDNES v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

Played at Widnes before 3,000 spectators. Widnes had the best of the open7ng exchanges, and a brilliant movement by Lally, Lambert, Reid, and McCarthy ended in the latter scoring at the corner. G. Aspey failed at the goal-kick. For a long time Widnes kept up a hot attack, and then Broughton broke away and Barr receiving a pass scored a good try. Harris failed at the goal. Half-time—Broughton 3 points, Widnes 3 points. .

The second half was all in favour of the Rangers, and it was very seldom that IVidnes got out of their own quarters. The Rangers' back, led by Hogg, showed splendid form, but Widnes put up a strong defence. In the last ten minutes Jones had his kick charged down, and Davies scored for Harris to kick a goal. Just before the whistle sounded Hogg dribbled under the posts and scored. Harris again improved. Result : Rangers 2 goals 3 tries (13 points), Widnes 1 try (3 points).

div.head: RUNCORN WELL BEATEN.
div.p: RUNCORN WELL BEATEN.

At Oldham on Saturday Runcorn lost their unbeaten record before 20,000 people. At the outset Runcorn attazked hotly, and throughout the match their for- wards had the advantage in the scrummages. and gave their half backs more opportunities of handling the ball than the Oldham pair got. On the other hand, the Runcorn half backs and three-quarters made little effective use of their opportunities, and were never really dangerous. The first score was made after about ten minutes' play, Deane .gaining a try for which Ferguson made the opening, and Wood placed the goal. Two points were added from a penalty kick, and before the interval Tyson-and Llewellyn each scored, Jardine improving the latter's try. Wood was injured just before half-time, and was ab•zent for nearly twenty minutes In spite of this handicap Oldham were greatly superior in finish, and in the second half tries were scored by Avery, Tyson, and G. W. Smith, and Jardine added the goal to the first of these. Runcorn made a big effort just before the finish, but could not penetrate the Oldham defence. Result:—Oldham 4 goals and 6 tries (26 points), Runcorn nil.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCII.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCII.

WARRINGTON "A" V. SALFORD ST. BARTHOLO- MEW'S.—Tbe Warringtonians had a remarkably easy task in disposing of Salford St. Bartholomew's at Wilderspool on Saturday. Soon after ihe kick-off Smith after a smart run scored at the corner. Cartwright next bluffed the opposition and crossed, and in quick succession Cartwright recorded two more tries, Mclntyre placing goals. Smith and Landor added tries and Mclntyre added the extra points. Half-time : Warrington, four goals six tries (26 points) ; Salford, nil. In the second half Warrington again demonstrated their superiority, and tries were notched by Smith. Landor, Mclntyre, Callendar and Smith in th• order named. Mclntyre placed three goals, the custodian thus having the fine record of placing seven goals in succession. Final: Warrington "A," seven goals eleven tries (47 points) ; Salford St. Bartholomew's, nil.

div.p: ST. lIELENS AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.

R VIANDS BROS. RECREATION V. PEARSON AND KNOWLES.—This match was played on Saturday on the ground of the latter club. Considerable interest was taken in this match and a keen game was anticipated but the spectators were greatly disappointed. Rylands' had the advantage of a strong wind during the first half of the game and taking the opportunity of this and some loose play on the part of P. & K. enabled them to register 3 tries during the first half. On resuming, Hannon for P. & K. opened out the game in splendid style but Tickle after a fine run was" grassed" at the corner. Undaunted they kept the" Wiremen " on the defensive the greater portion of this half, but were tot allowed to score. Ashton and Crawford were in turn held up on the line and nothing but bad luck prevented a score. Near the close the •' Wiremen " put on another try. This concluding the scoring. An unfortunate accident caused a gloom, when one of Rylands' forwards sustained a fracture of the leg. He was taken to the Infirmary and detained. The result of the game by no means represented the play and with the " Iron" team at full strength at the next meeting this decision may be reversed.

HOWLEY ATHLEWIC V. WARRINGTON ALBION RECS.

Played at Howley on Saturday ;before a capital attendance. The Albion team were short of C. Turner and H. Dutton, but Howley were at full strength, the team turning out as selected. A great deal of loterest was taken in the match because Councillor Howard who takes a keen interest in the Howley Club had promised to kick off. Howley won the toss and played against the wind. Councillor Howard started the game amidst great cheering. Soon, the visiting left wing forced a corner off Pendleton but the ball went dead. Howley began to sett!e down to their usual style and from a fine centre by Derbyshire, Cragg opened the sco7.:ng

for the homesters, with a shot from thirty yards dis- tance, which found the corner of the net. The visiting goalkeeper saved fine shots from Warren and Cragg. Howley were having all the play but the fine display of the Albions goalkeeper'would not allow them to add to theic score before half time: Howley 1, Warrington AO. In the second half it was soon seen that there was only going to be one team in it for Cragg again found the net with a Rood shot. Spooner was showing good form for the Albrons but met with little support from the others. Again the visiting goalkeeper had all his work cut out,in saving a shot from Cragg. Soon after, fine play -by Brown and Sankey resulted in Cragg getting his third goal. Howley had all the game, Cragg getting two more goals and Warren placing a penalty. Result Howley, 6; Warrington Albion 0.
WRRRINGTON ALBION v. PRESCOT ATHLETIC.

Warrington Albion encountered Prescot Athletic on Saturday, an the Liverpool-road ground, in a Liverpool District League match. There was a large attendance, the prominent visitors including the Mayor (Alderman W.J. Forshaw),Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall,Alderman Burton, Councillors Fulton-Smith, Ashcroft and Broad- hurst, Messrs. James Dodds and E. Draper. The following were the teams :—Albion : Wyatt, goal ; Sargent and Short, backs; Dilworth (captain, Dickenson and Whitefield, half-backs, Ritchie, Hunter, Thomas, Ball and Chester, forwards. Prescot Athletic: Whitehead, goal ; A.Leadbetter and Middlehurst,backs; Hunter, Robinson (captain), and •T. Leaclbetter' half- backs ; Crawley, Scotson, Dagnall,Prescott and Roscoe forwards.

Dilworth having won the toss, proposed to play to the Sankey goal. There was a spell of give and take play, enlivened by some smart combination onthe part of the Athletics, and it was not very long Lefore Crawley had a shot at goal but Wyatt cleared,punching the ball into midfield. Ritchie siezing an opportunity ran down and made a good attempt to open the Albions' score but was not successful, the ball just missing. Play vas of a very even nature and within a few minutes the custodians were called upon to defend their goals. Then for some time play got . into neutral territory neither goalkeeper being tested. Prescot attacked but Sargent kicked clear and a free kick to Warrington placed the Athletic on the defence. Ths Prescot forwards raced away bet Sargent was again a stumbling block. Ball tested Whitehead, who partially eleared and Thomas was unlucky in not opening the Albions' account. The home team were leaving decidedly the best of matters but Ball shot wide when in a good position. The Warrington forwards again got possesion but Hunter was rather slow to take advantage of tie opening and the visitors invaded Warrington's quarter. Not to be denied the locals again pressed and Ritchie sent in a beautiful centre which Cheaters turned to account. After this success the home team had the best of the argument and Ball sent in a Tom shot which 'Whitehead dealt with cleverly but was hurt in the clearance. He was able to resume after a little attention. Prescot now livened up and attacked but without success. Some nice com- bination between the Warrington forwards ended in Cheaters adding a second goal. J. Leadbetter opened Prescot's account from a close shot. Half-time score: Warrington Albions, 2 goals; Prescot Athletic, 1 goal. Resuming, play was in the visitor's quarters and Whitehead defended extremely well. During the excitement round the goal Leadbetter picked up the ball and attempted to clear but the referee noting this deviation from the rules awarded the Albion's a penalty which was turned to accound by Dilworth. Stung by their run of reverses the Athletics pressed very h ard, but were unable to get through. So the play con- tinued until within a minutes of full time when Cheaters, seizing an opening, ran to the goal and crashed the leather into the net with great force, his knee catching Whitehead on the thigh. The latter player was 'carried off the field. Final: Warrington Albion, 4 goals; Prescot Athletic, one goal. BOTELER. G. S. V. KING'S SCHOOL, CHESTER.—These teams met at Warrington on Saturday. At the end of the first half the Grammar School, who had had the best of the game, were leading 2-1. The result of the game was, however, a draw, 3-3. Ths most prominent players for the Grammar School were Murphy, at out- side left, and Browne at centre-half.

div.head: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
div.p: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
BY B. BENNISON.
ILLUSTRATED BY JACK DODWORTIL

If, as Mr. J. J. Bentley said at Oldham, the Players' Union refuse to break away from the Trades Federation, and insist upon "a strike clause" in their agreement, then the war be- tween the professionals and the Football Asso- ciation Will be tremendouely difficult to settle. The stipulation to strike in order to remedy real or imaginary grievances must hurt every sports- man; to refuse to play any game because things are not going smoothly smacks of childishness; it is a sort of "I -won't-play-in-your-yard" policy, and if it is pursued the Players will, in my judgment, regret what I venture to think is sheer folly. With the Players on many points-- the abolition of the maximum wage, the sweep- ing away of the transfer system especially—l 1/1 with them heart and soul; there is no logical reason why legislation should not be so framed that they will enjoy freedom- but the right to strike—never. Let us concede the right to seek to redress wrongs, many of which are ad- mitted, if you will, but let the game be saved from all the unpleasantness and sordidness attached to a strike.

What Will the Players Do? Of course, Mr. Bentley may be wrong in tell- ing the world that the strike clause will be in- sisted upon; but I have an idea that the speech made by the President of the League is based upon the best possible information. After what we have heard, it is imperative, to my thinking, that the Football Association and the Players

should meet at the earliest possible moment. We must not have an interminable wrangle. Peace must be secured if it is possible; if the Players and the Football Association cannot hit ?pop a common understanding that will not pre- judice the game as a game, as distinct from an out-and-out business, it is all the better that we should know. Whether the Football Association will be induced to consent to the Players' Union being affiliated with the Trades Federation I do not know. It is not likely that the Players will throw the Ttades Unions over; and, upon care- ful consideration, I do not think that it is abso- lutely necessary that they should do so, though one cannot but agree with the contention of the Football Association that the presence of a third party in a purely domestic quarrel is to he avoided. It is for the Players to declare their hand. We are told that they decided upon a plan of campaign at their conference at Birmingham. We are keenly desirous of knowing what that plan of campaign is. Aleanwhilo, one is restless because of the remarks of the President of the League.

Class Football at Brim. It is very pleasant to be able to record that while this war is being continued we have had evidence that Aston Villa and Everton can play the game in a way that is strictly in accord with the traditions of the two clubs. Their match at Birmingham went far to show that on occasion the high arts of the game have not been wholly forgotten. When one does soe really high-class football, not football that means merely a helter-skelter for points, one realises, what a great game Association football is. Perhaps it is too much to expect a general improvement in play, for the reason that clever
CLAI

footballers are spread over a larger number of clubs, and that with the retentiim of a fixed wage there is not the sa.rue inducement tc attain perfection as there used to be. Ido not for a moment with to suggcet that players arc content to remain at one dead level, but it is a fact—and I do not think it can be controverted-- that the idea of paying all men the same wage puts a premium on mediocrity. Ireland's Heavy Defeat.

Association football in Ireland does not make much headway, which is a fact that is difficult to understand, for if there ever were an enthu- siastic footballer it is the Irishman. Somehow he is slow to karn the game's lestons. The Irish League team, though they were very earinest and tremendously keen, were really no match for the English eleven at Oldham. In sixtccn years the best the Irish League players havç been able to do is to play a draw with England. That they will go on trying is a certainty; the Irish footballer is not discouraged by defeat.

There is not any great change in the position of the various League clubs, though it is resting to note that Sheffield United have found their way to the top of the First Divi- sion, and, what is more, have played two matches fewer than Newcastle United, who. I arn told, had just about as much As they could do to beat Bradford City. One cannot, help but re- mark upon the improvement shown by the Yorkshire team. It is all really wonderful; yet when one conies to study the personnel of the team thew need be no surprise at the most satisfactory position Which they occupy. The only cause for wonder is that they came near be- ing relegated last season.

New Centre for Manchester U::ited. Glossop, with their many amateurs, are close on the heels of West Bromwich. People at Glos- sop are beginning to think that the town will have a First League team again. It is well for
•OoT L 1 3iVlZ)c la-cce "

Glossop that they are supported by such a fine sportsman as Mr. C. H. Wood. He must have spent a small fortune in running the Glossop club. Blackburn Rovers are having quite a good time—so aro Liverpool; while Notts Forest are living up to the favourable impression they made at the beginning of the season. Woolwich Arsenal are very down in the clumps; Totten- ham and Chelsea are thankful .for small mercies. Manchester United are rather disappointing. I hear that they have completed arrangements for the transfer of Horner, the Kidderminster centre-forward, who is highly spoken of. New Brompton had a very big fight when they met Northampton. Last year's champions made it appear very strange that the Kent club arcs first in the comnctition. A defeat by seven goals to one after their :lathy p.2r:ormlnces must be very difficult for tho men of New Brompton to explain. Things aro looking up at lwall. div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.

A RECORD MAIN. There was a record entry of 528 for a main which has been held on the Bull's Head Green, for the benefit cf Mr. Robert Fairbrother, )\ who has been an invalid for many months. Mr. Fair. brother was for many years one of the most prominent of the Bull's head team, and assisted that organization to gain championship honours in the tourney promoted by the Lancashire and Cheshire Association. A I d a r man Evans thoughtfully pro- moted the main which proved a splendid success. Ihe competition was com- , maned early in September and the final was only reached on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the local veteran champion, George Ball, ben., who defeated P. Lawless by 13 points against seven. Mr. Ball is now in h:s 68th year, but he is wonderfully active and his victory after a keen fight was highly popular. Both bowlers had had an allowance of one start, and Lawless, taking advantage of the first throw of the jack, took a lead. Having secured the advantage Ball scored, by the aid of a series of good woods, a remarkable sequence of chalks, Lawless only recording another end, the final result being : Ball, 13; Lawlees,7. The winner has had a remarkable career as a trundler, and a quarter of a century ago he defeated Tom Hart, the acknowledged champion of England, on the green attached to the King and Queen, Padgate lane. During the past season he has assisted the Cemetery Hotel Club to secure the championship honours in the County Competition. He is held in the highest regard by all lovers of the ancient game of bowls in this district.
MR.
IALL.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT CRICKET LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT CRICKET LEAGUE.
Annual Meeting.

The annual meeting of the above- was held at the Crown ani Sceptre Hotel, Buttermarket-street on Tuesday evening, when Mr. J. F. Foster presided over a moderate attendance. The secretary read the balance sheet and commented on the work of the league, and the increased interest in cricket in Warrington since its formation. They had three applications for two vacancies, namely : Latchford Wesleyans, Stockton Heath Y.M.C., and Sankey. Latchford Baptists, had found it impossible to continue their membership and sent in their resignation with best wishes for the future. A vote of thanks was then passed to all the retiring officers and the following clubs were elected to make up the league for next season :—St. James', Rylands' Bros. Recreation, Cheshire Lines Engineers •Guardian Office, Walker's Brewery, Sankey Wire Mills,Whitecross Recreation, Latchford Wesleyans, and Stockton Heath Y.M.C.

_ The election of officers for season 1910, was as follows :—Chairman, Mr. J. F. Foster; viCe-chairman, Mr. J. Langley; hon. treasurer, Mr. R. .R. Lonsdale ; hon. secretary, Mr. J. Woodhead ; assistant secretary, Mr. W. Bennett; hon. auditor, Mr. A. 1. Newton, and a representative from each of the clubs to form a com- mattee.
