The execution of Senor A EUROPEAN FERROR raises some SCANDAL. doubt as to whether

Spain ought to be ranked among nations that are civilised. We can perceive no moral difference between such an event and simple murder. Even such a softening phrase as 'judicial murder" would not apply in this case, for Senor FERRER had no• proper trial. He was not taken "before a regular court. His judges were military officers. There was no evidence against him: He was prevented from making the best defence, which is the right of every man in every civilised country. He was treated from first to last as a destined victim. He might reasonably have entered the court saying to the military officers who had been appointed to condmt the mock trial, "Aye, CEesar ! I, who am about to die,

salute you." But even this brutal and insensate method of conducting a man to his death is not the worst asPect of the affair. The execution was hurried forward because it was perceived that the. method of the trial and the char- acter of the sentence would provoke the con- demnation of Europe. It was determined to anticipate all protests, and to make them ineffective in the most absolute sense. "A dead man," ;the Spanish authorities seem to have said, "cannot be resuscitated, whatever may

be said in his favour. Let us kill this man, lest we should be persuaded, or lest we should be alarmed into sparing his life:' The parallel case is that of the SULTAN •OF MOROCCO and _EL .ROGETL The SULTAN threw his relative, the Pretender,to the lion Whilst the European Consuls_were waiting without to protest to him against his cruelty. We see no moral difference between the Spanish and the Moroccan methods, though shooting is more merciful than torture by wild beasts.

Spain is obviously in bad hands. The ,war against the Riffs is a stock-jobbers' war. It is true that four men were murdered, and that a country isl under obligation to see justice done in such cases. Our •own Ashantee war was undertaken under rather less provocation. Happily there was no suspicion of stock-jobbing behind it. There was not the slightest ground for supposing that the events out of Which it arose were what is vulgarly known as a fake. In the Spanish case, however, there seems the least possible reason to doubt •that the mining speculators Wanted a war, and that the murder of their four men was one of the arranged preliminaries. The assassination of Senor FERRER by semi- legal forms is one of the direct consequences of the war. The war occasioned the Barcelona riots as a protest, and those who put down the riots seized on SENOR FERRER as a scape- goat, although he had taken no tart in them. It appears to have been alleged that the books used at his school had a " Modernist " tendency. That is a priest's reason. Then, as he admitted he had written more than sixteen years since a draft appeal on the occasion of the Madrid Congress of Free Thought, this was resucitated and treated as if it were a quite recent docu- ment. In addition, the "Modernist " character of his school books—that is, the quality which made them real school books —had produced the Barcelona outbreak! It is on such grounds as these that he has been put to death before the outraged feeling of Europe had time to express itself. Such an insensate exercise of power does not give us much confidence in the future of KING ALFONSO. That way, indeed, revolution lies.

div.head: St. John Ambulance Brigade.
div.p: St. John Ambulance Brigade.

The inspection of the men belonging—to the Royal Naval Auxiliary Sick Berth Reserve (R.N.A.5.8.R.) took 'place at the Police Buildings at 7 p.m. on Monday, by Staff Surgeon Bean, inspecting Medical Officer of the Naval Auxiliary Forces. Twelve men were present on parade (11 from the Crosfield Division and one from Head Quarters Divition) as were also Chief Superintendent Waring of the Warrington Corps, Superintendent Rose and Ist Officer Cawley of the Crosfield Division. The men were first put through the stretcher drill and treating and carrying patients. Afterwards questions on paper were handed to eadh man which embraced both first aid and nursing, and they were subjected to a severe examination. on the various subjects brought lorward• and came out of the ordeal very creditably. After the inspection Dr. Bean spoke to the men and complimented them on their efficiency. He said it was a great pleasure to him,.to come to Warrington to inspect a body of men who had acquired so much knowledge of first'uld and sick nursing and who were preptred to offer their service to the country. He alsd pointed out how dreadful would be-a naval war and what a large and efficient body of men would be required for. such an event. ,He expretsed a wish that when he came to Ntarrington- next year he would find a much larger number to inspect.

Colonel Hall Walker, ONE MAN----Two M.P. for' Widnes,' has PUBS. been making history in - a mild sort of way, and his name ought to go down to posterity as that of the Member of Parliament who courageously and originally suggested that there should be two public-houses for every workingman—" one where he worked and one where he lived." Mr. Dodds drew local attention to the gallant colonel's noble notion in a speech to the Women's Circle on Monday evenitrg, when he expressed surprise that the brewers did not want a half way house as well. "Toby M.P." seems to have been struck with the same idea as Mr. Dodds, and in the current number 'of" Punch" he thus satirises the Member for Widnes HALL WALKER so moved by diScovery of treason in our Midst that he contributed most original idea that has yet flashed through debate, Protest being made against alleged design of Government to extinguish small licensed houses, gallant Colonel deployed in their defence. Declaied axiom that Public-house is, perhaps next to garments, absolute necessity for working-man. _ "Fact is," he said, "every workingman requires two Publicrhonses—Pne near his 403nek one near his work." Member below Gangway, not to be but lone in generosity, suggested another midway, so that going and coming Weary Willie.might drop in. No ; HALL WALKER a man of moderate views. Not to be dragged into extremes. A public- house, say next door but one to his residence, another three doors distant from his workshop, should suffice any reasonable labourer. Committee had heard of the principle of One Man One Vote. Something novel about this development of One Working Man Two Public Houses. Adjourned to think it over..

Next to Socialism, the CAPITAL LEAVING favourite bogey with THE COUNTRY? Conservative speakers who wish to scare the electorate is to tell them that capital is leav- ing the country as a result of Liberal legisla- tion, and that our commercial ruin is within measureable distance. They make no effort to substantiate the statement, which is pro- bably not swallowed so innocently as they think, and like other bogeys has become so familiar as to be treated with just contempt. A reliable illustration of the flow of capital is afforded by the quick results accruing from Mr. Lloyd George's new Patent Act. This measure has already attracted £500,000 of foreign capital to this country, and the , amount is daily increasing. The annual meeting of the Trafford Park Estates Co. this week in Manchester also affords a striking object lesson to the men who talk so glibly of capital flying away. The Company has paid a dividend for the first time, •solely because more capital than ever before has been forthcoming for industrial developments on the banks of the Ship Canal. The chair- man referred to the success of their efforts in attracting capital from abroad and attributed it largely to the operations of the Patents Act. There are more indications to-day of an industrial boom than of corn- decay,a.nd the men who suggest that capital is not safe in England are either shutting their eyes to the facts or deliberately mis-stating' them. There is not, and never has been, any country in the world Offering such an outlet, and promising so safe a return for capital investment as , England. And once the Budget become g law there will be a great development of enter- prise which is bound to absorb capital to an extent, undreamed of. Finally the men who are so alarmed (sic) at capital going abroad take care to keep their own capital at home and live comfortably on its earnings. We can quote Colonel Hall' Walker as example; seeing that he told the people of Widnes on Monday that Capital )1;:as leaving the country "to the extent of Millions a year." 'Now,.his oWni,capital—as". a brewer—is pretty well taxed, but he does not sell out and transfer it to Germany, the United States, or Spain! Why?'
On Monday, when the

RUINING- THE Housing Tand Town TOWN PLANNING Planning Bill came up ScHEmE, for a third reading, the Lords seemed to be obsessed by a capricious spirit of ,mischief. An amendment to give compensation to the landlord for any loss which an arbitrator might decide that he had incurred through a Town Planning scheme restricting the num- ber or height of buildings on a piece Of land, had twice been rejected at previous stages. It was moved again, and although Lord Crewe warned the House that it would ruin, the Bill—no warning was necessary to tell any rational person that it would make any project of Town Planning impracticable—it was carried.
It is a strange thing, SACROSANCT but perhaps the chief CONSERVATISM. responsibility for it lies

with the- curious anomaly that when the Conservative Party is in Opposition the smallest minority has as much destructive power, thanks to the Lords' veto, as it would have if it were all but a majority ; however this may be, it is a strange thing that the Conservative Party has not been able all through the last four years to adjust its ideas,to the situation of a small 'minority in the representative Chamber. The Opposition are convinced that there is something sacrosanct about a Con- servative Party, and to attack their prin- ciples on a public platform, save with humble apologies and bated breath, is demagogy, mob oratory, vituperation, vulgar abuse, and a hundred other offences which is too tedious to enumerate. Mr. Lloyd-George's Limehouse speech made the Oppositian shudder and gasp, after the Newcastle speech they have been screaming and foaming. Yet what, after all, did Mr. Lloyd George do? He merely demonstrated, fully and with a mass of detail, that while the ground-,landlords were crying out that they were being plundered, spoiled, seques- trated (to use a term of the Comionwealth period), they had in reality been fleecing•the community right and left, if " fleecing: is interpreted in the sense of adjusting one's demands not to the value of the thing sold but the buyer's necessity; while the com- munity was only asking for a moderate con- tribution from the wealth it had itself created.
There are two Two IMPORTANT important points in Mr. POINTS. Lldyd-George's defence

of the land faxes which are liable to-be overlooked in the controver- sial stress upon other and more militant topics in it. The first is that the yield of these land.,taies- is certain to be progressive. It has been rpade a, ground of attack upon these taxes that their yield for the current year will be small—an attack which overlooks the obvious retort that if the taxes bring in little they cannot exact much, for these taxes are not like the duties advocated by Tariff Reformers, which would only contribute to the State a small fraction in comparison with the burden which they would impose. But if the present yield is small, there will be a continuous increase every, year. And, be it observed, while the Tariff Reform duties would tend to grow in amount' while their yield would decrease, the yield of these taxes

will be constantly increasing, without 4ny increase in the rate -of taxation. The second point is this: the Budget, by developing the resogrces of the country and improving the housing conditions of the nation, will increase the demand for land. Consequently this Budget, -which is said to be aimed at impoverishing the landlord, will increase his Wealth, while it takes a moderate toll for the State of this wealth which the State itself creates.

div.head: ..eNd•—--f NOTES AND NOTIONS
div.p: ..eNd•—--f NOTES AND NOTIONS
BUDGET MOTTO.
"These are times that touch moneyed worldlings with dismay." * * *

Mr. T. H. Sloan, Unionist M.P., from South Belfast who will be , remem- bered as a leading speaker at one of the Licensing Bill meetings in Warrington —has just been telling his constituents that the Budget is" honest and just." There has notzbe a single meeting against the Budget in .any constituency in Ulster, and Mr. Sloan vouched for the support of the democracy of the North of Ireland. * *

' • The way party leaders are being trotted round to bowling *matches, friendly society gatherings and the like, is becoming farcical. Sir' Gilbert Greenall and Councillor Fulton- Smith seem to be going the round regularly, and how they can attend to their respective duties as Shepherds, Buffaloes, Oddfellows and the like is a matter for increasing wonder. We are not surprised that they are beginning to want something for their trouble. Coun- cillor Fulton-Smith end6avoured to get a quid pro quo at the annual meeting of . Shepherds on Monday evening by delivering a political speech from the usually impartial position of chairman. He politely remarked that "of course, politics were debarred from the assembly," and having thus cleared the way he told the Shepherds (not in so many words) but quite plainly, that the Budget was Socialism and the only alternative Tariff Reform. They were also to attribute unemployMent to the fact that our orders were passing away to foreign competitors. We don't blame Mr. Fulton Smith—except for abusing his position as chairman—but the Shepherds and kindred associations ought to take more care about the nature of the speeches they invite their members to hear' if they wish to' maintain unity and secure progress. * *

gentleman who, we will hope, has gone to a better land, has given a sort of p6sthumous punch to Socialism. In leaving £6O to a former servant, out of an estate of £10,474, the testator directed that the legacy is not given free of legacy dut3;, which would have been the case "but for the fact that the husband of Caroline Mary Sugg (the legatee) holds Socialistic views, and ought, therefore, better to appreciate a legacy left to his wife which is subject to a heavy duty for the benefit of the State." * *

•This has been a week of rest from the Budget; rest necessary both for Parliament and the Treasury in the immense task of framing so great a measure. The sudden and tragic death of the Member for Ber- mondsey will. have given the public some idea of the strain through which Parliament has been passing. But such sacrifices are necessary if any considerable work is to be achieved for • the people of England. The bill as amended in Committee of the House of COMMORS has now been republished, and anyone who 'Cares to purchase it (Messrs. Wyman and Sons, Limited, Fetter-lane, ,E-C,price 9d.), will, be struck by the studied care and minute labour with which this gfeat measure has been drafted and redrafted. The last touches will be given to the bill on the report stage -next week, and then it will be ready for transmission to the House of Lords.

What will the House of Lords do with it? That is the question of questions at the present moment in English politics. The Constitutional position of this country is clear. The King acts under the advice of his Ministers. Therefore, we must presume that Mr. Asquith has been in this case rather the giver than the receiver of advice. And that advice will be that there can be no comprise in the assertion of the rights of the House of Commons to control finance.

* * * For let it be clearly understood that it is not the House of Commons which is the' aggressive party in this fight. The House of Commons is simply exercising those Con- stitutional rights of taxation which have bqonged to them for three centuries. It is the House of Lords which, through the mouths of many of its most conspicuous Members, ha 4 been uttering threats during the last few months. And what are all these threats about? It is not as if the House of Commons were proposing to do any- thing very atrocious, or even very drastic. An impartial observer would certainly imagine, at any rate, that the House of Commons was proposing to tax the land of the country to the marrow. Lord Rosebery with his talk of" ruined landlords," certainly gave that impression.

* * But that is far from the fact. On the contrary, so far is the House of Commons from wishing to tax the landlords to the marrow that they are not even laying any general taxes on land at all. These taxes are not on land; they are on land values. These taxes are not levied on the fruits of industry at all. They are levied.. on "Treasure Trove." Look at it in this way. Let it be supposed a man to-day buys at a proper times price a field of agricultural land. He keeps it for some years, and then one fine day when ploughing he strikes against a hard substance which he discovers to be a metal urn full of valuable Roman gold coins. By the law of Treasure" Trove he must deliver up his find to the Treasury for the Crown's benefit. It is an act of gracious custom that he receives reward for what the Crown retains to compensate him for his trouble, and perhaps to mark his honesty. * * * _

Now, instead of an tirnful of Roman coins, let is suppose a railway company comes by his land, and they make a station close adjoining. He finds " treasure" then in his land which is wanted for building purposes. If he had neither struck the Roman urn nor had a railway come by his land he would have been no richer. The State has rights over the whole Treasure Trove in the first case, and now it is asking for a part of the Treasure Trove in the second case. In the first case the man did something towards the development of the wealth. In the case of the railway he did absolutely nothing. Is increment value duty, there, a burden

So much for the land taxes. But of late there has been an effort to divert the agita- tion from the land taxes to the taxes on the "Trade." Those are denounced as "robbery." Now, do not be deceived by phrases. As a matter of faet, it is not too much to say that "the Trade" is making a very good thing out of these taxes.' In London, for instance,

they _raised the price of beer by 1/2cl. a glass -on July Ist. And yet the licence duties do not come into force until December Ist! Five months clear run without paying a penny to the Exchequer! The fact is that behind the cover of their pocket-handker- chiefs these people are picking the pockets of the public. It is the old story of the Walrus and the Carpenter with the oysters. "With tears and sobs he sorted• out those of the largest size." But the public are not oysters. They have seen more of life than the molluscs.

Women's Liberal Association. The annual tea and concert .in connection with this association will be held in Bold-street .Wesleyan Schoolroom on Monday ,evening. Miss Truda Ciosfield will give an _illustrated lecture on her travels in India. Sudden Death. , ,

Mr. Arthur Thomas Smith (52), a retired diver, who lodged at 25, Museum-street, went in a hairdresser's shop in Scotland-road on Saturday evening• with the intention of being shaved, but fell to the floor and expired immediately. Death was due to heart trouble. Cycling Fatality. • . A pedlar, named Robert Postlethxvaite, aged 40, of Warrington, was standing in the roadway at Acton Grange about 9.30 On Vhursday evening, when he was knocked down by a bicycle ridden by,James Fryar, of Padgate, and sustained such serious injuiies that he died an hour later.—An inquest will be held to-day.

Palatine Skating Rink. A grand summer and seaside carnival will boheld. at the Palatine' Rink, Wilderspool Causeway, on Thursday evening, when prizes .will be given for the smartest costume (lady), original costume (gentleman), and twot.step competition (lallY and gentleman). ' Adult School. The Warrington Adult School Federation which has been recently. formed hopes to have 12 Schools in the' town and district before long On Thursday evening not' the fortnightly' lectures held in the 'Adult School; Academy-street, will be continued, when Mr. ,J. C. Radley will give an account of the Poor Law Corn- Mission report. Y. Mr. A. J. Jolley will preside. Warringtom Man Found Drowned. • Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest at Padgate yesterday on Andrew Malcolm -(33), cabinet .maker, . lodging at 29, • Wellington-street; Warrington, whose body was found in .the river at Woolston on Wednesday. Deceased had been greatly de pressed through the death othis 'wife: A . verdict of "Found drowned" was returned.,

Empire Skating Rink. . The gross amount taken at the Empire Skating Rink on the opening day (Tuesday) was 147 is. Bd., including the following donations :—Lady Greenall £5 ; Mr, D. Cooper, £1; :Messrs, Wright, Garnett and Wright 10s. The expenditure incurred in print- ing &c., was £6 us. Bd., leaving £4O 10s. available for distribution among local charities. £3l .10s. has been handed over to the Infirmary and Dispensary; £8 to the Warrington District Nursing Association; and £1 to the Stockton Heath Nursing Association. The respective. treasurers of these institutions acknowledge the donations with thanks.

Death of Mr. Thomas Moores. Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Mr. Thomas Moores, 46, Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath, who passed away yesterday aternbon after about ten days' illness from septic pneumonia. Mr. Moores, who was sixty-six years of age, was up to a few years ago, one of Warrington's best known tradesmen. For a long 'period be carried on the business of a grocer and corn merchant in Irlam- street, but latterly he had lived in retirement. Ile IN as a staunch Churchman and at one time held the office of churchwarden at the Parish Church. In politics he was a Conservative. Much sympathy will be felt with the family (two sons and seven daughters) in their bereavement.

United Irish League, Warrington Branch. The winter session in connection with the above organization was commenced. on Sunday evening last in the League rooms; Winwick-street, with a limelight lecture by Councillor Owen Toole. The lecturer took for his 'subject " Beauty spots of Ireland" and dealt with it in a most exhaustive, instructive, and interesting mariner. The slides were excellent\ and. the .beauty of the views excited the applause and admiration of the large' gathering present. The lantern was manipulated by Messrs. Hill and • Jones. During the eveningvarious songs were contributed. Miss Macaleese sang splendidly "I bid you the top of the Morning" whilst Mrs. John Dolan gave "To the old Green Isle" and Mr. James Flynn" My Irish Home "effectively::: A vote of thanks to Councillor Toole and the artistes was accorded on the proposition of Mr. A. M. Crowe seconded by Mr. J. Fay., Councillor Toole proposed and Mr. M. Cunningham seconded a vote of thanks to the chairman (Dr. J. D. Liston).—On Sunday next Mr. J. C. Dalton--(President U.I.L. Chester and late of Warrington) will address a meeting in the League rooms on the Home Rule question. " PnvErtn. " FIRE GRATES Still unsurpassed, Inspection invited..—J. S. div.head: Presentation to P.C. Richard K. Wilson.
div.p: Presentation to P.C. Richard K. Wilson.

There was a large attendance at the Constitution Lodge of Oddfellows on Saturday evening, the occasion being the presentation of a Past Grand's Framed Emblem of Merit to Bro. Richard Wilson. Amongst those present' were Pro. G. M. George F. Freeman, Deputy Prov. G. M. Thomas B. Forbes. I.P.M. Lot Brookes, P.P.G.M, Bradshaw, Prov. C.S. Fred Webster, P.P.G.M. Ellis R. Clare, P.P.G.M. William Daintith, P.P. G.M. F. J. Whittle, P.P.G.M. Joseph Taylor, P.G. Henry Taylor, P.G. W. Holloway, P. G. Peter Lester, P.G. G, il: Warburton Steel, P.G. A. E. Burdett and other brethren. N.G. Mellor occupied the chair and P.G. Thomas Ellison officiated as V.G. After, the delegates to the, District meet- ing had given their report Prov. G.M. Free- man made the presentation in suitable terms. —P.G.G. H, Warburton Steel said that he could not allow the octasion to pass without adding his'testimony to the work of Bro. Wilson, He (the speaker) felt that some or the credit of Bro. Wilson reflected on him as he had prevailed upon P.G. Wilson to join the Order andlhad first proposed him as an officer of the Lodge.--P.G. Wilson said that he 4ppreeiated the honour, that had been conferred upon him and although he felt he had not done as much as he would have liked for the Order he was pleased that the little he had done had met with the appreciation of his brother OddfellGws. He could assure them that it was not his intention to sever himself from the, society and he would always be willing to assist the Lodge and the Order in general to the very • best of his ability. Applause). During the evening songs were given and (a very pleasant evening spent after which the N.G closed the Lodge with the usual ceremoty. -

- • Death of Mr. L. E - Newcombe. • • Many residents in "Warrington and Penketh will regret to hear of the death yesterday -in a London Hospital, of Mr. Leonard Erie Newcombe, second son of Mr. John Newcombe, Stockton Heath. The deceased gentleman succumbed from the effects of an operation on the brain. He was 37 years old, and was educated at the Warrington. Grammar School, subsequently , being articled to the late Mr. J. E. Wright, architect. He left Warrington about a dozen years ago, and settled down as an architect in Wolverhampton, where he married. The widow and five children strvive.him. "HERALD" KITCHM RANGES save 50 per cent of fuel.—Agent J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, 51 to 55 Bridge st.,Warrington.—Advt.. • School Children's Rounders Competition. There was a pleasing little cerembny at the Sacred Heart School on Tuesday afternoon when the silver rose bowl won in the rounders competition was formally presented by the donor, Councillor Fulton- Smith. Others present were ;—The Rev' Father Rockliffe, the new rector in charge; Mr. E. Plinston, one of the managers of the school; and Mr.- J. Moore Murray (director of education). A number of songs and solos were pleasingly contributed by the children, under the superintendence of the head mistress, Miss E. Dinsdale. Miss Haney acted as accompanist.— Father Rockcliffe said it was a very happy augury for him as this event was taking place just after his arrival in the parish, and it favourably impressedlim with the condition of the school of which he had the happiness to take charge. He had no doubt that if they entered into their work in the some spirit with which they entered . into their games. they would achieve success. (Applause.) Councillor Fulton- Smith then ddressed a few words of advice and ' encouragement t. the children, a ftcr which Margaret Reynolds, captain of the winning teat& stepped forward and addressing Councillor Fulton.. Smith, said: We, the children of the Sacred Heart School, wish to thank you for the honour you have done us to-day in coming amongst us and presenting us with this beautiful rose bowl, of which we are so proud. Hopinr, this will convey to-you our apprecia- tion of your-rovely -gift;' 'we remain,' yours very regpectfully, the children of the Sacred Heart School. (Applause.) The proceedings closed with the National Anthein.

Mr. J. Rabbltt In Llandudno Opera. Mr. J. Rabbitt, of Warrington, on Thursday week had the honour of being summoned by telegram to Llandudno to take the leading role of Colonel Fairfax in a performance of "The Yeomen of the Guard 4, at the Grand Theatre in aid of the Llandudno Cottage Hospital. Mr. D. Llewellyn Jones had been cast for the part, but owing to indisposition a few hours before the production it was found necessary to obtain a sub- stitute. Mr. Rabbitt, on the suggestion of Mr. Thornley-Dodge, who was taking the character of Jack Point, was• wired for. Mr. Babbitt hastily journeyed to Llandudno and practically without rehearsal enacted Mr. Jones's part, an effort which speaks well for Mr. Rabbitt's well-known resources as an amateur. Writing of his perform- ance, the "Llandudno Advertiser says:— " Whilst we have had no opportunity of hearing Mr. D.. Llewelyn Jones •in this production, we cannot imagine him giving'a more creditable pourtrayal of this most difficult role of Colonel Fairfax than that pourtrayed by Mr. Rabbitt, and When it is known that the gentlemen had seen neither score nor words for the last two years, it was a distinctly meritorious per- formance, and all concerned are deepy indebted to him for his prompt response to such a difficult undertaking: The audience were not slow to show their appreciation and at the conclusion of his first solo, most delight- fully sung, he came in for a most enthusiastic recall. and similar favours were bestowed upon him at each of his solo during the remainder of the production, and thoroughly deserved. There is no gainsaying the fact that, with few exceptions, he was the finest vocalist of the evening, and a distinct acquisition."
TABLE AND HANGING LAMPS, new designs now showing.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt.

Loyal Order of Ancient• Shepherds (A.U.) Warrington District. The quarterly meeting was held on Saturday at the Ironworkers' 110111e.Lodge,Alexandra Vaults. Amongst those under the presidency of Prov. Chief Shepherd W. Miles were• D.P.C.S. W. Taylor, P.P.C.S. J. Gillooley, P.P.C.S. L. Weir, P.P.C.S. W. Eckersley, P.P.C.S. J. Mather, P.P.C.S. P. L. Edgar, P.P.C.S. J. Hfrley, P.P.C.S. T. Miller, and P.P.C.S. James Parr (district treasurer). The accounts for the quarter were presented along with the auditors report and adopted. Bro. S. Blythe (Rose Bud Lodge) was elected auditor for the following six months. Bro. John Haley (Olive Branch Lodge) was nominated for the'vice-presidency ot the Lancashire and Adjacent Counties Conference and Bro. L. Weir (Sons of Mersey Lodge) was nominated for the Board of Management of such Conference. Bro. L. Weir was also nominated for a seat on the Order Executive. An interesting item was the presentation 'of a handsome li-alnut clock to P.P.C.S. Bro. J. Gillooley for services rendered during his term of office as Prov. Chief Shepherd. P.P.C.S. Bro. P. L. Edgar in making the presentation congratulated Bro. Gillooley on the success which had attended his efforts during his 'term of office and tendered to him the good wishes of all for his future welfare. Bros. J. Haley, W. Peers, L. Weir, W. Massey, T. Miller, W. Miles and James Parr supported the presentation with congratulatory speeches. Bro. Gillooley on rising to reply was received with enthusiasm. fle thanked the brethren for the hand- some testimonial and for their good wishes and said that any service he had performed for Shepherdry had been done as a matter of duty to the fraternity. He thanked the district officers and lodge officials for the courtesy shown him during his term of office and hoped to still continue to work for the good of the Order.

div.head: WARRINGTON SWIMMING CLUB. 26th Annual Gala.
div.p: WARRINGTON SWIMMING CLUB. 26th Annual Gala.
The Mayor's Attack on Aid. Bolton.

The Warrington baths were crowded last evening for the 26th annual gala of the Warrington Swimming Club. A programme of great attractiveness and been prepared, one of the features being an exhibition of life saving and ornamental swimming by the Liverpool Westminster Ladies' Swimming Club. These accom- plished ladies have gained numerous prizes, and their exhibition was a miniature gala in itself and was loudly cheered. .Among the local events was a 25 yards handi- cap for girls under 16 which was well contested by nine entrants. Various local championships were also decided, t.nd the gels was unquestionably one of the best ever promoted by the Club in the course of its lengthy career. * The Mayor (Alderman Porshaw) presided over the proceedings. The MAYOR during an interval said he thought the Corporation ought te afford better facilities for the children in order that they might learn to swim. He thought the baths were a disgrace to the town of Warrington. (Hear hear, and applause). As long as they bad Alderman Bolton as chairman of the Town Hall, Parks, and Baths Committee they would have nothing, done for them.

The results of the various events were as follows :- 50 Yards Schoolboy Championship of Warrington and District.—First prize, " Thornton" perpetual challenge bowl and gold medal • second, gold medal; third, gold centre medal. Ist, D. Cooper (Arpley-street) ; 2nd, J. Cross (Arpley-street) ; 3rd, S. Watkins (heath Side). Final Works Squadron Championship.—First prize. sir Gilbert Greenall, Perpetual Challenge Shield and four gold medals (presented by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart).; second prize, four gold centre medals. Holders, Co-operative Stores. Winners.; Crosfield's. 25 'Yards Girls' Under 16 Tlandicap.—First prize, ladies' silver brush; second, silver photo frame; third, flower holders. Ist, M. McCormack ; 2nd, M. Merchant; 3rd, T. Crannigan. 150 Yards Championship of Warrington and Dis- trict.—First prize, Licensed Victuallers' Perpetual Challenge Trophy and Gold Medal (presented by the Warrington and District Licensed Victuallers Associa- tion) ; second, gold medal •, third, gold medal. Holder: R. Allen. Winner :_R. Allen.

_ 50 Yards Members' Handicap.—First prize, rose bowl ; second, silver cruet; third, set of carvers ; fourth, prize clock. Ist, W. Dunn ; 2nd, J. Sanders; 3rd, H. Sisson ; 4th, J. Furnival. Final of the Grawd Squadron Challenge Shield.— Teams 8 a side to swim 4 lengths of the 43ath. Wigan (Holders) V. Everton. Winner: Wigan. Instead of the polo match between Everton (winners 'of the Liverpool and District League) and rest E League a mixed international team gave an exhibition of splendid water polo. The judges of the various events were Messrs. John Evans, E. Evans, E. Draper, J. Fulton-Smith, and W. Chalmers, Mr. J. N. Vernon (hon. sec.) and Mr. J. B Wilkinson (hon. treasurer) had pleasure of seeing their efforts rewarded by the success of the gala.
I SHALL have a few Choice DAMSONS this next week. McDERMOTT, "Cheapest Man Alive."

div.head: SHOP-BREAKERS CA
div.p: SHOP-BREAKERS CA

_ At the Borough Police Court on Monday, a young tr an named Frank Tracey living with his mother in Catherine-street was charged with breaking and entering the lock-up shop of 139, Bewsey-road and stealing there- from six silver watches, nine silver chains, one pair of opera glasses, five gold rings, a pair of gold earrings, one cameo breast pin, one gold breast pin, and a silk muffler, value in all £8 17s. Gd. the property of William Shields.—lnspector Williamson, said it was a cAse in which the police wanted a remand for eight days. The prisoner was only a young man living with his mother in Catherine-street. The prosecutor was Charles Shield carrying on business in Bewsey-road as a pawnbroker. The shop was a lock-up cne. Mr. Shield did riot reside there. In the early hours of that morning shortly after two o'clock, the occupier of the shop next to the prose- cutor's heard someone in Mr. Shield's shop, and on getting up and looking through the window saw the prisoner crouching down in the shop. He sz-nt for Mr. Shield and on his getting there, the prisoner bolted. Mr. Shield gave chase and with the assistance of the night watchman from Messrs. Greenings Works, caught him. On being brought to the Police Station and searched the stolen property was found upon him.— A remand of eight days was granted. ALLEGED THEFT OF IRON.—A REMAND.

Joseph Massey, 79, Liverpool-road and John Shaw 56, Wellington-street, were charged at the Borough Police Court on Monday with stealing, between Friday, September 30th, and October 9th, one ion, 3 quarters of iron and steel valued at 455. from Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. Ltd., the property of that company.—Mr. T. S. Steel, solicitor, said he was instructed to appear on behalf of the prisoner Massey, but was not at present able to proceed with the defence and he therefore asked for a remand for a week, also for bail to be allowed for both men. They were both men of good character.—The Clerk: The police have no objection to that.—The remand was granted, bail being allowed. At the Borough Court on Tuesday Joseph Tracey, the above prisonees brother, 9, Catherine-street, was charged with having some time between 10 and 11 p.m. on Saturday, October 9th, broken into and entered the lock-up-shop, 137,Bewsey-road, and stolen there- from threepairs of hair clippers, two pairs of rciseors, four lb, of thick twist, three lb. of other twist, one lb. of thin twist, and !lb. of " Perfection Flake" tobacco value £2 9s id., the property of William Turton. - Chief Inspector Williamson stated that a younger brother of the prisoner was charged at the Court the 'previous morning viith breaking into the premises of Mr. Shield, pawnbroker, who kept a lock-up shop next door to that of Mr. Turton, and he asked for a remand in order that the brothers might be tried together. It appeared that prisoner and his brother had been visit- ing the public houses in the town, and at closing time they went home together.—A remand was granted for seven days.
-ABANDONED ON A DOOR STEP. TWO MONTHS FOR NEGLECT.

At the Borough Police Court on Wednesday a story was told of a young male child being abandoned on a door step in Dial-street by its mother. The sequel was that Mary Ann Docherty, a widow, of Bolton's-yard, was charged with abandoning her young child in a manner likely to cause it unnecessary suffering and injury to heilth, and further with neglecting the same child.—Mr. A. Browne, who prosecuted, said prisoner had been a widow for two 7ears. She had three children, two of whom did not live with her because of her character, while the other one, Thomas, aged fifteen months—the one neglected, was kept by her. On Friday night about half-past ten, a Mrs. Jones, living at 26, Dial-ftreet, found the child on her door step in a most destitute condition. It was conveyed ta the Police Station and then taken back to• Mrs. Jones who looked after it during the night. Inspector Cox came on the scene and examined the child and found it filthy and verminous and presented a sorrowful spectacle.— Inspector Cox said he examined the child and found it in a o.eplorable condition.lis clothes,which were nothing but rags, were pinned around its body. The vermin were running all over the child's body. He knew the woman very well,and she would not stay in the Workhouse, but left the child to the mercy of the people. She had no fixed home at the present time and wandered from house to house. Her husband died about two years ago, and since than she had been wandering about. Her character was a very bad one.—Mrs. Jones. of 26, Dial- street, said she found the child on her doorstep at half- post eleven ou Friday night. It was in a shocking condition.—John Constable, an official of the Work- house, said the child's body was covered with blisters from the vermin.—Prisoner was sentenced to two mouths' hard labour.

EXTENSIVE SHOP ROBBERIES. A CHARWOMAN'S SERIOUS OFFENCE. The proceeds of a series of systematic robberies cc blob included numerous articles of lady's and gent's underclothing were displayed at the Felice Court on Thursday when Annie Palmer, married woman, 11, Church-street, was charged with stealing during the past twelve months goods to the value of £l7 19s. Gd. from the shop of Charles Maunfield, outfitter, Horse- market-street, and other articles 'rake £2 35., the property of the Misses Woods, Rylands-street—The facts as related by Mr. T. S. Steel who prosecuted were to the effect that for the past sixteen months the prisoner had been employed by Mr. Mounfield as a charwoman. She was also in the employ of the Misses Woodsat was her usual custom to clean out the shop once weekly. In consequence of certain information coming to the knowledge of the police Detective Reddington called at the shop of Mr. Monnfleld and interviewed the prisoner who made certain admissions. A basket which belonged to the prisoner was found to contain two new shirts and a further search at the donee station revealed other property secreted underneath her clothing. From inquiries it was ascertained that for some considerable time the prisoner had been in the habit of pawning new good-s. Some of them were pawned by neighbours at the prisoner's request. In the house there were no less than 117 pawntickets relative to property stolen from Mr. Mountield. Not only had the woman got other women to pledge the goods for her, but she had been selling them amongst her neighbours. In the course of the inquiries it was found that goods belong- ing to the Misses Woods had been pledged. So far as the police had been able to ascertain there was no reason for the woman to do anything of that description. Detective Reddington had shown diligence in making inquiries with regard to the thefts. The Chairman (Mr. J. Rymer Young) said there was no single extenuating circumstance in her case why she should have committed the thefts, and she would have to go to prison for eight months.

div.head: Warrington Borough Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Court.

MONDAY.—Before—Alderman Smethurst (chairman), and ;Messrs. W. Roberts, H. Thornton and G. Pilling. A MONTH FOR TIIEFT.—James Heaton, a stranger to the town, was charged with stealing a pair of boots value ss. lld, from the shop of 59, Buttermarket-street the property of William Bowden. Inspector Williamson said-the prisoner was before the court the previous Saturday and the case was adjourned in order to find the owner of the boots.—lt appears that Mr. Bowden is a boot dealer, csrrying on business in Buttermarket- street. At five o'clock on Friday afternoon he had six pairs of boots lying on the floor just inside his shop door. Subsequently he missed one pair. The same evening prisoner attempted to pledge the boots in a shop in Mersey-street and the occupant of the shop being suspicious, informed the police. Sergeant Heap took him into custody. He at first refused to give any answer with regard to the boots. Afterwards he was charged and admitted stealing the boots, saying he was in drink at the time.—A sentence of one month's imprisonment was passed. _ . .
TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. H. Roberts (chairman), J Rymer Young, C. Jackson Holmes and W. T.

Williams. NEGLECT OF WIFE AND FAMILY.—JOIM William Douglas, labourer, Cockbedge-lane, was charged with neglecting his wife and six children whereby they became chargeable to the Warrington Union. Mr. Shearer said the prisoner's wife and mix children were admitted to the workhouse on the Bth instant. Defend- ant lit that time was in full work and could have been earning a guinea a week. He,however, spent the money on himself, sometimes only giving his wife 4s. per week. Mr. F. H. Aukland stated that he gave the order as at the time the wife aid children were absolutely destitute and homeless.—Mrs. Dotkglas said the neglect had been going on for years. Defendant was sent to gaol for 14 days. EDUCATION CASES.—The following parents were fined as under for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—John Hickman, 39, Ashton-streed, fined 2s. 6d.; and Samuel Kean, 55, Howley-lane' is. 6d. W'EDNES'DAY.—Before Mr. J. W. Hayward (chairman,) Alderman Smethurst and Dr. Joseph. THE BEGGING NUISANCE.—John Williams, of no settled abode was charged with begging in Thynne- street the previous day.—P.C. Holland stated that he saw prisoner begging in Thynne-street. He was waiting for the commercial travellers coming out of Garton's Seed Depot. Witness beard him ask out traveller for money as he had walked from Knutsford and had nothing to eat and could not get work. Witness bad had several complaints about prisoner. He worked different districts of the town every day, he generally worked Wilderspool-road from house to house. He belonged to Stockport. He walked about 30 yards with the commercial traveller.—Prizoner was sentencel to three months hard labour.
THURSDA Y.—Beforo J. Rymer Young -(in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, W. Roberts, Dr. Naden, W. T.
Williams.
AN UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.—Frederick Sheard, a stranger, was charged with assaulting William Buck, milk dealer, Allen-street, and further with using obscene language.—The complainant stated that he was

in Bewsey-road on Wednesday afternoon delivering milk, when the prisoner purchased a halfpennyworth. An argument arose over the quantity and quality which ended in the prisoner throwing the milk in his face, and also struck him in the mouth with his fist. He then ran away, but was caught in Scotland-road, where he was given into the custody of P.C. W i Woods.—The chair- man n committing prisoner for one month said it was a most unprovoked assault. . ALLEGED THEFT OF ELECTRIC GLOBES.—Frank Hammond was remanded for seven days on a charge of stealing by means of a trick a number of electric globes, the property of Harry Bibby, Arpley-street.—The Chief Constable said that on October 2nd the prisoner went to the premises of the prosecutor and asked to be supplied with six lamps for a gentleman named Bibby in Latchford. Nothing further was heard of the lamps until Wednesday, when Detective Clough in making inquiries with regard to other stolen propert3 from St. Helens discovered prisoner's connection with the present charge. FRlDA.Y.—Befora the Mayor (chairman), Alderman Smethurst, Messrs. T. Locker and G. Pilling. THE THEFT OF BRASSES.—Edward Duffy Kendrick,a stranger, was handed over to the Liverpool Police on the charge of stealing a number of brass locks and handles.—The Chief Constable stated that the prisoner had been remanded until that day in order that the police might find the owners of the property. They had discovered that it bad been stolen from Liverpool. FINED FOR ASSAULT.—WaIter Brown,of 16,Battersby- lane, was summoned by his wife (Ellen Brown) for assault on the 11th of Oatober.—Complainant said the defendant abused her after she had been out and kicked her about the legs.—Fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. • Juvenile Court.

FRIDA y.—Before the Mayor (chairman) Alderman Smethurst, and Messrs. T. Locker, and G. Pilling. THEFT OF A PURSE.—CASE REMANDED.—Harry Forster a young lad of School Brow was charged with stealing a purse containing Cs. in money, end two Canadian postal orders, the property of Dianah Warrens 38, Blaine-street.—lt tippe:irs that at eleven o'clock the previous morning he went to the house of the prosecutor and asked her little daughter for her mother's purse. He then abscondel, He had been in the habit of going to the house selling firewood. The case was remanded for seven days.

div.head: Latchford Baptist Church.
div.p: Latchford Baptist Church.

The autumnal anniversary services were held at the above Church on Sunday, Rev. E. E. Walter, of New Brighton, preaching in the morning and evening. In the afternoon a children's musical service was held when special choruses and solos were creditably rendered by a children's choir, the soloists being Miss A. Grounds, Master A. Hamblett and Master W. E. Wilkinson. A duet "While you're young: was sweetly sung by Miss G. Jones and Master W. T. Wilkinson. The choir rendered the anthems "What are these ! " (Stainer) and "As pants the hart" (Spokr), Mr. Peter Harrison presiding at the organ. Miss Lee sang in the solo in the latter anthem very feelingly. The collec- tion amounted to £lO.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was a very good attendance at this meetiing on Sunday last. The Secretary presided and spoke upon "There shall te no night there." Night and darkness were the symbol of sorrow, trouble and bereavement. These we had in this life, but the nights of our experi- ence would pass away and we would enter into the fulness of joy in the eternal day. Mr. Himsworth gave the address upon "Sleeping and awake," the point which he emphasised being that the higher things of life are gained by wakefulness and watchfulness. Mr. Payton read the lesson and the Chairman led the prayer. Mr. Payton presided at the organ and also rendered as an organ solo" Cmrsalem" which was greatly enjoyed. The Chairman welcomed one new member. He also moved a vote of sympathy with Miss Sitncocks, who belongs to the Society, with an expression of hope for her recovery. The meeting closed with singing "I'll praise Him all the time."

div.head: Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission.
div.p: Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held at this mission on Sunday. Addressing the scholars in the morning, the Rev. J. S. Langley of Kirkham took for his subject the story of a farmer whose crops had failed and who returned thanks by sending some of his produce, wheat, as a thank-offering. The children very much appreciated the address. In the afternoon Mr. Langley spoke of the character of Jacob in contrast with Esau. The attendance throughout the day was very good. At the evening service the Mission was crowded, special hymns being sung by the choir. An anthem, "All the works of the Lord are good" (Nichol) was also rendered with good effect. On Monday evening a concert was given at the mission by the Excelsior Glee Party and others. There was a large and appreciative audience and the programme included :—Songs, Mr. J. Mather, Mr. Moon, Miss Mounfteld, Miss Silcock, Mr. W. H. Wallington; piano solos. Miss Pollitt ; glees Excelsior Glee Party; sketch, Mr. A. Trow. The accompanists were played by Mr. A. Trow. On the proposition of Mr. Holland, seconded by Mr. Rushton, and supported by Mr. Wall, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Glee Patty and others.

div.head: Wesleyan Bible Class League. Address by Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P.
div.p: Wesleyan Bible Class League. Address by Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P.

That veteran Parliamentarian, Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P., addressed a public meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Bible Class League in Bold-street Church last Sunday afternoon. There was a large con- gregation, which included most of the Bible classes of the local Wesleyan circuit. Mr. James Dodds presided and supporting him on the platform were Messrs. J. C. Holland and Dean and Miss M. Dodds.

The CHAIRMAN said they were privileged to have upon the rostrum Mr. Cameron, who was a close student of the Bible and who was of high character and spotless integrity. He was eminently fitted to speak to them upon the subject which they were supremely interested in—the Bible. Before he (the speaker) was born—and that was over sixty years ago—Mr. Cameron had been living for the intellectual, the Inc ail, and the spiritual welfare of those about him. In the county of Durham and over a wider area, the character and the life of their friend were spoken of with affection. He had laboured strenuously throughout his life and made himself in his district an everlasting name. Their friend had never lowered his flag, as he (the speaker) knew, for any popular cause or for any personal victory. In 1900 there was a great war and the Methodist Church on the whole was in favour of it as well as the people of the country. Mr. Cameron was one of the very few public men who said "1 am dead against the war; it is an abominable war." (Applause.) He fought his election on that war and was returned by double his majority. He (the speaker) did not think he was divulging any secret when be told them that the late Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman said to Mr. Cameron while walking down the Lobby, " My friend Cameron, if they had all been like you, I think we should have done very much better in the fight." Continuing, Mr. Dodds said that was what most of them came to realise. In 1906 Mr. Cameron was returned by a majority of 6,060 and the Labour Party had passed a resolution that so long as Robert Cameron lived and liked to represent that division they would never oppose him. That showed the splendid feeling of the miners who dominated that district. (Applause). Mr. JOHN MeAwritua then gave a splendid render- ing of " Behold I stand at the door. Mr. CAMERON, in the course of his address, said that the Gospel included God, truth, knowledge, politics of the right sort, and every good thing of course. The study of the Bible was the preparation for all studies, and if one knew the Bible well one had the turn of all literature at our finger ends. He would take for his text the following verse "The eyes of all wait upon Thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season." —Psalm cxlv., 15. It was not cant nor commonplace for him to say that was a wonderful book that could contain a text so simple, beautiful and clear as that. The assertion that God was centre of all things, pro- vider of all things, supplier of all that life required, —that He Himself had created in so simple a form. When they as Bible scholars thought about it they would know what the text meant, and how it had become what it had. The speaker illustrated the text by saying that when a farmer went to feed his birds " the eyes of all waited upon him." Proceeding, he said that God was the farmer in this universe—" the God in whom we all live, move and have our being." God was guiding the universe which He bad brought into existence. God was the inner force of everything, He was in all things and through all things. They were taught and accustomed to think of God as a Person standing outside,as a Man controlling the universe. The Apostle said a deeper thought—that He was in all things. Proceeding he said that life was a mystery What was that mysterious thing that we called life ? What could it be ? We might dismiss it. The mystery of mysteries lay there. Life was universal. It was everywhere and in a myriad of forms. What mar- vellous forces there were going on around us ! Those mysterious forces were creating the fish, the plants and the birds. On every bill there was life ; in every lane there were myriads of flies. All life had to be fed. Life took a thousand forms and culminated at last in the creation of a human being. What a Providence it was that found the necessary food for all life ! What a God we had! What a being it was that had the burden of all the creation. If their Bible studies did not stir them all to see the great Bible outside—the Bible of creation, moonlight, the sunrise and the sunset ; if their eyes were not opened he sometimes asked if • they used their senses. What a mistake it was to give them five senses and a glorious world and yet they were lost in their businesses, cares and sports. To the young men he

said that the real sport was the training .of the intellect to' see, and to grasp this great universe. As they used the gifts they had they would become stronger as they grew in years. The real religion was this: that we might learn to see gradually that there was a God; that there must be a Clod and though the clouds and darkness were round about Him yet righteousness and truth were the foundations of His thrGne ; that He was working out a mighty scheme and a mighty purpose and that His character was infinite in its power, infinite in its designs and therefore we, with our limited faculties, our childish natures,—infanta cry- 'ing for the light—could learn from that by faith and trust we found the meaning of the wondrous words of Christ "The poor in heart shall see God." Mr. Holland briefly thanked Mr. Cameron for his address and the meeting concluded after lasting an hour and a half and being very inspiring and successful in every way.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 16, 1909
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 16, 1909
Cairo-street Chapel.

There were good congregations at Cairo-street chapel on Sunday when harvest thanksgiving services were held. The decorations, although not on a lavish scale, were very tasteful. The preacher, morning and even- ing, was the Rev. R. S. Redfern, of Leigh. Harvest hymns were sung, and anthems were creditably rendered by the choir, that in the evening being "Sing to the Lord of Harvest." Mr. James Muir was at the organ. The preacher took for his text in the evening "For herein is the saying true, one soweth, and another reapeth. I sent son to reap that whereon ye have not laboured. Others laboured and ye have entered into their labours" St. John iv. 37 33. One of the lessons which the rev, gentleman impressed upon his hearers was that they were sowing for posterity, just as other men had - laboured and the present generation had enterei into their labours. But they had also to bear the weight of the legacy of the past, the indolence, folly and sin. All this legacy brought. with it a solemn responsibility. They bad to sow good seed for the reaping of those who would come after them. They bad also to root up the evil crops that were the fruit of the negligence of the past. It was in consequence of the indifference' of past generations to the education of the children that education was such a burning ques- tion now, and why they felt it necessary to spend so much money on it.

div.head: Bold-street Wesley Guild.
div.p: Bold-street Wesley Guild.

On Monday evening the opening social of the above guild (which took the form of a song social) was held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Schoolroom when about sixty members and friends assembled add spent a very pleasant time together. During the evening Miss Ker- shaw contributed a song entitled " The Flight of Ages" Mr. Bert Spruce following with one of his humerons pieces" 0, the agony," which caused much laughter. The gramophone selections given by Mr E. T. Jones included" Tne Pirates of Penzance." Mr.J. McArthur favoured the cempany with several songs one of which (by special request) he gave in the broad Scoth dialect "My am n folk." Another very interesting feature of the evening WAS the wearing of a badge by each person which represented the title of a song, and prizes were offered for the one who named the largest number of songs correctly, and one for the most ingenious badge. The first prize for the highest number guessed was secured by Miss Hodge, and Mr. F. Light obtained the prize for the most ingenious badge. Light refreshments ware served during the evening after which the time was spent in games and social chat with each other. The Rev. T. Miller kindly distributed the prizes. The syllabus of the Guild for the winter session is very interesting and instructive, every meeting being occupied with a good subject.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS
Band of Hope Union's Application Refused.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, Mr. G. Mather presiding. There were also present : Mrs. Collingwood, Mrs. Simpson, Miss Broadbent, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, W. Gill, R. Bolton, J. A. Rushworth, R. Lee, W. C. Brooks, M. IV. Seton, A. Brooks, R. Forshaw, E. b. Bent,J. Billinge, A. Bottomley (clerk), R. W. Peacock (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (superintendent of Cottage Homes).

div.head: NEW BUILDING.
div.p: THE NEW BUILDING.
• A number of tenders for the loan of £6,659 required for the erection of the now infirm block were opened and referred to the Finance Committee. ASSISTANT CLERK'S SALARY.

Miss BROADBENT moved that the salary of Mr. R. W. Peacock, assistant clerk, be increased from £lOO to £125. She said that when they had an officer who had their interests so thoroughly at heart as Mr. Peacock, it was to their advantage to retain him. He had saved the Board expense in many ways, notably in regard to the stationery bill, although they received much more literature than they used to do. Mr. SETON seconded and said Mr. Peacock was well deserving of the advance. Mr. BENT also thought the time had arrived when they should grant an advance to such a good and faith- ful servant. _ _ - -
The increase was unanimously carried, BAND OF HOPE UNION'S APPLICATION REFUSED.

Mr. W. A. BATLEY, of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope and Temperance Union, wrote asking the Board to grant him permission to visit the Padgate School to give a science lecture on" Alcohol and the human body" to the scholarsof ten years and upwards, in accordance with the Board of Education syllabus of lessons on temperance issued in June last. He sug- gested Wednesday, October 27th, as a convenient date. In a circular it was stated that for the past ten years the Union had retained the services of trained certifi- cated teachers with special science qualifications to give illustrated object lessons on alcohol and its effects on the human body. The lessons were strictly in accordance with school requirements and with the clde and they were free from ,such terms as" pledge" " drunkenness," " public-house" and the like. _ _
Mr. BENT moved and Mr. GILL seconded that the letter lie on the table. . _ _ _

Miss BRoADBENT moved and Mrs. Simpson seconded , that the necessary permission for the lecture be given. ' Mr. W. C. BROOKS: I propose that it lie under- neath the table. (Laughter). Miss BRoADBENT said the lecture was very interest- ing and instructive and she thought the children would enjoy it, Mr. MATHER : Wonld you allow any person interested on the other side to give a lecture showing the good that alcohol does? Mr. A. BROOKS: It does none. Mrs. SIMPSON : We c'll see the results in the striets daily. Mrs. rl/4—T.I_INGWOOD : Is the lecturesupported by the Board of Education? Mr. A. BROOKS : It is allowed, at all events. The CHAIRMAN: It is allowed by the Board of Education but very few village schools allow it now. The CLERK quoted the statement from the circular as to the lecture being in accordance with the code and avoiding certain expressions. Mr. BENT said he strongly objected to such docu- ments coming before the Board. Of course they could not really object to that but he did not believe in it at all. If they allowed the lecture to be given it would be bringing certain questions to the minds of the children. They saw the evil of over-indulgence every day but if alcohol did harm it also did good in a great many cases. He felt very strongly on the point and should press his resolution. Mrs. COLLINO"WooD supported Miss Broadbent's proposition on the ground that most of the children knew the effects of drink from their early childhood. The lecture would not in that sense he teaching them things they did not know. Most of the children in the Workhouse were suffering from the evil effects of drink and it was very necessary to train them up to know the evils of it.
Mr. JOLLEY : Is it not equllly necessary to train them to know the advantages of it?

Mr. A. BR,OOKES : There are none. MTS. CULLING WOOD : So far as I know, the only advantage is when it is recommended by doctors. Mr. SETON strongly resented permission being given. If they allowed one lecturer to come they would have to allow others.

Mrs. Stmesos : I think the children ought to be trained in every branch. Mr. SETON : They will get to know soon enough. Mrs. SIMPSON said a great many of the children were in the homes through their parents over-indulging, and it would be a pity not to teach them to have a determination to reist temptation and to know the evil of di ink. Some of the Guardians said alcohol hai good qualities, but it was far better when thera was danger in a thing to leave it entirely alone if they had not strength of will to resist. It was a subject the Board ought to take in hand and consider. It was for the good of the children, and it was the women and children who had to suffer from the evil. Mr. JOLLEY said the eloquent observations of Mrs Simpson pointed to a somewhat different conclusion to that which she had made her address in support of. If it was their duty to teach all these wonderful doctrines, why was it not part of the regular curriculum ? It was not necessary to import an outsid lecturer once a year or once in twa years if the Committee and the Guar- dians did their duty. He ventured to think that on the whole the Committee had done their duty, and that the children were constantly and regularly receiving such moral instruction as was necessary. He did not imagine that the moral tone of the school could Le very greatly assisted by the introduction of .a man who was preach- ing a particular propaganda .which certainly did not commend itself to the majority of. the Guardians. Mr. FOTISHAW : The objection. I have to it is that it is called science. It is a one-sided sort of science and it is a travesty of the word "science" to call them scientific lectures. On a vote being taken it was decided by 9 votes to 5 that the letter lie on the table. The following voted in support of the lecture being given :-111 iss Broadbent, Miss Collingwood, Mrs. Simpson, Mr. Billinge and Mr. A. Brooks. The CHAIRMAN did not vote and the other members supported the proposition that the letter lie on the table.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

WIDNES YOUTH'S DEATH. Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, conducted an inquiry at' Widnes Police Station, on Monday, touching the death of Harry Manifold, who resided with his sister at 5, Joseph-street, Widnes. He was employed as a milk carter at the Runcorn and Widnes Co-operative Stores. On Saturday the 2nd, he went to his work apparently in his usual spirits, but came home and complained of pains in the stomach. He complained that be had over- lifted himself on Saturday at his work. He afterwards went to Dr. Lindsay and was treated, and on the 7th he died at twelve o'clock. Drs. Lindsay and Edwards made a post-mortem, and said that in their opinion death was caused by the inflammation from the appendix. —The jury retired, and aftera lengthy absencefreturned a verdict that "Death was due to acute septic peritonitis caused by appendicitis, probably accelerated by a strain at his work."

RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. The fortnightly meeting of the above Council was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. T. Wright presided, and there were also present :—Messrs. J. Spruce, G. Egerton-Warburton, Admiral Jones-Parry, E. Britch, S. Woodward, A. H. Talbot, P. Booth, NV. M. Morris, H. Mynekyme, J. Hallows, P. Collins, J. Broome, T. Bretberton, G. Pilling, T. Antwis, J. Whitlow, H. Mawdsley, J. H. Davies, J. W. Weir, R. Nixon, G. F. Ashton (clerk), NV. C. Hough (assistant clerk), W. Diggle and J. Swinton (surveyors), J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances.)

div.head: WESTON PAROCHIAL COil ITTE E.
div.p: WESTON PAROCHIAL COil ITTE E.

At a special meeting of this cn-inr-niitee; Archdeacon Wood presiding, it was resolved that the water closet system be adopted for all property in the township, where there is sufficient water supply; that Mr. T. J. Jones be appointed Council's surveyor, to prepare plans and specifications for the laying of new sewers behind Clarkes-terrace, Beaconhill-view, Massey-view, Mather's-lane, and that tenders be obtained for the work.

div.head: WIDNE3 TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WIDNE3 TOWN COUNCIL.

It was reported at Tuesday's meeting- of the Widnes Town Council that negotiations were proceeding between the Gas and Water Committee and a private firm for the supply of electricity for lighting and power purppses in Widnes. The firm are connected with the Salt Union, and it is proposed to erect a large gener- ating station at Weston Point, near Runcorn, from whence the current would be transmitted at high tension across the Manchester Ship Canal and the Mersey to Widnes, where it would be transferred for lighting and power. The negotiations are not vet concluded, and, in the meantime; instructions have been given to the Council's engineer to prepare a municipal scheme at an estimated cost of £4,100. _

Councillor W. B. Clarke said that pressure had been brought upon the Council by the Board of Trade to take some steps or relinquish their standing under the provisional order they had obtained. It would be for the Gas Committee to decide whether the terms which would be submitted were to be accepted, or v; hether they were to continue holding the power under the order by erecting a Corporation electrical works. Councillor G. Davies expressed the opinion that not one member who considered the scheme but was aware that the Corporation would lose by it if they decided to generate the new luminant themselves. The recommendations of the committee to continue negotiations and also to prepare a municipal scheme were confirmed.

The Park and Cerneaary Committee submitted a scheme for the provision of bowling greens, cricket patches, and tennis courts in Victoria Park, at a total cost of £1,260. The greens will admit thirty players trundling simultaneously, and a pavilion, which can also be used as a shelter by the visitors to the park, will also be erected. A suggestion of providing swings and gymnastic equipment bad been dropped because it had been found on inquiry that St. Helens Corporation were discontinuing the experiment owing to the danger which such erections involved to children.

div.head: MAYORALTY.
div.p: THE MAYORALTY.

At a meeting following the Town Council, the Mayor (Councillor T. Smith) intimated, in reply to a deputa- tion which had waited upon h-im a week previously, that he would be pleased to accept the office for a second year. The decision was received with unquali- fied satisfaction. ENTHUSIASTIC BUDGET MEETING AT WIDNES . A huge mass meeting in support of the people's Budget was held in the Drill Hall, Widnes, on Monday evening. The spacious hall was well packed, and amongst the principals on the platform were Mr. Allan H. Bright, chairman Liberal Federal Council, and Mr. Max Muspratt. Mr. James B. Aitken, of Penketh, pre- sided. Mr. Muspratt, who was heartily cheered on rising, could not get a hearing for a minute or two owing to the welcome. He moved the following resolu- tion : —" That this meeting records its entire agreement with the proposals of the Budget (hear, hear), believing that without increasing the cost of the necessaries of life or hampering industry, they will secure for this and future years the money needed for the navy and for social organisatioa, will vindicate Free Trade, will relieve local burdens, and will promote land reform; that this meeting further pledges itself to support the Government in carrying the Budget into law, and in guarding the constitutional rights of the House of Commons." (Cheers.) Mr. Rigby Swift had said that the Liberal Government had done nothing. He (the speaker) only wanted to remind them of the Patent Law, the wiping off of forty millions of debt, which had placed finance on a sound foundation; the scandal of allowing school children to go from home without a bri akfast, and last, but not least, the old-age pensions. To stand before a Widnes audience and say that they had done nothing was insulting the intelligence of Widnes people. Liberalism did not believe in sweeping away all the old customs and the machinery of the past; but it did believe that there were a large number of social sores that had got to be remedied, and the policy of modern Liberalism was remedy and not revolution. (Cheers). Mr. Allan Bright stated that before long he hoped to support the candidature of Mr. Muspratt in that division. He reviewed the details of the, Budget,which the Tories described as confiscation and robbery. On the other hand, the Liberals struck a high note, which betokened a gr,sat era of advancement for this country. The alternative of the Budget was Tariff Reform which, if boiled down, meant taxation of the food of the people and the taxation of raw materials. The mangling of good measures that went on in the Upper House could not last much longer. (Applause.) Mr. Horace Crawford supported the resolution which was carried amidst tremendous cheering.—A vat?, of thanks to the chairman concluded one of the most enthusiastic meet- ings ever held in Widnes.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the above Board was held at the Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. T. Baxter presided and there were also present Messrs. J. Spruce, G. Egerton Warburton, Admiral Jones Parry, C. Britch, S. Woodward, T. Wright, A. H. Talbot, P. Booth, C. E. Linaker, sear., W. M. Morris, C. E. Linaker, junr. H. Mynekyme, J. Hallows, P. Collins, J. THE NEW MASTER. The Local Government Board wrote appr wing the appointment of Mr. and Mrs. Parsons as master and matron of the Workhouse at salaries of £7O and £3O per annum respectively. REPORTS _ . _ .

Mr. Britch, one of the agates who visited the Pantasaph Orphanage Home on September 30th, said they were perfectly satisfied that the home was con- ducted on the right lines. He thought the educational part of the institntion was up-to-date and evers thing that could be desired. He was sorry to say that the eight children sent to the home were not yet fit to be sent out. He moved the adoption of the report. Mr. Collins, another delegate, said be was very pleased with the method in which the children were brought up. The report was adopted. The report from the delegates who visited the North- Western Poor Law Conference held at Blackpool on the 24th and 25th September was also read. Mr. Spruce, one of the delegates, said the conference was highly interesting, and the discussions at times were of a heated character. From the discussion he was of the opinion that their relieving officers knew their work of relieving excellently. Mr. Linaker, jun., another delegate, seconded, and said that their Guardians had had a great deal of experience with regard to giving out-door relief, and he was convinced that they were working on the right lines.

The report was adopted. A. report was submitted by the late Master (Mr. Rollinson) with regard to inmate labour in the house in the course of which he said it would be advisable to get an all-round man to do the plumbing, painting and looking to the boilers, after %hat Mr. Morris said at the last meeting with regard to an explosion at the Toxteth Workhouse where two inmates employed were killed. That was, however, impossiple at Dutton as the boilers were kept at a very low pressure. • Mr. Spruce said the 'Visiting Committee had con- sidered Mr. Rollinson's suggestion as to employing an all-round man and it was resolved that they should advertise for a single man who had a knowledge of plumbing, fitting, and stoking of the boilers. He had not to be less than 23 years of age and to state salary required. It was decided by the Council to do this.

div.head: Fire in Winwick-road.
div.p: Fire in Winwick-road.

Shortly before three o'clock on Saturday afternoon the Warrington Fire Brigade was summoned to a fire which had broken out in a shed adjoining the Horse and Jockey, Winwick-road. The shed is sub-let by the landlord, Mr. J. A. Rushworth, to Councillor Cunnington. The brigade arrived on the scene in exactly seven minutes from the giving of the alarm, under the direction of the deputy-superintendent, Mr. Mr. Frank Turner. The flames had, however, got such a firm hold that the shed was destroyed, as well as its contents, _namely, two traps and a quantity of hay and straw. The damage, which is estimated at about £lOO, is not covered by insurance. The fire is supposed to have been caused by boys setting off fire- works in the vicinity of the building.

ANCIENT ORDER OF FORESTERS. Interesting Local History. For well over seventy years the Ancient Order of Foresters has pursued its good work in Warrington and it is at present one of the most prosperous and active of the many friendly societies. In ,order to trace the history of the Order in our good old town, we shall have to go back to the early days of the present century. The Ancient Order of Foresters was the outcome of a disruption of the Royal Foresters who were in existence in the year 1745 of which Order the oldest Court in the Warrington District was a branch Number 138. .'he disruption took place in the year 1833 when the above Court along with Man- chester and several other districts seceeded,and formed the Ancient Order of Foresters. It is interesting to note that the parent Order still survives as an organisation, its Supreme Court meeting annually. Its 22 Courts, 9of which have been opened since 1834, are chiefly in the North-West corner of Yorkshire, while the Ancient Order is now spread all over the Globe. In 1855, when the first Directory of the Order was published, there were 392 Courts and only 24 districts, among them being .Knutsford and Warrington with 8 Courts. As to the records of these ancient times and what was done we are at a loss to know, as books were not kept and the Govern- ment of last century had no confidence in men who met in secret, as they often laid heavy hands upon them, particularly in the years following the French Revolution. We find that in the year 1841 the 7th High Court of the Order' was held in Warrington, at which 344 delegates were present, when the late Bro. Richard Croughton was High Chief Ranger. EMPIRE SKATING RINK.
SUCCESSFUL OPENING.

Roller skating has come to the fore in Warrington with remarkable rapidity, and expectations are that it has come to stay. Devotees of the fascinating pastime are admirably catered for and Tuesday saw the open- ing of the handsome new Empire Skating Rink in Winmarleigh-street. The enterprise, a purely local one, is on an ambitious scale, the rink being one of largest in the kingdom. The building is spacious, lofty, and well lighted, and its equipment is on the most modern lines. The maple floor measures 1551 t. by 85ft. and in addition there is the rinkette—or "mugs' alley" as it is dubbed-118ft. by 16ft., where learners are initiated into the "art. Every provision is made for the convenience and enjoyment of patrons, and a well-appointed lounge, 701 t. by 201 t., with refreshment bar, adjoins the rink.. Tea rooms, cloak rooms and lavatories for ladies and gentlemen, and a gentlemen's smoke-room are also provided. The decoration of the building is in the best of taste, a striking feature being the introduction on the walls of the beautiful hand-paintings by Mr. F. J. Dell. Praise is due to the architects (Messrs. Wright, Garnett and Wright), and the following contractors for the admirable way in which the work has been carried out :—Builder, Mr. D. Cooper; steel work, Messrs. Forshaw and Son ; heating, Messrs. S. and F. Acton; lighting, Mr. 11. Bibby ; floor dressing, Mr.J.Gregory of Nelson; decorating, Mr. F.J.Dell ; and painting, Mr.Winstanley.
