div.head: OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: THE OPENING CEREMONY.

Lady GREENALL opened the rink on Tuesday after- noon in the presence of a large gathering. The build- ing wad gay with vane-coloured garlands and hapging baskets of flowers and presented a charming picture.. Amongst those present were the directors' Messrs. S. J. Beaman (chairman), J. T. Barton, W. Chalmers, W. Boothroyd and J. Finlayson, together with Mr. A. H. Clive (secretary) and a number of shareholders. Mr. A. H. CROSPIELD, M.P., wrote from Biarritz expressing regret that Mrs. Crosfleld and himsslf would be unable to attend the opening ceremony as they would not be back from the Continent until the even- ing. "I trust," added Mr. Crosfleld, "that the opening ceremony will be a great success, as it is sure to be, while you are so fortunate as to have secured the presence of Lady Greenall. I again thank you for kindly inviting us." - -

Mr: BEAMAYi extended a cordial welcome to the assembly. He regretted that the building had not quite been completed but they had been greatly pressed for time, and the directors expected that in a week or two everything would be in proper working order. The conditions of roller skating to-day were far different to what they were a generation ago, and he thought the public of Warrington would find, if they chose to honour the Empire rink with their presence, that they could enjoy the pastime and at the same time benefit to a large extent by participating in a healthy exercise. All those connected with the rink were local people, young and enthusiastic, and they could be depended upon to conduct their business on the best possible lines. (Applause.). ROMANCE OF A PRINCESS.

Princess Hohenberg, the morganatic wife of the Archduke Francis Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, has been raised by the Emperor Francis Joseph to the rank of Duchess with the title of Highness. At the time of his wedding the Archduke took an oath that he would not declare the Princess, an Empress or Queen, or his children as members of the Imperial House ; and this fresh honour from the Emperor is naturally raising much speculation in Vienna. 4"

Intsit PASTURE ARES.—Tho area in pasture in Ireland has increased by 59,811 acres over that of 1908. figures which bring into special notice the startling fact that in a country of 201 million acres in extent, con- siderably more than half, or, to be absolutely correct, 12,566,203 acres, is in pasture, and the employment given on that vast area is comparatively infinitesimal. It was soundly hoped, says "Avena," in "Farm and Home," when the Land Act of 1903 was passed, that has made such a large number of farmers owners of their holdings, that tillage would increase, and the country benefited by more employment being given, and emigra- tion of the youth of both sexes gradually stopped. These hopes have been disappointed, the decrease in all crops in Ireland in 1909 having amounted to no less than 25,479 acres, showing that ownership of the land, instead of developing a taste for tilling the soil, has,on the very contrary, lessened it to a very serious extent.

div.p: FWARRINGTON $ CHAPTERS. > THE MAN MAN WITH THE HOE.

We wrote in this column not long ago a brief account of Jean Francois Millet and his "Angelus." Those who found interest in the story therein told may appreciate the glimpse we are able to give of another of his less-known though much-debated pictures "The Man with the Hoe." _ _

We need not repeat Millet's life-history save to recall the days when after many disappointments he went back to the soil and lived the life of a peasant. It was while toiling at the growing of vegetables on his little farm that he painted the pictures which have made him famous for ever.

Small wonder that his paintings reflect the hard And monotoTmg life of the peasantry and small wonder that sadness seems to brood over them. Millet was .but giving expression to the sadness of his own life. With the " Angelus " on the easel he was painting sign boards and growing cabbages to eke out a scanty living. He had 'been in the large world of the cities and offered his best work only to be bitterly disappointed and had returned a bereaved and a saddened widower to live the life of an obscure peasant. As such he lived the remainder of his days and as such he died, but in his closing years .he painted the small pictures which have ensured him enduring fame. Did Millet dream that such would be the case when he worked at them? We do not think so. He allowed his heart to speak, that was all. He had seen life at its hardest and there surged within a passion of sym- pathy for the toilers and sufferers of the field.

The picture we reproduce has been the most criticized of his works. " The Gleaners" and" The Angelus" are field scenes but the figures are picturesque and attractive. It is not so with " The Man with the

Hoe." Critics attacked it severely as repulsive, socialistic and insulting. But while the artists were railing, the common people were acclaiming it, without_ knowing why, a work of genius. It represents labour in its sternest,cruellest form. This man has used his limbs to the neglect of his mind and is fastened to the clods of the field. His limbs are racked, he has grown to his hoe until it seems to be part of his body ; he is at the level of the beast that drags his plough. That such a figure should jar upon sensitive minds was inevitable. The hollow eyes, low forehead and senseless gaze haunted them and they vented wrath upon the artist and wrote bitter things. But Millet was undisturbed. His picture was a mute appeal for the downtrodden and those out of whom social conditions were crushing heart and life, and he calmly waited until its meaning should become clear. It was not an appeal to the eye, but to the heart. In the noble letter, to Sensier he wrote: " Some tell me that I deny the charms of the country. I find much more than charms. I find infinite glories. I see as well as they do the little flowers of which Christ said that Solomon in all his glory was•not arrayed like one of these. I see the halos of dandelions, and the sun which spreads out beyond the world its glory in the clouds. But I see as well, in the plain, the steaming horses at work; and, in a rocky place, a man all worn out, who han ' ! you have heard since morn- ing, and who tries to straighten himself a moment and breathe. The drama is sur- rounded by beauty." Millet was conscious of the beauty of the world, but he was conscious of the world's tragedies, and in his own way pleaded for the sufferers. Condemned by the critics, his pictures spoke so strongly to the heart as to be soon recognized as masterpieces. The painter went to an early grave crushed in the battle of life, but his pictures live to make their mute appeal, and in years to ' come when we have meted out 'social justice and toilers receive their due, the world will treasure them as ranking among the educa- tors of the race. A. M.

div.head: TH THE HOE.
div.p: TH THE HOE.
"THE MAN W

The rift of dawn, the reddening of the rose ? Through- this dread shape the suffering ages look; Time's tragedy is in that aching stoop ; Through this dread shape humanity, betrayed, Plundered, profaned, and disinherited, Cries protest to the Judges of the World, A protest that is also prophesy, 0, masters, lords, and rulers in all lands, Is this the handiwork you give to God, This monstrous thing distorted and soul-quenched? How will you ever straighten up this shape; Touch it again with immortality; Give back the upward looking and the light; Rebuild in it the music and the dream ;- Make right the immemorial infamies, ' Perfidious wrongs, irremediable woes? 0 masters, lords and rulers in all lands, How will the Future reckon with this man? How answer his brute question in that hour When whirlwinds of rebellion shake the world ? How,will it be with kingdoms and with kings— With those who shaped him to the thing he is— When this dumb Terror shall reply to God, After the silence of the centuries ?
tW

Bowed by the weight of centuries, he leans Upon his hoe and gazes on the ground, The emptiness of ages in his face, And on his back the burden of the world. Who made him dead to rapture and despair, A. thing that grieves not and that never hopes, Stolid and stunned, a brother to the ox? Who loosened and let down this brutal jaw? Whose was the hand that slanted back this brow? Whose breath blew out the light within this brain? Is this the Thing the Lord God made and gave To have dominion over sea and land; To trace the stars and search the heavens for powers; To feel the passion of Eternity? Is this the Dream He dreamed who shaped the suns And pillared the blue firmament with light? Down all the stretch of Hell to its last gulf There is no shape more terrible than this— More tongued with censure of the world's blind greed More filled with signs and potents for the soul— More fraught with menace to the universe. What gulfs between him and the seraphim! Slave of the wheel of labour, what to him - Are Plato and the swing of Pleiades? What the long reaches of the peaks of song,

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.

SALE. V. STOCKTON HEATH.—These teams tried con- clusions at Sale on Saturday. The visitors attacked at the outset, and Banks opened the score with a clever back-handed shot. Jessop equalized with a fine effort, and Thornby increased Sale's score from a melee. Jessop scored again very smartly, and Battersby added another._ Baiteraby scored again from a corner, and Thornby scored from a penalty bully against R. Pier- point, who had the misfortune to drop his stick. Sale led at half-time by 6--1. On resuming, Battersby scored from a corner ; Jessop ran through from the half-way line, and Battersby and Barnes each scored. Result: Sale, 10 goals; Stockton Heath, one goal.

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.

The political barometer changes from hour to hour. No one can more confidently prophesy an early General Election now than it was possible to do a few weeks 'ago. The visit of the Prime Minister to the King, in spite of attempts to disassociate it from the Budget, has, without a doubt, been con- nected with proposals for an arrangement by which conflict between the Commons and the Lords 111,3 r be averted. Cabinet ministers are very definite and very bold in their declarations that there are to be no more concessions, but that the Lords will either have to take the Budget or leave it as it is presented to them by the House of Commons. It is neither wise nor safe for Mr. George and Mr. Churchill to make these statements. They sound too much like whistling to frighten away the ghosts. Moreover, it will not be Winston Churchill and Lloyd-George who will have the final word in this question. The Prime Minister will have to decide whether he will resist the interference of the Peers and force an issue, or whether once more the difference shall be settled by a, compromise which gives away the heart of the Bill and leaves the House of Lords in a stronger position.

div.head: AN INEVITABLE FIGHT.
div.p: AN INEVITABLE FIGHT.

The settlement of the Question of the right of the Peers or the People to decide on matters of government cannot be indefinitely postponed. Nothing has occurred since 1884 which would 'provide a better battleground for a fight against the Peers than this Budget; for the protests of the Dukes have. made it a measure, in popular opinion, of a far more revolutionary character than it really is. If the Prime Minister ha received suggestions from the King in favour of some compromise which would satisfy the Lords, and if such a compromise is accepted, then the Liberal Party might as well fold up its tents and steal away from the political arena as swiftly as possible. THE LONDON BYE-ELECTION.

The death of Dr. Cooper, M.P. for Bermondsey, creates a vacancy which will lead to a very interesting bye-election. The late member was a Liberal of a very inde- pendent and somewhat eccentric type. His contempt for the official Liberal was never exceeded by that of the most rabid Socialist. He held his constituency in his own grip. He was the Liberal Association, the registra- tion agent, and M.P. all in himself. He had the most perfect organisation in London, and he did all the work himself with the assist- ance of his daughter. He used to send to the local papers long reports of speeches he had made to the Liberal A spciation, the said speeches having been written out and delivered by himself.

div.head: LABOUR CONSTITUENCY.
div.p: A LABOUR CONSTITUENCY.

His death finds the Liberals in a difficult situation. They have no organisation, and there is no Liberal Party in the constitu- ency. The Labour Party is stronger in Bermondsey than in any other London borough. At the last municipal election they put up nine candidates and returned them all. Since then they have won seats at bye- elections. They have one of the seats for the London County Council. It has been well understood for some time that when Dr. Cooper retired the Labour Party would contest for the Parliamentary repres6nta- tion. With their position in the borough it would be impossible for them to forego their claim. A SPLENDID CANDIDATE.

Fortunately the Labour Party have a candidate of ,exceptional suitability. For the last fourteen years a Quaker doctor has been working among the poor people of this miser- able quarter of London. He has been the leader of the Progressives on the Council, and is now the L.C.C. representative. His nature and his experiences have made him a Socialist, and he is now the chairman of the local I.L.P. He is the man who will carry the Labour flag in the coming contest, and his ability, his character, his record, his popularity ought to make him an acceptable candidate for every section of progressive thought. THE FALLING WAGES.

Last Saturday all the daily papers made a great display of the Board of Trade figures about changes in the rate of wages. Their facts arc somewhat belated, as all this infor- mation was available months ago, and I made it part of my case against the imposi- tion of the tea duty some weeks since. But some of the Tariff Reform journals use the fact that wages are going down to decry our Free Trade policy. This is really not fair argument. The same thing is going on in both Germany and the United States at present, and the cause is not in the fiscal policy of any of these countries, but is in conditions far more deeply rooted than a system of import duties. Wages are going down, it is true, but all the while profits from trade are going up, and that is surely not an evidence of the decline of British trade. To assign wages reductions to free imports is to connect two things which have little or no relation to each other. THE OSBORNE CASE.

The law courts will shortly re-open after the vacation, and soon after it is expected that the decision in the Osborne case will be given by the House of Lords. This case, it may be remembered, raises the question of the legality of Trade 'Union levies for Parlia- mentary representation. If the decision is adverse to the Trade Unions it will cause a good deal of inconvenience, coming, as it will, possibly, on the very eve of a General Election. The Labour Party has consider- able funds in hand, and these, it is surmised, will not be affected by an 'adverse decision. The Trade Unions will have to get over the difficulty by making the contributions to their Parliamentary Funds voluntary instead of compulsory. Some of them have done that already, and the response, I understand, is quite encouraging. THE MINERS' CANDIDATES.

The :Miners' Conference last week con- firmed their previous decision to join the Labour Party, and to run their candidates at the next election on the Labour Party ticket. They have paid their fees to the Labour Party, and also their first year's subscrip- tion to the , Parliamentary Fund. With the adhesion of the miners, the Labour Party now practically embraces the whole of the Trade Unions of the country. It is less than ten years since the Labour Party was formed, and few persons would have been so daring then as to prophecy that in ten. years the Labour Party would have a mem- bership of nearly two millions, and have in Parliament 48 members run by affiliated Trade Unions. It is a wonderful achieve- ment, the greatest, I think, in modern demo- cratic history. THE INSURANCE AGENTS.
Every member of Parliament— -has. been overwhelmed lately with letters from insur- ance agents about a Bill which is now before

Parliament. The Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress has been blocking this Bill in accordance with instruc- tions from the Trade Union Congress. On a motion from the Insurance Agents them- selves, the Congress last year passed a resolution instructing the Parliamentary Committee to take steps in regard to alleged gambling in human lives. This the Com- mittee did, and the result was the speech of Mr. Shackleton at the recent congress, and the resolution for the appointment of a Royal Commission. This speech and action have brought strong remonstrances from the insurance agents, but they ought to remem- ber that the action of the Congress was taken on the initiative of their own Union.

.Negotiations have been going on, and a satisfactory settlement will probably be arranged. The insurance agents need not alarm themselves. Neither the Trade Union Congress nor the Labour Party has any desire to injure them ; but on the contrary as an affiliated body, the insurance agents are entitled.to and will receive consideration and support from the Labour Party in every thing which is reasonable and just. So far as I know the Labour Party will give a unanimous vote for the Second Reading of the Bill. The question of the appointment of a Royal Commission is one which the President of the Board of Trade must settle, and in coming to a conclusion he will pro- bably be guided by the opinion of the Registrar of Friendly Societies.

This League is now entering upon its third season, and there are more Clubs participating in the Tourna- ment than ever before. This in itself speaks well for the interest taken in the matches which are played under the auspices of this League, and all the Clubs affiliated are preparing themselves and enrolling new players in the hope of proving victorious. The matches are played on Thursday evenings throughout the winter and no doubt will attract a large amount of attention, not tnly from the participants, but out- siders. The season has very good prospects in view, and it will only need a continuance of that entkusiasm which ligs marked past semons to assure a record measure of success. div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

King Charles' Pension.—After th 3 investigation of various claims, it has been decided that Miss Mary Elizabeth Withington is entitled, if living, to If the pension given by King Charles 11 to the farmer Richard Pederel, in gratitude for hiding him in the foliage of an oak tree after the battle of Worcester in 1651. For seven generations the pension of £lOO a year was paid without interruption, and in 1859 it was shared between James Withington and Robert MacLaren. The latter is still living, but Withington went abroad in 1860, and has not been heard of since. Many claims have been put forward to his half of the pension, but it has been decided that the heir is Miss M. E. Withington, born in Octok.er, 1873, to James and Emma Withington, of 7, Taylor-street, Lacester Although every search has been made for her, she cannot be found. •

Abdul Hamid's Downfall.—The music-hall stage is always open to the hero or heroine of a nine day "wonder," even if it is only the mysterious disappear- ance over a cliff of a lady motorist. But it is not only in this country and in America that this is the case, and it seems that several of the wives of the ex-Sultan of Turkey have appeared on the stage in Vienna, being reduced to the necessity for earning money for their living. Great and complete is the downfall of Abdul Harold. His household has been turned adrift, his effects sold, and his palace at Yildiz Kiosk turned into a shilling admission show place. In one respect there is a resemblance between the ex-Sultan and our own King George IV. of whom Greville said that he never gave away anything, and that when he did his wardrobe represented the accumulations of ftfty years, and realised £15,000. It appears to have been the same with Abdul Hamid, and among the personal effects he left behind at Yildoz Kiosk, were no fewer than 2,000 waistcoats, besides hundreds of boxes of wearing apparel.

Badge Wearers.—There is talk of a coming craze for the wearing of badges and flags. An American city has instituted a League of Politeness the men enrolled wearing a button bearing the letters L.P., intended to signify that the wearer is willing to give up his seat in a public conveyance to a lady, and will on every occasion behave like a gentleman. The scheme has evoked the suggestion that there should be a Women's League, the members of which should wear a T.Y. (Thank you) button. All this savours of machine-made politeness, which is not worth much, but in London the propaganda is being carried further, and a number of the men and women members of "The Round-about Club " have started a" flag "section. The object is to dispense with the formality of an introduction in social ettiquette. You display two tiny silk flags in your buttonhole, and if you meet man or woman similarly decorated you recognise them as if they were already acquaintances. You can, however, decline to talk by wearing the flags turned down which would mean that you are engaged for the present. It is a novel and interesting idea, especially to educated persons depressd with a sense of souial loneliness, but it seems scarcely likely to be taken up by people of modest and retiring dispositions. Old English Fairs.—The Mop Fair, which is held annually at Stratford-on-Avon, on October 12th goes back to very ancient times, and still presents the attrac- tions which the itinerant showmen always have to offer. Another of these ancient fairs was the old Dish Fair at York, held on St. Luke's Day October 18th. This was chiefly for the sale of wooden dishes, ladles, and so on, and an enormous wooden spoon used to be carried round Mickle Gate to attract attention. It is probably that custom which was in ridicule of the commonplace wares sold at the fair and gave rise to the contemptuous use of the wooden spoon in presenting it to the least successful in games and sports. St. Luke's is also called Whip Dog Day, and refers to the quaint offices of dog-whipper and sluggard-rnaker, in church, usually the duty of the sexton. In some places the whip for driving dogs out of church is still preserved, as is also the wand used for waking sleepers during the sermon. This bad a fork at one end for the men, and a foxes brush at the other to arouse lady sleepers more courteously.

narm—ana, above all, I'm not going to lock you up. When I have told you what I want to tell you, you can walk out of this place— a free man."
"Sounds all right," said the man. "Any zonditions "
"One or two," replied Baxendale.. "There are questions I want to ask you—things you must tell me. After that, 11l judge what is best to be done. In the first place—your name?"
John Baxendale knew that if the man gave the name of " Rufus " the matter was settled for all time. He waited in an agdny. "My name isn't a pretty one," replied the man.. "It's Rufus—Rufus__ Cridge.'
John- Baxendale bowed hi 's heal He kyym the worst now, at all events. "How have you lived?" he asked. "You are a young man. What has your life been?"

"The soit of thing that you wouldn't un- derstand," retorted Cridge, with a grim laugh.. "I began badly—and I've gone on worse: I'm not whining _about it, vcu'll un- derstand," he add/A., with some .ferceness. "It's the only life I've known, and there are few of my trade that can work as well as I .do. I was caught to-night because I was taken, by surprise; otherwise you wouldn't have got me,"
"You speak well—almest like a gentle- man," said Baxendale.

"I was carefully brought up," said the man, with a sneer. "At any rate, I MPH:, to school; and what I didn't learn there I 'war taught by—well, never mind who taught me. At any rate, it was a woman." "You've led this sort of lire as long as you can remember?" said Baxendale. "I have. It's the only life I've ?known. I've lived in the under-world. I've mixed with forgers and thieves and others of that kidney from the beginning. Young, you say? Yes, I'm young enough,- but I've eeen the in&11of a prison more than once. That's funny, isn't it? Born on the same day—and looking as like each other as .two peas--and yet you here, cradled in swansdown, and living soft and easy; and me with. a number, and warders to watch me—caged like a beast! It's a- funny world!" "Do you believe in justice?" demanded Baxendale, suddenly. "Answer me!" "Not from men," retorted the other. "Well, you're going to ace an act of jus- tice done to-night," said Baxendak. "While you've been talking, I've been making up my mind about you. There's something in you that calls to me—heart to heart—as no other man could 'call. Come here!"

The man shambled to his feet, and strode across the room towards where John Baxe.,,n- dale stood. And now, indeed, the two faces, side by side, in that silent room, furtively watching each other, were dreadfully alike. Baxendale took the man by the arm, and twisted him round; and so stood with him, side by side, before the mirror. "Look there!" " exclaimed Baxendale. "Did you ever see a likeness like that?" The man shuddered and laughed a little hysterically, and put an arm before his eyes. "I don't half blue it," he muttered. "1 feel as if I was bewitched." He tore away his arm from the other's grasp, and went back to the table, putting the length of it between Baxendale and himself. "Who the deuce are you?" he snarled, like .a frightened dog. "I am your brother," said John Baxen- dale, turning away from him with a shudder. "Brother? You?" The man laughed in a queer fashion, and looked at Baxendale, and at the costly room, and at his own shabby garments. "What are you talking about? Are you one of those Socialist fellows, level- ling everything up or everything down? Is that the sort of brother you mean?" John Baxendale shook his head. "No. I mean a flesh-and-blood brother—born of the same mother. Rufus, you and I are each twenty-five years of aee to-night; and you have lived your life— " "The life of a dog," broke in the other man, bitterly. "While I have lived a life of ease and plenty. To-night we meet for the first time since our babyhood; to-night we stand face to face, with our roads meeting once again." Rufus Cridge stood looking at him with a puzzled expression on his face. He Deemed to be arranging the details of this extra- ordinary business in his mind—turning it over and over. When at last he spoke, it was half to himself.

"That was what he said—years and years ago," he muttered. "But I didn't take any notice of it then; I didn't believe it was any- thing but her ravings. A child lost and mourned for—some old vengeance only half completed! Yes, that was what she said._"_
"Who was it 'said that?" asked Baxendale.

"Mrs. Cridge—my mother," said the man. "She was not your mother at all. She stole you when you were a baby. I've heard the story for the first time to-night. Scarcely an hour ago I heard for .the first time that you had even- had an existence. And now you break into my house—" "Hold hard! Hold hard!" exclaimed the man, with a cunning grin. "Not so much of my house, •if you please. Twin brothers, it seems to me, should share. More than that, there should be a bit over for me, seeing that you've had five-and-twenty years of it, while I've gone On short commons. Your house indeed! It seems almOst to me .as if I'd broken itito my own."
"I have told you that I mean to do justice to you after all these years: I mean to let you understand that I am going to right an old wrong, and make reparation. But it must be done in secret."

"I -don't see there's anything to be secret about," retorted Rufus. "You and me have only got to stand side by side, and anyone will beliOve what we say. It's a rum sort of world, when you come to think about ft. Half-an-hour ago I was cracking a crib, ,on the chance of lifting something, and with the prospect, if I got caught, of landing myself in gaol again. And now I'm standing with my own brother, in my own house, and no one has the right to say anything to me about to-night's work. It's lovely!" He broke off with a short laugh, and helped himself insolently to the spirits on the table. Yet there ras about him still something of the old furtive look—something of the fear that he might by some strange chance return in a moment to what he had been before. He still watched John Baxendale, and still seemed to listen for any sounds in the house. "I am so strong about the necessity for secrecy," said Baxendale, "that I have made up my mind that only on my own conditions shall you enjoy what is yours by right. If you refuse those conditions I turn you out of this place, and leave you to go back to your own life. The likeness I shall declare (even if we are ever brought face to face again) to be an accidental one. Now, what do you ry? " "Lt's hear the conditions," said the man, a little sulkily. "After all, it's a poor way to treat a brother whom you haven't seen for five-and-twenty years. But I suppose you're top dog, and you must do as you Pe." "The thing has been kept secret all this time on account of my father—l should say, our father. It was an old wrong, and the woman, Johanna Cridge, did her best to avenge it. But that wrong must not be dragged out into the light of day now. For five-and-twenty years there has been one Bax- endale—there must be one still, and one only. Do you understand that? " "Not quite; but you can go on," said the man.

"I am so eager to do what is right that I intend to have the whole of my property valued—everything that I possess in the world, down to the last farthing. When that is done, it shall be divided into two equal parts; and one part shall be yours. With that you shall go abroad, to whatever country you select, and shall start there under fresh conditions, and as a rich man."

"You seem pretty anxious to get rid of me," said the man after a moment's pause. "Why can't I live quietly in England?" "Because the.ne is always the danger, now that you know the secret, of others knowing it also," replied Baxendale. "But for such an accident as has happened to-night you would never have known at all, unless the woman you have believed to be your mother —Johanna Cridee—had told you. Doubtless

she meant to tell you some day, for Der own purposes; but it rests with us now—you and T, Rufus—to do the thing decently, and yet save our father's nanfe. I'll deal justly with you, and your fortune will be a large one, but for everyone's sake you must not remain in England now that you know the truth." Rufus Cridge laughed. "It's not a bad notion for me to get out of England," he said; "perhaps I've made it a bit too hot for me—one way and another. Well, there's another twenty-five years before me—and perhaps a bit more added on to that, if I'm careful—and, by heaven! I shall have seen a bit of life. Come, my brother," he added, banteringly, "when do we start this pretty little game of share and share alike?". "Practically at once," replied Baxendale. "I wan to do the square thing—but it muss be done in secret. Now, tell me, have you any ties—anything that binds you to Eng- land?" The man frowned at the table for a moment or two; spoke at last without raising his eyes. "Nothing that I won't be glad to get rid of and be done with—now that I'm a gentleman with money," he said. Of course, there's one or two that may think they've got a claim on me," he added; "but I think you can leave me ,to settle them in my own way. We've got ways of dealing with people in my line of life that are not quite of the kid glove order, you understand. It's a rough-and tumble world with its. I could shew you a thing or two that would surprise you, my gentle brother. You may have heard of it—dreamt of it—talked about it—but I've lired it:"

"Poor wretch !" murmured John flaxen- dale, looking at the shabby forlorn figure before him. ." Almost it See m s as though I should take upon myself some of your burdens— should live, for an hour or two,. at leaet, the life you have lived so long. I would like to understand_ it ; I should pity and sympathise with you the more."

" Why not?" suggested Rufus, thrusting his face towards his brother, and speaking "You've known one ele of life; the other half of you—that's me—has known the other. Come and see it; come and un• dimtand it."

John Baxendale looked at him for "to moment, and hesitated; then, on an impulse he stretched out his hand to the other man • "I will," he said., "Take me to the plact where you've Jived. F.;ihew me the people who have been your friends in poverty. Let me understand how you have existed at all I don't want you- to be afraid of me. Ever if it's too late to feel towards you as a brother might have done, I am your friend." "I'm not afraid of you—and it's very kind of you," retorted Rufus Cridge, ironically. "Only it won't do, you know, for you and your shadow to be seen together. That won't do at all. You'd better let me go first, and you can follow. You can easily find the pine* —it's in London." "I'll come at once," . said Baxendale. eagerly. "There's a man in the house here —my solicitor—and he is going to London by. a very early train. I can go with him." "I've always got my suspicions about solicitors," said Rufus Cridge, shaking his head. "They're no good to anyone—least- ways, they've never been any good to me. Besides, won't he think it funny, your start- ing off early in the morning like that Wouldn't it be better if you came later in the day?" "Yes, of course it would," said John Bax- endale. "Bc.sides, I'm going to lunch with. some people to-morrow—or, rather, to-day," he added, with a glance at the clock-. "Yee, I'll come on later in the day. Give me the address."

" Middleton's Rents, Lambeth," said Rufus Cridge. " Ask for Mrs. Cridge. Every- body knows her down 'there. It's not what you'd call an aristocratic place," he added, with a grin; "but, you re,e, we've got to put up with what we can afford." "I'm going to change all that, Rufus," said Bairendale. heartily. "Yes, I'll bet you are," said Cridge, with a meaning nod. "Now let me get out of this place. I've got a feyv miles to walk before I get on my road to London." "You'll want money—to take you there," suggested Baxendale, going to a desk in the corner of the room and taking out some nacs. "How much shall I give you?" "What you give me will be in gold," said the man, waving the notes aside. "Can't you see me walking into a place and trying to change one of tho§e, and perhaps some officious busybody tracing it to you, or to your bank? Not much—we can talk about notes later."

John Baxendale put back the notes, and gave Rufus Cridge all the money he had in his poehets. In the very act of putting it away in his own pocket, Rufus Cridge crcssed to the fireplace, and stared at a portrait of Evelyn Kaylor standing there; nodded at it, and then turned to 13axendale. "That's a likelv looking girl," he said. "That's the lady who's to be my .wife,"' said Baxen4ale, shortly. "Very nice—very pretty!" Cridge nodded many times over the portrait, and laughed again. "Well, brother, it looks to me as if you'd had all the luck of it, so far. My turn'e coming—eh?" "Yes, your turn's coming now," said John Baxendale. At that moment there was a curious shuff- ling sound of footsteps outside the room: then the handle of the door was turned, and rattled. John Baxendale remembered, with relief, that he had turned the key in the lock. He put his finger on his lips in token of silence to the other man, and then spoke loudly: "Hullo! Who is it?"
"Only me—Felix Goode," replied the voice of the old man. "Can't you let me in for a moment? "

"No—not now," said Baxendale, glancing uneasily at his brother. "I don't want to be disturbed. I'm buss going- through some papers. Is anything the matter?" "No. Only I thought I heard voices, and so came down. Are you alone?" "Of course I'm alone," retorted flaxen- dale. "Why don't you go back to bed?" Really,, my dear John, you're most dis- courteous,, replied the voice of the lawyer, with a note of irritation in it. "And I can't for the life of me see why you can't let me in. I can't sleep, and, apparently, you're in the same boat."

John Baxendale looked helplessly at the other man; and then a sudden idea flashed into his mind. This should be a test. He would, in a sense, ge..4 an expert opinion con- cerning this extraordinary likeness in feature and gesture, and even in voice. He caught Rufus Cridge by the shoulders, and rapidly whispered to him.

" I want to find out if the .likeness between us is as great as we believe. Stand behind that chair—that tall one—fold your arms on the top of it, and rest your chin on them, so that he sees your face only. So!" Baxen- dale rapidly turned the chair, so that it faced towards the door, and yet hid the man that stood behind it save for his face. "Now, I'll open this window, and get behind the curtain. When he comes in, speak to him, and get him to turn round to close the door. Then I'l. change places with you, and you can alip out, and away." 'You're a sportsman, you are!" exclaimed Cridge, in a whisper. "All right, I'm ready."

"Wait a minute, and let you in," John Baxendale called. Then he stepped noise- lessly to the door, and softly turned the key; stole past the other man, and, got behind the curtain that shrouded the window. Scarcely a yard divided him from his brother. "Now call to him," he whispered. Rufus Cridge glanced over his shoulder for a moment, to be certain that Baxendale was out of sight; then, with his face just appear- ing above his folded .arms, ,he called: You can come in." -

The door slowly opened, and Felix Goode came in. He glanced at the man leaning over the back of the great chair, and smiled and nodded. "You've kept me a deuce of a time waiting, John," he said. "Well, now that you are in, you might shut the door," said Rufus Cridge. "Very well—very well," returned the old man, with a laugh. He turned with the slowness of age to- wards the door, and in that moment, when his back was towards Cridge, John Baxendale slipped from behind the curtain, and noise- lessly changed places -with his brother. As he passed him, he whispered for a moment: "I'll be with you to-night." And then tilt)
otner man waelpite, and he etood waiting for the, lawyer. _ _

"Did you speak?" demanded Goode, turn- ing his head swiftly. No," replied :John Baxendale, realising now how completely this man, who had drifted in out .of a world of which Baxendale knew nothing, was like Baxendale himself. The old man sat down, and prosed on and on, talking about nothing of any deep in- terest, and evidently striving to keep himself awake. By-and-bye he slept quietly in his chair, while John Baxendale sat watching him and deciding that, for the present at least, he would not tell the old man of the happenings of that night. In the days to come he vc_as to repent that decision bitterly over and over again. But he did not kniA that then. He only told himself that the lawyer would in all probability be strongly opposed to any scheme which meant the division of the property between Baxendale and his brother. And, after all,. Baxendale's ideas of justice were his own, and concerned himself only. Towards morning the old man awoke, and apologised for having troubled his young host, and went off to his room. In due course he drove away in the dog-cart to the station; and John Baxendale went back, to get through the day as best he-- could until the time came for him to pay a visit to that mys- terious place known as Middleton 's Rents, Lambe th.

As he had promised, he, lunched with Evelyn and her aunt,. and afterwards walked in the woods with Evelyn. But he scarcely knew what he said to her, and he answered her remarks merely it random; for he was thinking of that other man who had gone limping out of the house the night before— that man who walked in the image of John Baxendale, and was destined to play some part in the life and history of John Baxen- dale. It was a curious feeling that Baxendale had: that thought that Of himself he was not complete, and could not, as other men, take his place in the world on the strength of his own personality. He did not like that at all. Late in the afternoon, taking no luggage with him, and saying nothing to anyone, he set off for London. A few people saw him at the station, and knew him; the stationmaster and a porter or two touched their caps as young Mr. John Baxendale took his place in the trttin. But in London no one knew him, and he went out of the great terminus and into the streets, and became a unit among myriads of other units.

With some difficulty he found Middleton's Rent S—a vile slum in the midst of mean and narrow streets. He was looked at curiously; and a constable of whom he asked the way glanved at his questioner for a moment, and murmured a warning. "Best be careful 'ow you go down there, sir," said the man. "They're a tough.- lot there. I'll keep an eye: on the Rents. • If you don't come out again, I'll get a mate, an' 'ave a look for you." John Baxendale found the house, asked for Mrs. Cridge, and was directed up a filthy, common staircase. He kneched en a door, and entered a room; saw an old woman bend- ing.over a fire, despite the' heat of the room, and a couple of men lounging at a window. Turning quickly as he got into the room, ,he came face to face with his brother Rufus.

"Ah ! there you are," he said.j "The' seem suspicious of you outside. There's a constable waiting at the top of the court. He says if .1 don't COM 3 out soon, he and another constable will come down to look for me. Of course, he doesn't und,.if6tand-"

Rufus Cridge was making signs to someone behind. As John Baxendale turned he sud- denly received a crashing blow, that seemed to cause the old woman at the fire, and the two men at the window, and the broken table tr gyrate and dance, and then to come tumblin- all about him. lle tried to cry out; strove to save himself from falling. Then the room was blotted out, and he seemed to sink away and away into some dark depths that had no

ending. - "Now, then, what the deuce are you stand- ing about there for?" demanded Cridge, swiftly. "Get these clothes off. I've got to change with him in a couple of minutes, un- less we want the police down here. Hurry, now!"
Rapidly they stripped the unconscious man, while Rufus Cridge, chuckling to himself, tore off his own clothes, and donned those that belonged to John Baxendale. (To be dontinued.)

div.head: MS FATHER'S SON.
div.p: MS FATHER'S SON.
BY TOM GALLON
Author of " Tatterley," "Dicky Monteith," "Kiddy," "A Rogue in Love," "Fate's Beg- gar Maid," "The Charity Ghost," Ste.

SYNOPSIS OF OPENING CHAPTERS: The guests have separated -after the dinner which celebrates John Baxendale's inheritance of his fortune,. and he has told Evelyn Kaylor, the beautiful girl he is to marry, that he has not a care in the world. Yet there is a strange foreboding of coming ill. He feels practically certain that someone is prowling about the grounds. When the last guest has retired, Felix Goode, the family lawyer, begins the unfolding of the sinister secret which is to alter the whole tenour of John Baxendale's life. I% revenge for a wrong which his father did to a woman name"' Johanna Cridge she had stolen away one of twp sons, leaving the awful message that, just as her life had passed into darkness and evil, so should his. He should be educated, and yet trained to a life of infamy. That brother of John Baxen- dale may now at any time confront him. This story is told him at his father's request, under his crying injunction that it shall be preserved a secret. Baxendale, when on the way to his room, hears a sound in the drawing-room. Entering, and go- ing to one of the windows, he confronts and seizes a burglar, to find himself face to face with a man in his own likeness.

div.head: CHAPTER IL
div.p: CHAPTER IL

John Baxendale's other self—the man who had sprung in so 6trangely out of the dark- ness—proved but a poor opponent. After but a momentary struggle he dropped to his knees, and cried for quarter. _ _ _
1` Look out, you're Choking me! Take your hands away, curse you ! " . _

John Baxendale flung him aside with some- thing of loathing, and turned to the open window. 'Standing there, half in and half out of the room, the better to get a breath of fresh air, and looked back at the man slowly rising to his knees and to his feet. And more than ever he saw himself, in 601110 shabbier, more degraded form, crouching there before him, and as yet wholly uncon- scious of who he was, and what he was, in relation to Baxendale. Baxendale had had a momentary shudder when first he heard the man's voice; there was so little difference be- tween that voice and his own; it was, in fact, almost like a huskier echo of his own tones.
"Who are you? here?" he demanded.
What are you doing

The man got to his feet, and tugged for a moment at his neckcloth -where Baxendale's hands had been. "You can call me what you like," he retorted; "burglar—or thief—or anything else. You can pretty well guess what I came here for. If it comes to that, we're both young men—pretty much of an age, I should fancy. Why in this rotten world should you have the best of everything, and me nothing? Tell me that." "I suppose you wanted to equalise matters a bit, eh?" suggested Baxendale. "That's abditt it," said the other man. "Take me all round, I've been trying to equalise things a little all my life—in a hun- dred different fashions that you wouldn't un- derstand. If I've failed this time—" He had been but watching his opportunity. He made a sudden, crouching rush noiv, with the intention of slipping past Baxendale out into the darkness. He aimed a svtinging blow at the other man as he reached him, but Bax- endale was too quick for him. He caught the man's arm and gripped, it, and flung him back into the room. "No, you don't," said Baxendale, quietly. "I've something to say to you." He stepped into the room as he spoke, and so stood in the full light. The man wavered, with his arm up, as if to protect himself, and looked at John Baxendale with a new interest; then lowered the arm, and touched himself here and there in a vague, faltering way, as though to be sure of something. F_inally, he came quite close to ,John Baxendale, and looked at him as a Man might look at something weird and uncanny. "Heavens!" he whispered.
"Who aro
you? " "That's what I'm going to tell you," re- plied the other, closing the window and fastening it. "I'm not going to hurt you. Come with me—and make no noise."

The other man pullee his shabby clothes about him, and again adjusted his neckcloth. He looked sharply round, as if suspecting a trap, or seeking a way of escape. Baxendale opened the door of the room, and jerked his head as a sign to the other to go out; fol- lowed him closely, and pointed the way to the smoking-room. The man, with glances over his shoulder, went a pace or mo ahead, and so entered that room in which that night his story had been told. Baxendale followed, closed the door, and turned the key in it. He had time now to examine the intruder; had opportunity, with the -remembrance of that story in his mind, to note, line by line, the exact and startling resemblance the man bore to himseilf. In a ghastly fashion, he even saw the man give a little quick turn 'to the corner of his moustache—a trick for which Evelyn had often laughed at him. The man was thinner, and not so well nourished as John Baxendale; and the eyes had a hunted, shifty look, as of one who had lived much by his wits, and had been something of an Ishmael. The man glanced round the well-furnished room, and shrugged his shoulders, as though, in a sense, he contrasted the place with some surroundings of a very different character with which he had been acquainted. Then he glanced at John Baxendale, and once again touched his own face, and looked down at his own body, as though contrasting him- self with the man with whom he had been so strangely brought face to face. Baxendale, watching him, saw him turn swiftly, as some thought assailed him, and look keenly in the mirror; then look with equal keenness at Baxendale himself. _ _
"Strike me dead!—but we might be twins ! " he exclaimed, in a_ sort of _whisper.

"True—we might; he twins," said dOhn Baxendale, steadily. And it seemed then as though for a moment Baxendale had a vision of the young mother in whose arms as babies this man and himself had lain. "There are strange likenesses between men in the world," he added. The man pondered that question stupidly for a moment or two, looking at Baxendale suspiciously, as though he thought his senses might be playing him a trick. Then he seemed to dismiss the idea, with a careless shrug of his shoulders. He glanced at the table where the decanters and glasses were get out.

- "Before you ring for your servants, or send for the police, or whatever you mean to do, you might let me have a drink," he said. "When a man's been tramping miles, as I have, and lying in ditches, and what not; when a man's heard your infernal dogs straining at-their chains with the longing to get at his throat—he's apt to have a dryness. 80, by your leave—" "Help yourself," said John Baxendale. The man poured out a generous quantity, and drank it down; smacked his lips, and nodded. In the very act of setting down the glass he paused, and looked again at his captor; then set down the glass, and laughed. 'Yes—we might be twins, guv'nor, ' he said. "Though, if that was the case, you'd have to have been born twenty-five years ago to-night. They tell me this is my birthday— as if birthdays mattered aaything to !" "I was born twenty-five years ago to- night," said John Baxendale, quietly., 'l've been celebrating my birthday to-night. ' "I saw the lights, and heard the music," said the other, with a nod. "Doesn't it strike you this is rather curious—l mean you and me, as like as two peas, born the same day, standing face to face here, at this dead hour of the night? Rum go, isn't it?"

"There's nothing so very strange about it," said Baxendale, slowly. "I told you just now that I had something to say to you —that's why you're here now. You've no- thin to fear: . I'm not Roil= to do You any

div.head: CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL COLLEGE.
div.p: CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL COLLEGE.
Opposition to the Proposed Extension.

At a meeting of the Cheshire Education Committee at Crowe, on Monday, the Agricultural Committee brought forward a iesolution for extending the Agri- cultural and Horticultural College at Holmes Chapel,nt a cost not exceeding £6,000. It was stated that the college had now been affiliated with the Manchester University, and it was necessary that accommodation should be provided for not less than sixty students, with the requisite staff. Mr. S. Gleave, an agricultural representative, objected to the expenditure of £6,009 on extensions of the college. As representing an agricultural con- stituency, he said that Holmes Chapel could never be made a centre for farmers' sons. They had already spent £14,000 on the premises, and they proposed to spend another £6,000. What would they have to show for it? The premises did not belong to the county. He asked them to defer the question until next March, and make it a test question with the electors. The recommendation of the College Committee was adopted.

div.head: SIR JOHN BRUNNER'S ADVICE,
div.p: SIR JOHN BRUNNER'S ADVICE,
Even-handed Justice to Dukes and Artisans.

Sir John Brunner, M.P., who has represented North- wich for 21 years, took formal leave of the Liberals of his constituency on Saturday. In the course of a speech Sir John said he had been before them as an employer for 36 years, a lover of industrial peace. (Applause.) He had been a lover of international peace, and he hoped his successor would be a fighter for peace. (Applause.) He asked them to 14 their politics be manly, and to carry out the rule which he had always held up before himself, the rule of even-handed justice to all men alike, to the great, to the poor, to the dukes, to the wealthy manufacturer, to the shopkeeper, the artisan—. to all even-banded justice. (Applause.) He asked, too, that they would never he snobs. How did the principles of manliness and fair play apply to the present situation? Did they intend that they would govern through their elected representatives in the House of Commons ?—(" Yes ")—or did they intend that ridiculous institution at the other end of the lobby should govern? He said seriously, bound to every syllable, the Howe of Lords as at present con- stituted was not only the most ridiculous but was the meanest and most mischievous institution in all the country. (Applause). What would they sly in the House of Commons if man after man were to got up and propose amendments to a Bill in order to suit the circumstances of his own particular estate, in order to serve his own pecuniary interests? (Appian .e.) That was the spectacle they bad_had_before_them_in the House of Lords.

The House of Lords was the willing and subservient tool of the Tory Government,. but when the pcople desired to make a great advance m civilisation then the House of Lords was there ready to resist, mutilate and destroy. (Applause).

He eferred to the death of Mr. Charles William Jones, a fl whose unostentatious charity many living to-day "Itd grateful remembrance of, a man %la°, in his day and tifileration, bad done good work and done it quietly, though it was none the less highly valued. TfiE REV. R. W. B. WHITEWAY ON SABBATH
ObSERVANCE,

nig was the suNect of a sermon in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Lynon, cn Suncay evening last The preacher took his text frem Neherciah ii. 15. After speaking of the shameless elireg •rd of the Sabbath among the people of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah and the e,easures be took to remedy the evil Mae preacher Laid he Was afraid th ngs were not much better in our own times. What the National Convention of France could not do in its attempt to destroy the Sabbath as a day of worship he was afraid was being accomplished in more subtle ways, and means, in our own land. In all parts of the country Sunday excur- sion traies were Icing run to an extent that El veers ago would not have been tolerated. Indeed ro Railway Company would lave run them fur the simple reason that they would not have raid experses of coal. I oblic-houses. clubs and soops are open. Golf links and tennis courts are crowded with p'ayers. In the towes 'buses and tramcars are as busy as on any other day of the week, and this entails an enormous amouct of compulsory labour. All this shows the tending of the age. God's holy day is fast beconing a day of business and pleasure. Are we not on the high- road to a Continental Sabbath ? If so, then the outlook for England is dark indeed. Nothing gives a\caore certain evidence of the decay of a nation's greatness and honour than a disrsgird of God's day of rest. 'Remember the Sabbath Day to keep it holy," He said. And you can no more mistake the law of God with impunity now than the old Hebrews could. World to God that the words of Jeremiah could ring in the ears of England to-day, " \That evil thing is this, that ye profane the Sabbath. Did not your fathers thus, and did not God bring evil on the people and on the city ?" He did not hesitate one moment to say that the way a large number of people in Lymm were spending their Sabbaths was dishonouring to God; rod it was certainly not dignifying to themselves. He referred to those who were to be seen every Lord's Day on the golf links and tennis courts. And when they considered that many of them bad been at some time connected with the Christian church, if appeared all the woree. One would have thought thet would have learned to set a better example to tbeiy fami"es and friends. But it nes not so. Observance or God's law ,s the very bed rock of all national morality and prosperity. Edmund Burke the great Commoner said long ago. "A nation that neglects the Sabbath sinks to Barbarism and ruin." Righteousness exalteth a nation and there was no righteousness in golf and tennis playing and gardening on Sroday as I saw many people doing in Lyme. Destroy the Sabbath sea day of worship, and you distroy it eventually as Li" day of rest. you destroy it altogether, and it becomes what you have it on the continent. "Don't mistake me" he concluded "I am not pleading for a Puritan Sabbath. But I confc as that if I had to choose between a Prri` -n Sabbath and a Continental one, I should prefer the former, es being more safe and more in keeping with the law of Heaven. The experience of ell huiran history in the past goes to show that those Sabbaths are the best, the fullest of hope for the nation, and the fullest of blessing for ourselves, that are spent in worship and not in mere recreation, or pleasr-e, or idleness. No man can ever be what he might be, or what he ought to be, or what God wishes him to be, who holds lax views of God's Holy Day, or in any way profanes it. I appeal then to all who can hear me and I would make the same appeal to those who outside the walls of this place 'Remember the 'Sabbath day to keep it holy.' For your erica sake, for the sake of the nationel life and character of England, for the rake of those around you, and the children that are to come efter yor, consider this subject, set your- selves right on this question. See that you lose not your hold on the sanctity of the Sabbath. Observe it yourselves as a day of worship end teach your children to do the same, and the prows() of Gosl's blessing shall not fail you."
THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL. ANNUAL PRIZE-GIVING.

The annual prize-giving at Lymm Grammar School took place on Saturday arternoon, a numerous company being present.—The past year has been one of unusual importance in the history of the school, for it has witnessed changes of greatest significance. These were referred to by the key. G. B. Thurston in his opening speech as chairman. First of all he said, they had to welcome for the first time ladies on their board of government. They had succeeded, after throe long years of corrections, in adopting finally a new scheme for the school. That scheme had very far-reaching con- sequences. It placed them in what he hoped wasva permanent position for many years to come. The ;resent school was constracted to educate perhaps at the most seventy scholars, and for the last three or four yews they had had considerably over a hundred. After a great aeal of pleasant negotiation, the County Council had met the governors' wishes in a very open rad liberal spirit, and they might hope, perhaps before next "Speech Day," to Pad the school increased to double the size of what it was now. The County Council had promised to pay all expenses on a condition —which he need not mention—the governors very quickly acceded to, and they would commence building he hoped, 'I a very short time. . The Rev. C. Great, who some years ago was head- master of a famous school at Keswick, but left to institute a co-educational board school at Harpenden, 1 seer London, distlibuted the prizes and spoke on cc-education, of which hehas made a special school. 1 Mr. Cecil H. S. Wilson, the headmaster, in the dowse I of his 3rd annual report surd the past year had unq.ues- tiorsbly witnessed the highest academic distinctions which the rt.hool had yet at.ained to. It was all the more seisfactory to record those gratifying successes, because they were not so much the result of individual brilliancy, but were rather due to the excellent example of application and hard work set by the senior membrrs of the school. lae chief honours gained" during the year included the following :—Two candi- dates rassed the Northern Universities' Matricula- tion Examination ; four candidates passed the Senior Oxford Local Examination, two of them in honours, and three other candidates passed in four and a half out of five sections ; four candidates out of five pr ed the julior Oxford Local Examination; tbre candidates obtained bank clerk- ships and one a Civil Service clerkshia direct from the r Ihool, and one candidate was awarded a bronze star by the Royal Drawing Society. 0. De Jong and R. Wilks deserved er soh' credit as being. the first candidates to pess the Matz.; mlstion Erammation direct from the school. Special credit was also due to Bertba Goffin and Doris Czookes, who obtained honours in the Senior Local Exe-ninatior, the latter gaining the distinction of being one of .the three youngest candidates in England to obtain honours. The bronze star of the Royal Drawing Society awarded to Kenneth Brookes meant that he was among the first hundred in the United Kingdom out of several thousands of competitors The work of rine other candidates from the school was also especially r )mmended. div.head: LYMM WOMEN LIBERALS
div.p: LYMM WOMEN LIBERALS
Opening Social

Liberalie.n among the women of I.a..nm took a step forward in June Ir et when at a garden party held in Mr.F. H.Smith's grounds a Women's Liberal A ssooiation was formed. About 150 ladies jay:led the Association at its inauguration and on Threse ay evening last,When opening social for the winter session was held in the Congregational schoolroom, the membership was about 190—very gcod sign:. The officials are :—Mre Crossley (president), Mrs. Jones (chairman of the committee), Mrs. Gotobed (secretary), and Mrs. Brookes (try esurer.) Mr. Crossley presided over the social and she was supported on the nlatform by Mr. W. J. Crossley, M.P., Mr. and Mrs. F. Milne, Bliss Smith (Grange-over-Sands) and Mrs. Jones. 1. The procee iings opened with a Liberal song. Mrs. Crossley, who is an exceptiore"y good speaker, said that the gathering made her feel proud that she was the president of the Associatior She was proud that they should show themselves in that guise before her husband, becarce at the garden party held at Ye. Smith's a few months ago he was not able to be present as he was in London. They as a young risociation Fad progressed splendidly in so short a time. They all knew how good it was to band themselves, and to be ready for work. She believed in banding together so that they could inform themselves upon (Afferent sub- jects. They could not possibly know about things rnless they took the trouble to read or listen when somebody came to speak to them. (Applause.) It was not always easy for them to know the rights and w tongs of a question unless they listened to others who had studied it. They as Liberals were very proud of the great achievements of the Liberal Government. notn ithstending what their opponents raid. Of course it was very regrettable that the Liberal Government had spent a long time on measures that were rejected by the House of Lords.—two Education bills and the Licensing Bill. There had bc an a great fuss about the Chinese being left on the rand. Thoee who were there had hid to work out their time of contra et On the 9th November 1905 when the Liberals came in power there were 73,0(9 and in December last 1,800. At the end of January there would be none at all. The Liberals had given self-government to South Africa. There was not a continental nation thet was not foil of astonishment and adreiralion for such a thing as that. Referring to old age pensions granted by the Liberal goverament,she said there were 670,000 people who were at that moment receiving the pensieo. There were some who said that it Was only a re., tint measure—she believed her husband was one or them rid he wanted the age to come down to 65. (Applause). It was only the thin edge of the wedge. Their opponents_ said they were little Englandeh; and did not care for the Army and Navy. They cared as much as their opponents. Their opponents said that None of the money that was being raised world go to the NA% r, whereas £3,00,00 extra were going to the NAN y this year. The" Times"—the great Conservative newspaper—on October 4th praised Mr. Haldane and said that he had brought the regolar army into a higher state of efficiency than it bad been for meny years. There were also Labour Exchanges proposed by the present Government and Insurance- for workmen, which would be contributed to by the mastehe men and the State and then in times of unemployment the worhnen would not be objeets of charity, but would have some- thing to fall back upon. (Applause.) They felt proud that the Liberals had done those things. Concluding she empFesised that the Liberals stood for Free Trade. (Applause). Miss Smith made an extremely piaetical spe, .h and she illustrated her points very forcibly by placing: on the table and comparing with the English, various groceries used in France. She honed they would not think she had come to make a little present, she said as she placed the articles on the tables amidst laughter, or to sell those articles to them. She was going to compare the prices and quantities of our articles to those of France. She maintained that it wor'd be a veif disastrous thing if the Consereatives come into power for they would put taxes upon food and our soap. B9':01:1, cheese and butter would be texed and then they would say it was to make trade better. They as North country folks knew that that was a fallacy and it world not improve trade. She then made her comparisons which were as follows:— stone of flower, England is. 9d.; France 3s. 7cl ; tea, England le. Bcl France, (same quality) 4. 2e ; lump sugar, England, 2id., France 5d.; coffee, (ready roasted), England is. Bd., France, (in the green berry) 2s. 4d.; rice, England 3d, France, 5d.; rago, England, 4d., Fiance 7d.; golden sy ..ap, England, 2id.. France, 5d.; oatmeal 2d., France zie ; flu) spif Engband id., nance g,nger bread nuts, 7d., France, 11d.; currants, Englane, 4d. France, 6.d.; Jam, England, 7d Fiance ICld. ; meshing soap, 3d., France, 4d. Concluding ter list she said that the French list came to 15s. 6d. and the English Bs. 7d. She asked her audience to remain firm to their principles of Free Trade and not let the Proteotionists' insidious whispers catch their oars. if they would just think of what she had told them they would remember what a good thing Free Trade was. (Applause.) At this period Madam Louie Fidler, of Blanchester, rendered Tell me my heart" After this refreshments were partaken of and then Madam Fidler rang "Prima Donna. As tin encore she rendered "Joe an' me." This was followed by a duet by Madam Fidler and Mr. J. H Brazendale (of Manchester and Lymm), entitled "Where are you going to my pretty maid," which evoked considerable amusement and admiration. This ' was Madam Fidler 's first visit to Lymm and her a brilliant soprano voice of extraordinary flexibility and resonance made a great immesion. Miss Wise, of Manchester, was the accompanist. Mr. Crossley said ho noticed they had sung a ye.] encourag:ng song to a Welsh tune. Their march was to a Welsh tune and he thought it would be carried on. It was an excellent Welsh tune and it was sung by a most able man. (Applause). He had been told by wife that he was not to speak dry politics that right. (Laughter). He was entirely in her bends that night,if not &ways. (More Laughter). Continuing he said they had listened to a most entertaining speech on Free Trade He alas not one of those who believed in the grocery bill of 20 years ago.but Miss Smith had given re a it,- 1 living instance of the prices in protected countries compared to 011"1" One knew a good deal about Protectierist countries. They knew something about Germany, and they knew that in Germany they bad to ray lls. duty on corn. They had got free transport on the canals and rivers, and they covld get imported wheat very cheaply from the ports upon those canals and rivers. Now they were urging the Govern- ment of Germany to put .4% tariff on the canals. They said that us, was not enough for them, because they could get it up the canals cheaply. Then they would have to pay more for the corn, which would give them an excellent profit. Referring to the Budget, Mr. Crossley said that the/ bad thought all along that the poor had paid t)o great a share in indirect taxation. That Budget gave them hope that in a few years it world bring in so much money that they would be able at lest to give the people a free breakfast table. Mr. Snowden nede a speech owing to the tea duty of sd. not being taken off. He (Mr. Crossley) thought it was one of the most unfair speeches that Mr. Snowden bad made. The fact was that it was very paiefel to the Government to keep the sd. per lb. upon tea. They would very much like to see it off,but it con id not be done that yea -.Considering the way they were trending in regard to taxation they were hoping that only luxuries such as tobazco, whirky, beer, etc, would be taxed. (Applause). The statement that the Government were determined that the Budget should be law and that there woad be no compromise in the matter was received with loud cheering. Mr. R. H. Gotobed, in proposing a vote of tbarks to Mr. and Mre Crossley, Mrs Smith, and to the ladies, took the opportunity on behalf of the men's Libeiel Association of congratulating the women upon thh successful inaugaration of their Association. He also expressed the hope that they would co-operate together for the strengthening of the I ;bend rause in that district. Mr. J. D. B. Smith seconded and the motion was carried heartily.

Several letters were then read from the G.P.O. Sur- veyor about the closing of the Penketh Post Office at 12 noon on Pink Holidays. In reply to the Clerk, the G.P.O. Office, but this arrangement world not be interfered with. In the circumstances your Council may prbaps ag,...ee to the proposed relief from 1 to 7 on laursdays. With regard to the question of open'ig the Penketh Sub-Post Office for public business on week days at 8 r in. instead of 7.0 a.m., I find that the present arrange- ment must be maintained as the Sub-Postmastir. . is required to be in attendance to hrnd out a 'private bag for a Pm who send for it between 7 a.m. and 8 a.n-

Nation in Arms."

Sir,— With reference to the letter in the "Examiner"of October oth under the heading " A Nation in Arms," I write to say that I do not wish to reply at length to "Labor Omnia Vincit," for the tenets of Socialism are so obviously antagonistic to the real interests of the working man that it is unnecessary to argue the question, but I should like to point cut that it is the rich and the so-called "leisure ' people who would sacrifice themselves in the event of universal training. The working man has everything to gain by the system proposed by the National Service League. His place would be kept open for him; he would have a healthy, interesting holiday with free board and lodgings, and he would have fresh air and whole- some surroundings in the places of crowded town homes.

I would ask your correspondent to read the address of Dr. Arthur Shadwell, , author of " Industrial Efficiency," at the recent Church Congress. He admits he had strong Socialist leanings in his early days, but he denounces Socialism, as represented by the Socialist organisations of to-day, and says that "Socialism is the mortal enemy of Christianity.

-e • To your other correspondent, who puts his entire confidence in the Navy, I would say that most of our Admirals strongly advocate a Home Defence land force as well as that at sea ; and they would be the last to do this if it were not necessary.—Yours etc., ANTI-WAR.

div.head: Provision of a Dock.
div.p: The Provision of a Dock.

Sir,—l am obliged to Mr. Jones, of Liverpool, for his criticism of my letter as the subject is well worth ventilating though I suggest he failed to fully grasp its contents. I think too, it might have occurred to him that if the Ship Canal Co. at one time promised to make a dock, there must have been some weight in such a scheme. And also as to the suggestion of its being a financial failure it is usual for •Someone to predict, that with respect to all projects—and if this class of person were much listened to, very little in the world indeed would be accomplished. As a matter of fact with reference to the financial aspect of the case the evidence is overwhelming to the contrary.

It must be borne in mind too that the Ship Canal is now practically in the hands of the Manchester Corporation. It is therefore their policy to develop Manchester not Warrington. In fact Warrington and Manchester on this matter are rivals and it is therefore for Warrington to develop its own resources, and these resources are certainly in this respect much superior to Manchester's. I have not nor do not suggest that Warrington should at once make a dock. What I did suggest and re-iterate, is that Warrington should at once take the preliminary steps, viz, by acquiring the old river bed and a large quantity of land adjoining. I sug- gested this being done now as already a portion has fallen in the hands of builders and more will follow. I simply named this as a warning to the town as I felt it my duty as a citizen to do so.

With regard to the volume of trade in Warrington, Mr. Jones is very much at sea on this point. I think if he were conversant with the amount of its river and canal trade, which is fast increasing, he would be surprised. As a matter of fact to-day, if it were not for certain hindrances and lack of facilities, the trade could and would be immediately augmented. There are many men in Warrington like myself who state that .the town is not making the best use of her natural advantages, because we realise that given facilities, new industries would be brought and spring into her midst.

What is the Advertising Committee of the Warring- ton Corporatian doing! While Warrington has slept other towns have been wide awake, and induced foreign firms to plant works in their ,midst, and have derived benefits through the wise use of Lloyd-George's Patent Act.—Yours faithfully, .
E. ENGLAND.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADESMEN'S ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADESMEN'S ASSOCIATION.

The Annual General Meeting of the Warrington Tradesmen's Association was held in Messrs. Toft's Assembly Rooms yesterday afternoon, Mr. W. T. Williams, JP., presiding. The report of the executive stated that during the year much steady work had been accomplished. A reduction had at last been made in the price of electricity and judging from the printed report of the electrical engineer the experiment has proved a wise one, as the executive in its petition predicted it would. The executive also asked for a reduction in the price of gas, and it was pleasing to be able to report that the Gas Committee has seen its way to make reduc - Cons in the prices charged for this commodity. Regarding the proposed window display exhibition,the matter was at present in abeyance, but they would see by the report sent out what was in the minds of the executive on this question. The Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster had honoured the association during the year by placing the president for 1909 (Mr. W. T. William 3) on the Commission of the Peace for the borough. The financial statement shewed that the Association is in a highly flourishing condition, the balance in hand amountinz. to .£3O 19s. . _

Mr. W. rr. WILLIAMS in proposing the adoption of this report and statement of accounts referred to the steady progress of the Association, and briefly touched on the several matters which had engaged the attention of the Association during his term °fa:ace as President. There was no doubt that the Association had become a very useful body. It was not endowed with selfish motives but was anxious to serve a good purpose to the town and at the same time safeguard the interests of the local tradesmen. The question of the disposal of shop refuse and the charge made by the Corporation was a sore point with the members, but he was not without hope that even yet they would be able to convince the Corporation of the unfairness to tradesmen of this charge. The Executive had suggested the Association- becom- ing affiliated with the National Chamber of Trade, and this he felt sure the meeting would approv• of. It was a very strory, and influential body, the membership' numbering about 100,000, so that they would see it was a combination which could not be ignored whenever it raised its voice in any direction for the general good of the tradesmen. It had now engaging its attention the telephone system, and what was very important to them as tradesmen, the rating of business premises. Mr. J. CRITCHLEY seconded the resolution which was carried.

It was a happy idea which promoted the inaugura- tion of these concerts a few years ago, and that they have filled the long-felt want was evident from the crowded attendance at the first concert of ths season which was held in Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom on Saturday evening. The committee, with Mr. E. Plinston as secretary, has made admirable arrange- ments for the winter and if Saturday's programme may be taken as a criterion the success of the concerts should again be assured. The:Apollo Quartet Party gave expressive interpretations of " Love me and the world in mine" and "The dear little shamrock," and were rewarded with rounds of applause. Mr. J. W. Willett was heard to advantage in " Roses," " Ailsa mine" and "The Sailor's grave," and Miss Silcock who possesses a sweet voice, sang with pleasing effect "Laugh while you may" and "The. professor's love story." Master Millington, a promising violinist, gave solos very creditably; and Mr. S. Aukland, created great merriment with "I kept on waving my flag"
