BRABAZON EMPLOYMENT SOCIETY. Sale at Grappenhall. The annual sale of the work done by the inmates of the Warrington Union Hospital, in connection with the useful and beneflcient scheme of the Brabazon Employ- ment Society, was held on l'hursday at Grappenhall Hall (by kind permission of Mrs. Frost.) The work consisted mainly of embroidery, tablecloths, rugs and baskets, and certainly reflected great credit upon the workers. The flower stall was in charge of Miss Norton. The general stallholders were the Brabazon ladies, who are as follows :—Mesdames Dutton, Fair- dough, Frost, W. Furness, Hankey, Smith, Misses N. Fairclough, Broadbent, M. Broadbent, Appleton, Nellie Davies, Lister-Kaye. Concerts were arranged by Miss Norton, and interest- ing and varied programmes were submitted. Miss Broadbent in submitting her report said they bad had a satisfactory Brabazon year, though two of their best workers, David Morris and Thomas Ilanran had died since their last sale. However, they had the satisfaction of feeling that their declining years were greatly cheered by the work the society had given them. Hanran had just won a blue star of merit at Lady Meath's annual exhibition of Brabazon work in London hut when she went to tell him about it she found he had died the night before. There was a man called William Morris who, if he did not possess quite all the artistic gifts of his great namesake, certainly possessed his energy and enthusiasm. He was never idle for a moment and a blind boy was in attendance cutting the wool in lengths for his rugs. There was quite a young man condemned to spend the rest of his days in the hospital. He was absolutely deaf and could not read so the embroidery which he did exceeding well was his one amusement. A young woman subject to fits, also destined to end her days in the institution was a beautiful worker. If she were short of materials before the end of the week she almost shook her fist at her. (Laughter). She (Miss Broadbent) fancied many of the inmates imagined that the Brabazon ladies made a good thing out of the Society. One soon learned not to worry about such misapprehensions. Besides it was rather touching of inmates to work so hard if they really thought they (the ladies) got the money. (Laughter.) She was pleased to tell them that the days were over when she woke every morning wondering how on earth to make both ends meet. They could now pay their way, but they wanted to do far more than that, and she could promise them that they would spend wisely any money sympathisers were good enough to give. Already they helped some of the people when they left the hospital. They wanted to do it on a larger scale. They could imagine that it was difficult for a man or woman, after a long illness with no money and with shabby clothes to make a fresh start in life. They also wished to spend more money on sending cases in the early stages of consumption to the sanatorium. They had had so many kind gifts this year that it was impossible to mention them all, but she must allude to the handsome presents of books they had received irom Mr. Darwall. They were indeed acceptable as they had now three libraries, one for the house, one for the ig; hospital and one for the mitses. She would like to mention a new member of the Brabazon ladies.

Mrs. Dutton Fairclough, (who was a great acquisition), also Miss Ethel Appleton full the Misses Lister-Kaye who worked most devotedly at the Hospital Library and took the whole management off her hands. With regard to the finances the totel income amounted to £l4 17s. id., including £27 72. 113 d., proceeds of the sale of work in October last. The largest items of expenditure were £26 2s. Id. for materials and making up work and 211 17s. to men on leaving and to sana- toriums. There was a balance in hand of 13s. 10d. Mrs. Marshall, in declaring the sale open, said that those who had visited the Workhouse 'Anew what sad and sorrowful faces were there. Many of them were there through themselves, others through the faults of others. That Society had brought a flash of light into their live 3 which otherwise would be very dreary. She would like to congratulate them on the blue stars they had won at Lady Meath's exhibition. There were yet the golden stars and golden cross for them to get. They at Coniston had got the golden stars and no doubt it woutd not be long before they had them at Warrington. She had much pleasure in declaring the sale open. (Applause). Mrs. Collingwood, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Marshall said they welcomed her very heartily and especially as she was so intimately connected with the work. (Applause). The Rev. H. V. Pigot (Rector of Grapponhall) seconded.

The motion was heartily carried. Mr. Hickman proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Frost for opening her premises to them that afternoon. That was the first time she had done that kind of thing and she was always willing to help anything good. He would like to pay a compliment to the workers who had done that beautiful work. He was struck with the artistic work that had been done for that sale, and com- paring the work of previous years he thought there had been very great progress made. There was very great credit due to Miss Broadbent and the other ladies who had taught the workers. (Applause). Mr. Bolton in seconding said that Miss Broadbent was hardly away from the place. (Laughter and applause). Mr. J. A. Rushworth supported. The motion was heartily carriel and then the sale proceeded with.

div.head: Gandy—Henshall.
div.p: Gandy—Henshall.

A pretty wedding which aroused considerable local interest took place at Latchford Wesleyan Church on Tuesday, when Mr. Edward Gandy, M. 8., Ch. 8., son of Mr. and Mrs. James Gandy, of Enfield Hall, near Warrington, was married to Miss Mabel Henshall, daughter of the late Mr. R. G. Henshall, and Mrs. Henshall, Fairfield-road, Latchford. The bride and bridegroom are both members of well-known and respected local families, And the bride has made a reputation. in musical circles, her successes in the amateur operas of the Warrington Musical Society being fresh in the minds of the public. A large congregation assembled to witness, the marriage ceremony. The church had been very tastefully decorated with choice flowers by Mrs, John Strange, and presented a very bright and festal appearance. The Rev. John Gunnell was the officiating minister. The hymns "The Voice that breathed o'er Eden" and "0 Perfect Love" were sung. Miss Hartley was at the organ and played the "Bridal March" from " Lobengrin " and. Mendel- ssohn's "Wedding March." The bride, who was given away by her brother, was handsomely attired in a Princess robe of white chiffon taffeta. She wore a tulle veil and wreath of orange blossom and her bouquet was composed of lilies of the valley and white heather. Miss Gertrude Henshall, sister of the bride, was in attendance as brides- maid. She wore a pale blue frock with hat to match and carried a bouquet of pink roses and lilies of the valley. Her ornament was a gold watch bracelet, the gift of the bridegroom. Dr. Eames, of Stoneclough, acted as best man. After the ceremony the bride's mothcr held the reception in the Latchford Wesleyan Sunday School, a large number of guests attending. Later the newly-married couple left for North Wales where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride travelled in a mole face cloth dress trimmed with rose panne velvet, with rose coloured hat and mole squirrel coat. Many handsome presents were received. •

div.head: Hulme—Blackstock.
div.p: Hulme—Blackstock.

There was a pretty wedding at St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, on Tltursday, when Mr. James Herbert &time, of Lovely-lane, Warrington, was married to Miss Jessie Blackstock, daughter of the late Mr. George Blackstock, of Hood-lane, Sankey. The Rev. J. R. Jones, Vicar of Sankey, officiated The bride is an esteemed member of the church choir and great interest was taken in the wedding; a large congregation assembling. The hymns "The voice that breathed o'er Eden" and "Father of life con- fessing" were sung and Miss Emily D. Jeans, who presided at the organ, played Mendelssohn's "Wedding March." The bride was given away by her brother, Mr. J. Pierce Blackstock (London). She looked charming in a dress of ivory silk poplin trimmed with spotted net and Soutache trimming. She wore a Brussels net veil surmounted with a wreath of orange blossom, and carried a shower bouquet of lilies of the valley, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Miss Maud Blackstock (sister of the bride) and Miss Mabel Howarth (niece of the bride). Miss Blackstock wore a white serge Princess robe with hat to match, and her shower bouquet was composed of chrysanthemums and Neopolitan violets. Miss Howarth was attired in white embroidered maslin, threaded with mauve, with large velvet hat to match, and carried a basket of chrysanthemums, Neopolitan violets and lilies of the valley, the gift of the bride- groom. Mr. T. Harvey Ketiyon discharged the duties of best man. The reception was held in the schools, Great Sankey, and later the happy couple left for Blackpool where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was an amethyst cloth costume with large velvet hat trimmed with sable and wings. Many beautiful presents were received, the bride's present to the bridegroom being a gold signet ring, while the bridegroom's gift to the bride was a crown Derby tea service.

div.head: Mr. John White, J.P.
div.p: Mr. John White, J.P.

The will of the late Mr. John White, J.P., of Moore Hall, Moore, who suddenly died on Friday, August 6, has been proved at ;£5,050 gross and £5,401 net. Testator left 50 to his executor, I.lr. H. Seeker. He bequeathed all his real and personal estate upon trust to pay the income to his wife for life, and then 50Gt to his godson, Henry John Seeker; .-E.200 to Henry B. Melville; to the Rev. W. div.head: TORCHLIGHT TATTOO.
div.p: TORCHLIGHT TATTOO.
NOVEL MILITARY DISPLAY AT WARRINGTON.

The roll of the drum, the blare of brass, and the skirl of the bagpipes enlivened the streets of Warrington on Thursday evening and thousands of townspeople gathered to witness the =arch of seven military bands and detachments of Territorials to the Victoria Park where the torchlight tattoo arranged by the 4th Battalion (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment was held. The event was unique for Warrington—in fact when it was first announced most people were somewhat mystified as to what form of entertainment they might expect. Hitherto the 'wOtd •" tattoo" had been chiefly • applied to a • form of personal decoration but ' 'there was a vague notion that it had also some pecutair. Military signific- ance. However, SpeculatiOn was set at rest by the full description of the,function-whiolipilgaied in our columns, showing that the tattoo, in realiti a bugle call which ends the routine of the soldier's day, can on. occasion be made. into, quite .an imposing spectacular affair, with massed bands and' torch bearers. The chief object of holding a grand tattoo in Warrington was to stithulate recruiting in the Territorials. Incidentally it served to maintain the interest of the men iu Territorial duties in the usually- somewhat dull interval between the annual encamp- ment and the winter season,-for the drills incidental to the display have been entered into with fine enthusiasm.

The bands made their way through (tensely thronged thoroughfares to Victoria Park and a large concourse of spectators followed in their wake, with the result that the spacious enclosure was soon well-lined. There was something wierd in the scene. The inky darkness was relieved by a few torches and other illuminants and the long path which cuts across the park was lined with boy scouts and members of the Church Lads' Brigade who had the cheerful task of holding small lamps for the guidance of the visitors. Here and there one caught glimpses of groups of Territorials with torches not yet kindled, waiting in readiness for the signal to begin operations. A grand stand had been erected and here were seated many -piikainent townspeople, including the Mayor and Mayoress. At about eight o'clock the lights on the ground were extinguished and a hush of expectation fell on the crowd. Presently a rocket shot into the air and then a bugle call rang out. Hardly had the sound died away when the familiar strains of "God Bless the Prince of Wales" were heard, and the band of the 4th Pattalion South kancashire Regiment appeared on the scene, followed by about forty. torch bearers. They made a circuit of the field in smart style and took up a position in the centre, the effect being novel and even stirring. Then the band of the 9th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment with attendant torch bearers, seemed to spring up magically from another quarter and went through a similar manceuvre, their marching tune being" The British Grenadiers." And so it was with the remaining bands. The 10th (Scottish) Liverpool played Blue Bonnets over the border " ; the 8/40th Regimental depot band struck up "Here's to the , maiden of bashful fifteen" ; the band of the Army Service Corps next gave " Wait for the Waggon " ; and the sth Battalion South Lancashire h Regiment declared spiritedly " I'm 95." Last all came the pipers of the 10th (Scottish) Liverpool Regiment playing 'Cock o' th' North ", and a mighty cheer went up, for the Scots are great favourites. When all the bands and the 300 torch bearers had mustered in the centre of the enclosure, the massed bands, under the baton of Mr. Richardson, struck up "Long live the King" and the torch bearers went through a series of evolu- tions. The spectacle as the masses of flaring torches passed and re-passed and wound in and out in bewildering array was one of striking brilliance. The evolutions went on while the bands played "May Blossom," " El Capitan " and "Under the Double Eagle," and the pipers added a capital march. Then one by one the bands left the field to make way for the third part of the display. Camp fires were lighted, a bivouac was formed, four maxim guns were placed in position in readiness for emergencies, and the troops reclined as if in slumber. Away iri the distance a lurid glare for a few moments lit up the enemy's camp. A band played "Abide with me" and then all was quiet and dark. Very soon, however, one of the sentries Wil9 heard challenging a stranger, shots were exchanged, and the whole camp was roused. The rattle of maxims and the bursting of shells gave a realistic impression of warfare but, of course, the enemy was vanquished, England was once more victorious, and the hostilities closed with "Rule Britannia." The massed bands played the National Anthem and the display was at an end. It had all been very vivid, picturesque and exciting by turns, and the crowd went away much impressed. All they had to complain about was the bitterly cold wind which swept across the ground, but they had stuck to their places manfully, and the whole affair was a great success. Bands and torch bearers formed into -procession and returned to town, the Warrington Territorials making the streets resound with lusty cries of "Hello, Bill ! " which they seem to have adopted as a kind of regimental war song. At the Drill Hall meat pies, lemonade and beer were served out and as the exertions of the evening had developed keen appetites the refreshments were attacked with quite as much vigour as the enemy in the sham-fight.

It was a source of regret that Major General Bethune was unable to attend the tattoo,owing to a slight accident which befel, him at the French military manoeuvres. Brigadier Verschoyle was present and other visitors included Colonel Mac Fie, of the Liverpool Scottish. The local officers on parade were :—Colonel J. D. Fairclough, Majors B. Fairclough and Appleton, Cap- tains Crosfield, Smith, H. G. Roberts, Williarhson, Layton and Owen; Lieutenants Monks,Eric Fairclough, Whittle, Egerton Fairclough ' • Second Lieutenants Henshall, Adams, Townroe and Skinner ; Captain and Adjutant G. R. Mott; Sergeant-Major Ingram. The Chaplain (Rev. W. Bracecamp) also attended.

The contingent of the Church Lads' Brigade, to the number of about 200, was in charge of Captain Brooks, and GO boy scouts, from Warrington and Stockton Heath—chiefly from' the suburb—were directed by Scout Masters Bairstow, Prince and Starkey.
Great praise is due to Sergeant Major Ingram upon whom most of the work of organization devolved.
The proceeds, after paying expenses, are to be devoted to local charities and regimental institutions.

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.

Warrington A.C. had a nice muster, chiefly novices,for an ordinary run from headquarters over about 61 miles of varied country. Sub-captain It Holbrook and .1. Parsonage acted alternately as pace and whip with the result that the pack were kept nicely together thus helping the young runners who were out for their first cross country run. Under the circumstances the pace was fairly kept up throughout the run until nearing the finish when some of last season'a novices had a dust up over the last furlong with the result that H. Clayton finished four yards in front of C. Smith and S. Hol- brook, R. Whittaker was a yard behind the Bitter pair. F. Mountield was the most prominent of the beginners whilst J. Twiss and G. Nicholson shaped well. After the run a committee meeting was held and a sub-com- mittee appointed to manage the annual dance which has been fixed for Friday, November 12th. To-day's fixture is an ordinary pack run from Bridge Inn at 3.30 prompt. Visitors are cordially invited and anyone intending to become a member should at once communicate with the hon. secretary, W. Price, 78, Allen-street, so as to qualify for coming races.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNITED HARRIERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNITED HARRIERS.

The first ordinary run of the above club took place from the headquarters, Black horse Inn, on Saturday last when a very enjoyable afternoon was spent in a go-as-you-please run across the country for about seven miles. The runners arrived home after a lapse of about 50 minutes. More accommodation has been made at the club-room owing to the large number of members this season, therefore visiting teams will have plenty of room. A word of praise to our Secretary for winning the muster prize in the opening run from Rylands' Recreation Ground. May he have the honour of seeing his club bring the Junior Championship again to War- rington. An ordinary run takes place to-day from headquarters at 3.30 p.m., when three packs will be sent out—slow, medium, fast. Prospective members cordially invited.

div.head: LIBERAL VAN CAMPAIGN.
div.p: LIBERAL VAN CAMPAIGN.
Opening Meetings this Week.

A Liberal Caravan Campaign has been inaugurated in Warrington and their first meeting, which was a great success, was held in Elizabeth-street in the Whitecross Ward on Tuesday night. There was a good attendance the meeting being presided over by Councillor J. Hawthorn, one of the Warrington representatives in the Council. A very able speaker in the person of Mr. A. H. Ainsley. of Manchester, addressed the meeting in the absence of Messrs. 11. Lewis and James Kendal. His arguments, were of so convincing a character that the resolution in favour of the Budget put at the close of the meeting was passed unanimously. The CHAIRMAN said he was pleased to see so many stalwarts in the Whitecross Ward who were prepared to brave the weather on such a night as that in support of the Budget, and he look it from their attendance, that it was their determination to “e the Bill through. They had met at a critical time in the political history of the country. The Budget had passed through the House of Commons and had passed into the Committee stage. Next week it would pass on to the report stage and if the Lords decided to throw it out, then, as Mr. Lloyd-George said in his brilliant speech at Newcastle on Saturday, the people of this country would have to decide the future. The existing Land Laws and the Enclosure Acts might be taken as fair samples of the way the Lords had looked after their interests at the expense of the people. They had opposed, owing to the luke-warmness of the people, many of the most beneficent reforms on the Statute Book, and they had thrown out many bills of reform which would have been for the good of the country. There was a long account against them, and if they were so unwise as to throw out the present Budget, the wrath of the people would not be appeased until the power of the Lords had been broken. It was not very long ago that they heard them shouting for eight Dreadnoughts. "We want eight and we won't wait" was the cry. The Government ordered them, and they were now asking the Lords to " foot " a por- tion of the Bill. The Lords were very angry about it, and had already stopped subscriptions to charities, football clubs, and other institutions of that kind. The Government were determined to place the burden of taxation on the broadest backs. The man with the broadest acres wanted the working man to tax himself under the specious pretexts of Tariff Reform. The word for reform was never put to a worse use than when applied to a raid on the poor man's cupboard, by the tax upon his bread, meat, and other necessaries of life. (Applause.)

Mr. AniseEY the course of his speech gave a review of the Budget illustrating the Chancellor's methods of obtaining his money. He said the Chancellor of the Exchequer wanted 16 millions of money. They might think that it was a large order, but what was the money to be used for ? Take the question of the Navy. The Chancellor of the Exchequer demanded three millions extra to be used for the purpose of strengthening the Navy. In March last they would remember, they had a " Naval Scare " brought about by the other party, saying that we might wake up some morning and find our little isle in the hands of the Germans. He was very glad to say that the cry had ceased, and the attempts to frighten the people had finished. speaking about Old Age Pensions he said he was sure that every- body there would support the idea of providing money for the carrying out of the system of Old Age Pensions They had been in the air for a considerable number of; years. The Chancellor of the Exchequer required av sum of eight millions for the purpose of carrying on his scheme which had been a wonderful boon to many, worn-out industrious men and women. Even the small sum at present was very welcome. He believed that if the present Government were returned to power they would have Old Age Pensions extended to paupers. (Hear, hear). Some people had been sufficiently fortunate and thrifty during their earlier life and he did agree that men who had hem unfortunate, or unthrifty, were also entitled to the pension. (Applause). If they supported the Government that. principle of pensions would be developed. The speaker then proceeded to speak upon the scheme of afforestation and said that we in England had allowed the planting of trees to die out and if we wanted timber we had to buy it from other countries which had taken good care to develope their growth. Experts had told them that the scheme of afforestation would be very profitable in the country and would employ a large number of people, and so it was the Government's desire that a sum of ,money should be set aside for developing the scheme. Coming to the land question he said the Government were going to value the land and do it properly, and that the taxes would be levied fairly and equitably. He then gave an instance of the unfair assessment with regard to the Marquis of Bute's castle and a tailor's shop at Cardiff and said the Marquises castle stood on 11,000 square yards and was assessed at £917. whereas the tailor was assessed at £23 more. In consequence of this the tailor was compelled to charge a great deal more than he would if his land or shop was assessed fairly, as compared with the land of the Marquis. They did not want to tax industry: they wanted to tax monopoly. (Applause, and a voice: "That's it.") Continuing be Said they did not want to interfere with the progress of agriculture, or to keep land out of the market. Mr. Ainsley then spoke at length on the mining royalties and referred to Mr. Arkwright a relative of the inventor. On lesrning of the terms with regard to royalties pro- posed by the Budget, he called his tenants together and threatened them that if the Budget was passed he would leave the country, as be would be unable to live. After everything had been deducted he would still have £1,300 per year, or £26 per week, and if a man could not live on that sum per week be ought to die. (Laughter). lie said he would go to California (a voice: "Send him to Siberia"). Concluding the speaker said be would have to pay a bigger royalty there than he did in England. (Applause). On the resolution being put to the meeting it was passed unanimously. Alderman EVANS and Councillor WILKINSON proposed and seconded a vote of thanks to the chairman and speaker. Councillor WILKINSON gave an illustration of the rise in land values in that particular neighbourhood and mentioned that when the authorities desired to acquire land off Lovely-lane for the purposes of a new schoolland recreation ground £6,000 was asked. The land was farmed for generations at a rental of £2.5 a year. Mr. Lloyd-George's aim was that instead of all that increased value going into the pocket of the landowner ' the community should participate in it. The resolution was heartily agreed to. Last evening a meeting was held at the end of Thelwall Lane, Latchford, when Councillor Kendal of Manchester delivered an address. Mr. P. O'Brien presided.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.

Considerable interest is being taken in the approach- ing Municipal Elections, and there is promise of several contests. In the Latchford Ward Councillor NV. J. Wilson (C) will be opposed by Mr. Thomas Hewitt (L). The Conservatives are bringing forward Mr. W. H. Bellian as their candidate in Whitecross Ward where the retiring representative, Councillor Barton, will not seek re-electron. In Bewsey Ward Councillor Owen Toole (I) will again come before the electors and we understand the Liberals will not oppose him. The Conservatives have nominated Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins as their candidate in Town Hall Ward, Councillor Lord being the retiring member.

div.head: LIBERAL WARD MEETINGS. FAIRFIELD WARD.
div.p: LIBERAL WARD MEETINGS. FAIRFIELD WARD.

A meetipng of the Liberal Committee for this ward was held on Tuesday evening. Mr. George Walker presided over a good attendance which included Coun- cillor Locker and Mr. J. Howes junr. The question of contesting the ward in opposition to Coun ciltor Vernon (C) was discussed and several names were mentioned. A deputation was appointed to wait, upon these gentle- men to obtain a suitable candidate. WHITECROSS WARD. This committee met last evening under the presi- dency of Alderman James Evans. Three gentlemen were suggested to be interviewed as possible candidate in place of Councillor Barton who declined an invit ation to stand.
